Still wondering

Common questions

How deep should over-toilet shelving be?

8 to 10 inches. Any deeper and you will knock your head standing up. Start the lowest shelf about 24 inches above the cistern so the lid still opens fully, and you get roughly 30 inches of otherwise dead wall back.

How much clear floor does a small bathroom need?

21 inches in front of the toilet and 30 inches in front of the vanity. Protect those two measurements first and fit storage into what is left — which is exactly why almost everything in a small bathroom has to be shallow or wall-mounted.

What bathroom storage works without drilling?

A freestanding over-toilet etagere, a leaning ladder shelf, tension rods and tension corner caddies, over-door hooks and organisers, a narrow freestanding cabinet, and a rolling cart in the gap beside the vanity. Adhesive hooks work too, but check the weight rating against your wall finish.

Are hooks or towel rails better in a small bathroom?

Hooks, comfortably. A hook takes about 3 inches of wall; a rail takes 24 for the same towel. In a room where wall space is the only space you have, that is a trade worth making almost every time.

How deep is a recessed bathroom niche?

3.5 inches — the depth of a standard stud cavity — so it costs no room depth at all, which is what makes it the best answer to bottles on the shower floor. Check for pipes and wiring before cutting, and avoid external walls in cold climates.

How do I stop open bathroom shelving looking cluttered?

Aim for roughly 70% closed storage to 30% open, use matching baskets with one per category, decant soap and lotion into matching bottles, roll towels rather than folding them, and leave some shelf deliberately empty.

Bathroom Vanity Decor Ideas

Bathroom vanity decor ideas that stay tidy — the tray method, mirror sizing, what to display versus hide, and seasonal touches that survive humidity.

A bathroom vanity is a small surface that has to hold daily essentials and still look good. Most fail because everything lives on top of it.

The fix is a simple rule about what earns a place on the counter, plus a tray.

The rule: three things on display

Only three categories belong on a vanity surface:

  1. Something functional and attractive — a soap dispenser, a toothbrush holder
  2. Something living or natural — a plant, dried stems, a stone dish
  3. Something soft — a folded hand towel

Everything else goes in a drawer or a cabinet. Toothpaste, razors, skincare, hairbrushes — none of it earns counter space.

Use a tray

The single most effective vanity move. A tray groups the things that must stay out into one object.

Sizing: roughly one-third the vanity width for a single sink, or one tray per sink on a double.

Materials that survive a bathroom: marble, ceramic, metal, sealed wood, rattan. Avoid unsealed wood and anything with a fabric base.

Put on it: soap dispenser, a small plant, a candle. That’s it.

The tray also means you can lift everything off in one movement to clean.

Decant what you display

A branded plastic bottle looks like a product. The same soap in a ceramic or glass pump looks like decor.

  • Hand soap and lotion in matching pumps
  • Cotton buds and pads in small glass jars
  • Bath salts in a jar with a wooden scoop
  • Toothbrushes in a ceramic cup, not the plastic one they came with

This is the change that makes a vanity look styled rather than just tidy, and it costs very little.

Mirror sizing

Width: the mirror should be roughly the same width as the vanity, or slightly narrower — never wider.

Height: centre it at about 60–65 inches from the floor, or centred on the vanity itself.

Clearance: leave 4–8 inches between the top of the backsplash and the bottom of the mirror.

Shape: an arched or round mirror softens a boxy bathroom. A large rectangular mirror makes a narrow room feel wider.

Lighting

Bathroom lighting is usually the worst in the house — one overhead fitting casting shadows straight down onto your face.

Best setup: two sconces either side of the mirror at 60–66 inches, which lights your face evenly rather than from above.

If you only have overhead: add a small lamp on the vanity if there’s a socket, or a battery-operated one.

Bulb temperature: 2700–3000K. Warm enough to be flattering, bright enough to see properly.

What to add for warmth

Bathrooms are all hard surfaces — tile, ceramic, glass, mirror. Softness is what makes them feel finished.

  • A folded or rolled hand towel in a colour that isn’t white
  • A small rug or bath mat with texture
  • A woven basket on the floor or a shelf
  • A wooden or stone dish
  • A plant — pothos, fern or eucalyptus. Humidity suits them.

Plants that thrive in a bathroom

The humidity that ruins other things is perfect for these:

  • Pothos — trailing, tolerates low light
  • Boston fern — loves steam
  • Spider plant
  • Air plants in a small dish
  • Eucalyptus stems hung from the shower head (not a plant exactly, but it smells wonderful and lasts weeks)

Seasonal touches

A vanity can be refreshed in three minutes:

Spring — a small vase of tulips, a light-coloured towel Summer — greenery in a clear jar, a citrus-scented candle Autumn — dried stems, an amber glass dish, a deeper towel Winter — eucalyptus, a brass tray, a warm-scented candle

Keep the tray and the soap dispenser. Change the towel and one small item.

Under the vanity

Everything you took off the counter has to go somewhere.

  • Stacking drawers rather than one shelf
  • A U-shaped organiser around the pipe
  • Clear containers, one per category
  • A tension rod with spray bottles hanging
  • Adhesive hooks inside the door

Common mistakes

  • Too many products on display
  • Branded packaging left visible
  • A mirror wider than the vanity
  • Overhead-only lighting
  • Nothing soft or living in the room
  • A tray that’s too small to group anything

Double vanity

Treat each side as its own zone. One tray each, mirrored arrangement, and a shared item in the centre — a plant, a tray of towels, or a candle.

Symmetry works particularly well on a double vanity. Two matching sconces, two matching mirrors, two matching trays.

The formula:

Tray + decanted soap pump + small plant + one folded towel in colour + warm sconce lighting.

Five elements, everything else in a drawer, and the vanity looks finished in about ten minutes.

Bedroom Ideas for Young Boys

Bedroom ideas for young boys aged 3-8 — layouts, storage, paint colours and themes that grow with them instead of needing redoing in two years.

The hard part about decorating a young boy’s room isn’t finding ideas. It’s that a room designed for a five-year-old stops working by the time he’s eight.

Dinosaur wallpaper, a race car bed, a full theme — all lovely, all outgrown fast and expensive to undo. The approach below gives you a room that looks great now and adapts later without repainting.

The rule that saves money: theme the cheap layer

Split the room into two layers.

Permanent layer — paint, flooring, bed frame, storage furniture, curtains. Keep these neutral and grown-up. These cost real money and shouldn’t change.

Temporary layer — bedding, wall decals, cushions, art, rug, toy bins, lampshade. This is where the dinosaurs, rockets and diggers live. All of it costs under a few hundred and can change in an afternoon.

Do it this way and the room evolves from dinosaurs to football to gaming without a single tin of paint.

Layout for a small boy’s room

Most kids’ rooms are the smallest in the house. Priorities in order:

  1. Clear floor space for playing — this matters more than furniture at this age
  2. Bed against the longest wall, ideally in a corner, to free the middle
  3. Storage at child height so he can actually use it
  4. A small desk or table for drawing, from about age five

A single bed is 38 x 75 inches. In a 9 x 10 foot room, pushing it into a corner leaves roughly 6 x 7 feet of open floor. That’s the playing space, and protecting it matters more than adding another dresser.

Paint colours that work now and later

Skip primary blue. It reads as “toddler” and dates fast.

Colours that hold up as he grows:

  • Deep navy on one wall, white on the rest — looks smart at 5 and at 15
  • Sage or olive green — calm, works with almost every theme
  • Warm grey or greige — the safest neutral, lets the bedding do the work
  • Muted teal — more interesting than blue, less babyish
  • Off-white with a dark accent wall — the most flexible option of all

If you want colour without commitment, paint the lower third of the wall in a deeper tone with a simple wood rail as the break. It hides scuffs at kid height and looks deliberate.

Storage that a young child will actually use

This is where most kids’ rooms fail. Storage designed for adults doesn’t get used by children, so everything ends up on the floor.

Open bins beat drawers. A five-year-old will drop toys into an open basket. He will not open a drawer, place items inside, and close it.

Cube shelving units with fabric bins are the workhorse of a young boy’s room. Low, open, and each bin gets one category.

Height matters: anything he needs daily goes below 40 inches. Above that is for storage you control.

Label with pictures, not words, until he reads confidently. A photo of Lego on the Lego bin genuinely works.

Under-bed storage on castors doubles your capacity in a small room. Use it for the toys in rotation, not the ones in daily use.

Toy rotation — the thing that keeps it tidy

Young boys accumulate toys faster than any storage can hold. The fix isn’t more bins.

Keep about a third of the toys accessible. Box the rest and store them elsewhere. Swap every few weeks. He’ll play with the rotated-in toys as though they’re new, and the room stays manageable.

Bed options by age

Age 3–5: A floor bed or low single. Safety rail if he moves a lot. Skip the themed bed — it’s the most-regretted purchase in kids’ rooms.

Age 5–8: Standard single. A mid-sleeper (bed raised about 40 inches with storage or a desk underneath) is excellent in a small room and doesn’t feel babyish.

Sharing: Bunk beds work from about age six for the top bunk. Look for a solid guardrail and a properly angled ladder rather than vertical rungs.

Wall ideas that don’t cost much

  • Removable decals — the cheapest theme change there is, and peels off cleanly
  • A pegboard painted the wall colour, for medals, hats and craft supplies
  • Picture ledges at 40 inches — displays his own artwork, and swaps out weekly
  • A growth chart — one thing you’ll keep
  • Framed art of his interests — cheaper and more grown-up than posters
  • Magnetic or chalkboard paint on one small section

Lighting

Three sources, layered:

  • Overhead for general light — a simple shade, nothing that dominates
  • Bedside lamp with a touch switch he can operate himself
  • A nightlight — warm amber, not blue-white, which interferes with sleep

Add blackout curtains or a blind. Young children sleep considerably better in a properly dark room, and it’s the single most practical upgrade in a child’s bedroom.

A reading corner

A small rug, a floor cushion or beanbag, and a front-facing book display at his eye level. Front-facing matters — children pick books by the cover, and a spine-out shelf gets ignored.

It takes about 3 x 3 feet of corner and does more for reading habits than any amount of encouragement.

Making it feel like his room

Involve him in two decisions only — the bedding and the wall decals. Give him three options for each and let him choose.

He gets ownership. You keep control of the expensive, permanent choices. Everyone’s happy.

Quick plan for a young boy’s room:

Layer What to choose
Paint Navy, sage or warm grey — not primary colours
Bed Standard single, corner position
Storage Open bins below 40 inches, picture labels
Theme Bedding, decals, rug only
Lighting Overhead + bedside + amber nightlight
Extras Blackout blind, reading corner, picture ledge

There’s a big difference between a coastal bedroom and a beach-themed one. The first feels calm, airy and expensive. The second has anchors on the cushions and a sign that says “Beach: 2 miles.”

The good version is mostly about light, texture and a restrained palette. Here’s how it’s built.

The palette

Real coastal rooms are far more neutral than people expect. The blue is an accent, not the base.

Base (60%): warm white, cream, sand, pale oat. Not bright white — warm off-whites catch light better and feel softer.

Secondary (30%): natural wood, rattan, jute, linen. This is where most of the character comes from.

Accent (10%): soft blue, sea glass green, or a faded denim. Small doses.

What to avoid: navy-and-white stripes everywhere, bright turquoise, primary red. These are what tip a room from coastal into themed.

Shades worth sampling: Pale Oak and White Dove (Benjamin Moore), Sea Salt (Sherwin-Williams), Shaded White and Pale Powder (Farrow & Ball).

Texture does the work

Take the colour away and a coastal room still reads as coastal, because of the materials.

  • Linen — bedding and curtains. The single most coastal fabric there is.
  • Rattan and cane — headboard, bedside table, a pendant light, a mirror frame
  • Jute or sisal rug — the base layer
  • Weathered or limed wood — driftwood tones rather than orange pine
  • Cotton in a waffle or gauze weave
  • Woven baskets for storage
  • Ceramic and stoneware — matte, not glossy

Five of these in one room and it reads coastal without a single blue thing.

The bed

Headboard: rattan or cane is ideal. A whitewashed wood frame, or a linen upholstered headboard in oatmeal, works just as well.

Bedding: white or cream linen. Slightly rumpled is the point — crisp and pressed reads as hotel, not beach house.

Layers: duvet, a lightweight cotton or waffle throw folded across the bottom third, and cushions in cream, sand and one soft blue.

Skip: shell prints, anchor motifs, anything with a starfish on it.

Windows and light

Coastal rooms are defined by light more than anything else.

Sheer or light linen curtains — the look is light filtering through, not blocking it. Hang them high, near the ceiling, and floor-length.

Woven or bamboo blinds — texture plus light control, and very coastal.

White shutters if you have them.

If the room is dark, add a large mirror opposite the window. Light is the whole aesthetic, and a dark coastal room just looks beige.

Flooring

  • Pale wood — whitewashed oak, limed timber, or a light engineered board
  • Jute or sisal rug as the base
  • A soft flatweave layered on top in cream or a faded pattern

Dark floors fight the aesthetic. If you’re stuck with them, a large pale rug covers most of the problem.

Walls

Keep it quiet. Coastal rooms are calm.

  • One large piece of art — an abstract seascape, a horizon line, a photograph of water. Muted tones, not vivid.
  • A round rattan mirror
  • Shiplap or beadboard panelling painted warm white — genuinely coastal, adds texture
  • Framed botanical or grass prints
  • Dried grasses in a ceramic vase

One or two of these. The empty wall is part of the style.

Lighting

  • A rattan or woven pendant — instantly sets the tone
  • Ceramic or wooden table lamps with linen shades
  • Warm bulbs, 2700K

Avoid chrome, glass globes and anything shiny. Natural materials throughout.

Plants

Coastal-appropriate greenery keeps it fresh:

  • Olive tree in a large pot
  • Palm — kentia or parlour palm
  • Eucalyptus stems in a vase
  • Dried pampas or bunny tails
  • A trailing pothos on a shelf

Terracotta, stoneware or basket planters. Not plastic.

The cliches to skip

These are what turn coastal into kitsch:

  • Shells in glass jars
  • Rope and anchor motifs
  • Signs with beach-related words on them
  • Starfish anything
  • Bright turquoise
  • Navy and white stripes on every surface
  • Ships’ wheels, oars, lighthouses

One or two natural objects — a piece of driftwood, a single large shell on a stack of books — is charming. A collection of them is a gift shop.

Storage that fits

  • Woven baskets under the bed and on shelves
  • A whitewashed wooden chest at the foot of the bed
  • A rattan or cane bedside table
  • Open shelving with linen boxes

Natural materials again, so storage becomes part of the look.

Coastal on a budget

The style is cheap to achieve because it favours simple, natural things:

  • White or cream bedding from anywhere
  • A jute rug is one of the cheapest rug types
  • Thrifted baskets and wooden bowls
  • Dried grasses last for years
  • Paint an existing dresser in warm white
  • Cane webbing to update a plain headboard

The formula: warm white walls, linen bedding in cream, rattan headboard, jute rug, woven blinds, one large muted seascape, warm bulbs, and one soft blue cushion.

Not a shell in sight, and it will read as coastal from the doorway.

A bedroom rug does three things: it softens the space, adds warmth underfoot, and makes the room feel finished. A rug that is the wrong size or in the wrong position does the opposite — it makes the room look smaller and the layout feel unresolved.

These ideas cover the specific decisions that make a bedroom rug work — size, placement, material, and style — with practical guidance for every room type.

1. Size the Rug Correctly

The most common bedroom rug mistake is choosing a rug that is too small. The rug should extend at least 18 inches beyond the sides and foot of the bed. For a double bed, that means a minimum of 8 x 10 feet. For a king, 9 x 12 feet.

A small rug floating in the middle of the floor makes the room look smaller, not larger.

2. Place the Rug So Both Feet Land on It

When getting out of bed, both feet should land on the rug. This is the practical test for correct placement. If the rug only covers the area at the foot of the bed, it is in the wrong position.

The rug should sit under the lower two-thirds of the bed, not just at the foot.

3. Use a Low-Pile Wool Rug

Low-pile wool is the most practical material for a bedroom rug. It is soft underfoot, durable, easy to vacuum, and does not trap as much dust as a high-pile rug. It also looks better for longer than synthetic alternatives.

Avoid shag rugs in bedrooms — they trap dust, are hard to clean, and flatten quickly.

4. Try a Flatweave Rug for a Modern Look

A flatweave rug — kilim, dhurrie, or a simple woven cotton — is lighter, easier to clean, and less expensive than a pile rug. It works well in a modern or minimal bedroom.

Flatweave rugs can slip on hard floors — use a non-slip underlay.

5. Use a Jute or Sisal Rug for a Natural Look

A jute or sisal rug adds a natural, textural quality that suits a neutral or earthy bedroom. It is durable and relatively inexpensive.

Jute and sisal are rougher underfoot than wool — they work best in rooms where the rug is more decorative than functional.

6. Choose a Neutral Rug for Longevity

A neutral rug — cream, oatmeal, warm grey, or natural — works with almost every color scheme and is easier to update around than a patterned or brightly colored one.

A neutral rug also makes the room feel larger than a dark or heavily patterned one.

7. Use a Patterned Rug as the Room’s Focal Point

A patterned rug — a Persian, a geometric, or a bold abstract — can be the focal point of a simple bedroom. Keep the rest of the room calm and let the rug do the work.

Choose a pattern with colors that appear elsewhere in the room — in the bedding, curtains, or art.

8. Layer Two Rugs for a Bohemian Look

Layering a smaller patterned rug over a larger neutral one adds depth and a relaxed, layered quality. Use a flatweave or kilim as the top layer over a jute or sisal base.

The top rug should be roughly half the size of the bottom one.

9. Use a Round Rug for a Softer Look

A round rug in a bedroom with a lot of straight lines and rectangular furniture adds a soft, unexpected quality. Place it at the foot of the bed or in a reading corner.

A round rug works best as an accent rather than the main rug under the bed.

10. Choose a Dark Rug for Warmth and Drama

A dark rug — charcoal, navy, forest green, or deep burgundy — adds warmth and drama to a light bedroom. It also hides dirt better than a light rug.

A dark rug on a light floor creates a strong contrast that grounds the room.

11. Use a Vintage or Antique Rug

A vintage or antique rug adds character and warmth that a new rug cannot replicate. The faded colors and worn texture suit almost every bedroom style.

Vintage rugs are often available at lower prices than new rugs of the same quality.

12. Add a Non-Slip Underlay

A non-slip underlay prevents the rug from moving on hard floors and adds a layer of cushioning. It also extends the life of the rug by reducing wear on the back.

Choose an underlay that is slightly smaller than the rug so it does not show at the edges.

13. Use a Runner on Each Side of the Bed

Two runners — one on each side of the bed — are a practical alternative to a large rug in a room where a full-size rug is not practical or affordable. They provide the same underfoot warmth where it is needed most.

Choose matching runners in the same material and color.

14. Place a Small Rug in a Reading Corner

A small rug in a reading corner — under a chair and a floor lamp — defines the space and adds warmth. It does not need to match the main rug exactly, but it should complement it.

A round rug works particularly well in a reading corner.

15. Clean the Rug Regularly

A bedroom rug collects dust, skin cells, and allergens quickly. Vacuum it at least once a week and have it professionally cleaned once a year. A clean rug looks better and lasts longer.

Rotate the rug every six months to ensure even wear.

16. Use a Rug to Define the Bed Zone in an Open-Plan Room

In a studio apartment or open-plan bedroom, a rug under the bed defines the sleeping zone and separates it visually from the rest of the space. This is one of the most effective zoning tools in an open-plan layout.

Choose a rug that is large enough to extend beyond the bed on all sides.

17. Match the Rug to the Room’s Warmth Level

A warm-toned rug — cream, caramel, terracotta, or rust — suits a warm neutral bedroom. A cool-toned rug — grey, blue, or green — suits a cooler palette. Matching the rug’s warmth level to the room’s overall tone creates a cohesive look.

Test a rug sample in the room before buying — colors look different in different lighting conditions.

Final Thoughts

A bedroom rug works when it is the right size, in the right position, and in a material that suits the room’s use. Start with the size — bigger than you think — and the placement — both feet on the rug when getting out of bed. Everything else follows from those two decisions.

An accent wall in the bedroom does one job: it makes the bed feel like the intentional focal point of the room. When it works, the whole room looks more designed. When it does not work, it just looks like one wall was painted a different color.

These ideas cover the approaches that consistently look expensive — from a single coat of dark paint to textured plaster and wood panels.

1. Paint the Wall Behind the Bed a Deep Color

A deep color — navy, charcoal, forest green, terracotta, or dusty plum — on the wall behind the bed is the simplest and most effective accent wall approach. It costs one tin of paint and a few hours.

Keep the other three walls white or a warm off-white so the accent wall reads clearly.

2. Use Limewash Paint for Texture

Limewash paint creates a soft, mottled texture that looks like aged plaster. It adds depth that flat paint cannot achieve and photographs beautifully. It is also easy to apply — no special tools required.

Apply it in two thin coats with a wide brush, working in random directions.

3. Add a Wallpaper Panel

Papering one wall costs a fraction of papering the whole room. Choose a large-scale botanical, geometric, or abstract print. The scale of the pattern matters — small prints on a large wall look busy rather than bold.

Measure the wall carefully and order 10% extra for pattern matching.

4. Use Vertical Shiplap or Tongue-and-Groove Panels

Vertical wood panels add height and texture to a bedroom wall. Paint them the same color as the wall for a subtle effect, or a contrasting color for a stronger statement.

MDF panels are cheaper than real wood and easier to cut and install.

5. Create a Fabric Headboard Wall

Upholstered panels or a large piece of fabric stretched over a frame and mounted behind the bed creates a soft, hotel-like accent wall. Use a linen, velvet, or boucle fabric in a neutral or muted tone.

This approach also improves acoustics in a hard-floored room.

6. Use a Plaster Effect Paint

Plaster effect paints create a textured, layered finish that looks like real plaster. They are applied with a trowel or sponge and dry to a matte, slightly uneven surface.

The technique takes practice — test on a piece of board before applying to the wall.

7. Add Horizontal Paneling Below a Chair Rail

Horizontal panels below a chair rail (roughly 36 inches from the floor) add architectural detail to a plain room. Paint the panels a slightly darker shade than the wall above for a subtle, layered effect.

This approach works particularly well in older homes with high ceilings.

8. Use a Geometric Paint Pattern

A simple geometric pattern — arches, diamonds, or a color block — painted directly on the wall adds visual interest without wallpaper. Use painter’s tape for clean edges.

Keep the palette to two colors — the wall color and one accent — to avoid it looking busy.

9. Mount a Large Piece of Art

A single large piece of art — a canvas, a framed print, or a textile — mounted on the wall behind the bed creates a focal point without any painting or papering. The art should be roughly two-thirds the width of the bed.

Hang it 6–10 inches above the headboard with the center at 57 inches from the floor.

10. Use Dark Wallpaper With a Metallic Finish

Dark wallpaper with a subtle metallic or satin finish catches the light differently at different times of day. It adds depth and luxury without looking heavy when the room is well lit.

Use it on the wall behind the bed only — it can feel overwhelming on multiple walls.

11. Add a Stencil Pattern

A repeating stencil pattern in a tone-on-tone color scheme adds texture and pattern without the cost of wallpaper. Use a slightly darker or lighter shade of the wall color for a subtle effect.

Secure the stencil firmly with tape to prevent bleeding.

12. Use Reclaimed Wood Planks

Reclaimed wood planks mounted horizontally on the wall behind the bed add warmth and texture. The natural variation in the wood means no two walls look the same.

Seal the wood before mounting to prevent dust and splinters.

13. Create a Gallery Wall as the Accent

A carefully arranged gallery wall of framed prints, photographs, and small objects can function as an accent wall. Use matching frames and a consistent color palette to keep it looking cohesive.

Lay the arrangement out on the floor before hanging anything.

14. Use a Bold Geometric Wallpaper

A bold geometric wallpaper — large hexagons, wide stripes, or an oversized grid — on the wall behind the bed creates a strong graphic statement. Pair it with plain bedding and simple furniture.

The simpler the rest of the room, the bolder the wallpaper can be.

15. Add Wainscoting for a Classic Look

Wainscoting — raised panels on the lower half of the wall — adds architectural detail that looks expensive and is relatively straightforward to install with MDF and a mitre saw.

Paint the panels and the wall above the same color for a modern take on a traditional detail.

16. Use a Curved Arch Shape

A painted arch shape on the wall behind the bed — either a full arch or a half-arch — adds a soft, architectural quality. Use a slightly darker shade of the wall color for a subtle effect, or a contrasting color for a bolder statement.

Draw the arch with a pencil and string before painting.

17. Use Grasscloth or Textured Wallpaper

Grasscloth and textured wallpapers add a natural, tactile quality that flat paint cannot replicate. They work particularly well in bedrooms because the texture softens the space.

Grasscloth is harder to clean than painted walls — avoid it in rooms with young children.

Final Thoughts

The best bedroom accent wall is the one that makes the bed feel like the intentional center of the room. Start with the simplest approach — a single dark paint color — and only add complexity if the room needs it. A well-executed simple idea always looks better than a complicated one done poorly.

  • Linen and cotton are the most versatile curtain fabrics for a bedroom.

Curtains are one of the most impactful elements in a bedroom, and the most commonly done wrong. The fabric, the length, and especially the hanging position all affect how large and finished the room feels.

These ideas cover the specific decisions that make bedroom curtains look expensive and intentional rather than afterthought additions.

1. Hang the Rod High and Wide

This is the single most important curtain rule. Hang the rod 4–6 inches above the window frame and extend it 6–10 inches past each side of the window. This makes the window look larger, the ceiling feel higher, and the room feel more spacious.

Curtains hung at the window frame make the room look smaller and the ceiling lower.

2. Let the Curtains Touch the Floor

Curtains that stop above the floor look unfinished. The most polished options are curtains that just touch the floor, or curtains that pool slightly (1–2 inches of fabric on the floor). Avoid curtains that hover 2–3 inches above the floor.

Measure from the rod to the floor before buying — curtain lengths vary significantly between retailers.

3. Add Blackout Lining

Blackout lining improves sleep quality by blocking early morning light. It also adds weight to the curtain, which makes it hang better and look more expensive. It can be added to almost any curtain fabric.

Blackout lining is especially worth adding in east-facing bedrooms that get early morning sun.

4. Use Linen for a Relaxed, Natural Look

Linen curtains have a slightly textured, relaxed quality that suits almost every bedroom style. They filter light beautifully and look better as they age. Choose a natural, undyed linen or a warm white for the most versatile option.

Linen curtains wrinkle easily — this is part of their character, not a flaw.

5. Use Velvet for a Luxurious Look

Velvet curtains add warmth, texture, and a sense of luxury. They also block light and sound effectively. Choose a deep color — navy, forest green, charcoal, or dusty plum — for the most dramatic effect.

Velvet curtains are heavy — ensure the rod and brackets are rated for the weight.

6. Choose a Neutral Color for Longevity

White, cream, warm grey, and natural linen are the most versatile curtain colors. They work with almost every wall color and are easier to update around than a strongly colored curtain.

A neutral curtain also makes the room feel larger than a dark or heavily patterned one.

7. Use a Patterned Curtain as the Room’s Focal Point

A patterned curtain — a large botanical, a geometric, or a subtle stripe — can be the focal point of a simple bedroom. Keep the rest of the room calm and let the curtains do the work.

Choose a pattern with colors that appear elsewhere in the room.

8. Use Eyelet Curtains for a Clean, Modern Look

Eyelet curtains hang in even, regular folds and suit a modern or minimal bedroom. They are easy to hang and slide smoothly on the rod.

Choose a rod that is slightly thicker than the eyelet diameter for the smoothest movement.

9. Use Pinch Pleat Curtains for a Tailored Look

Pinch pleat curtains have a more formal, tailored quality than eyelet curtains. They suit a classic or traditional bedroom and look particularly good in velvet or a heavy cotton.

Pinch pleat curtains require more fabric than eyelet curtains — order accordingly.

10. Layer Curtains Over Blinds

Layering curtains over a roller blind or Roman blind gives the window both light control and a finished look. Use the blind for daytime privacy and the curtains for evening warmth and style.

Choose a blind in a neutral color that does not compete with the curtains.

11. Use Sheer Curtains for Soft Light

Sheer curtains filter light without blocking it, creating a soft, diffused glow. They work well in bedrooms that do not need full blackout but benefit from some privacy.

Layer sheer curtains under heavier curtains for a flexible light-control system.

12. Choose a Rod in a Finish That Suits the Room

A brass rod suits a warm, traditional bedroom. A matte black rod suits a modern or industrial bedroom. A natural wood rod suits a Scandinavian or earthy bedroom. The rod is a visible part of the window treatment — choose it deliberately.

Avoid chrome rods in a warm bedroom — they look cold and disconnected.

13. Use Tie-Top Curtains for a Casual Look

Tie-top curtains have a relaxed, casual quality that suits a coastal, boho, or country bedroom. They are easy to make from fabric if you want a custom look.

Tie-top curtains do not slide as smoothly as eyelet or pleat curtains — they work best in rooms where the curtains are not opened and closed frequently.

14. Add Curtain Holdbacks or Tiebacks

Curtain holdbacks or tiebacks keep the curtains open during the day and add a decorative detail. Choose a holdback in a finish that matches the rod — brass, matte black, or natural wood.

Position the holdback at roughly one-third of the curtain height from the bottom.

15. Use Two Panels Per Window

Two curtain panels per window — one on each side — always look more generous and finished than a single panel. Each panel should be at least as wide as the window when closed, so the curtains cover the window fully.

A common mistake is buying curtains that are too narrow — they look skimpy when closed and do not block light effectively.

Final Thoughts

Bedroom curtains work when they are hung high and wide, reach the floor, and are made from a fabric that suits the room’s style. Start with the hanging position — that single change makes more difference than any other curtain decision.

Bedroom Ideas for Small Teen Rooms

Small teen bedroom ideas that handle sleeping, studying and hanging out in one room — zoning, desk setups, storage and letting them own the space.

A teenager’s bedroom has to do three jobs a child’s room never did: sleep, study, and be somewhere friends can sit. In a small room those three compete for the same floor.

The rooms that work solve the zoning problem first and worry about style second.

Zone the room into three

Even in 90 square feet, you can create three distinct areas:

Sleep zone — bed, bedside surface, a light they control.

Study zone — desk, chair, task light, somewhere for books. Facing a wall or a window, not the bed.

Hang zone — floor cushions, a beanbag, or just clear floor with a rug. This is the one people skip, and it’s why teenagers end up sitting on the bed with friends.

The zones don’t need walls. A rug, a change in lighting, or the orientation of furniture is enough to make them read as separate.

The desk is non-negotiable

Homework on the bed is bad for both study and sleep. A desk is the single most important piece of furniture in a teen’s room.

Minimum size: 40 x 24 inches. Below 20 inches deep, a laptop plus a notebook doesn’t fit.

Height: 29–30 inches.

Clearance behind: 30 inches to push the chair back.

Where it fits when there’s no floor:

  • A floating desk mounted to the wall — clear floor underneath
  • A narrow console, 16 inches deep, along a wall
  • A desk built into the closet, doors removed
  • Under a mid-sleeper bed
  • A fold-down wall desk that closes when not in use

Bed options that free up floor

Mid-sleeper — bed raised about 40 inches with a desk or storage underneath. Doesn’t feel childish the way a bunk does, and it effectively doubles the room’s usable footprint.

Bed with under-drawers — replaces a whole chest of drawers.

Ottoman bed — the entire base lifts for storage. Best capacity of any option.

Daybed against a wall — works as a sofa during the day, which solves the hang zone at the same time.

Drop a size. A single bed instead of a double frees about 16 inches of floor, which is often the difference between a desk fitting and not.

Storage for the volume teens generate

Clothes, sports kit, school stuff, tech, and the things they collect.

  • Wardrobe to the ceiling — a short wardrobe with boxes on top wastes a foot of storage
  • Under-bed drawers on castors
  • Over-door hooks and rails
  • A clothes rail if the wardrobe is full — styled, it looks intentional
  • Wall shelves above the desk at 18 and 30 inches
  • A laundry basket by the door, not in a corner

Lighting, three sources

Teenagers use their rooms late and for everything. One overhead light doesn’t cover it.

  • Overhead on a dimmer for general light
  • A task lamp at the desk — warm, adjustable, essential for homework
  • A bedside light they can reach lying down
  • Plus something atmospheric — LED strip, fairy lights, a floor lamp

The atmospheric layer matters more here than in any other room in the house. It’s how they make the space feel like theirs.

Let them own the walls

This is where you hand over control. It’s also the cheapest part of the room.

  • A pinboard or pegboard — anything can go on it, no damage to paint
  • Picture ledges — posters and photos lean, swap freely, no holes
  • Removable wallpaper on one wall
  • Cheap frames for posters — turns them from clutter into decor
  • LED strips in the colour they choose

Give them the walls and the textiles. Keep control of the paint and furniture. That’s the deal that works.

Somewhere for friends to sit

If there’s genuinely no floor:

  • A daybed instead of a bed
  • Floor cushions that stack in a corner
  • A beanbag that squashes under the desk
  • A window seat if there’s a recess

Even 3 x 3 feet of clear rug reads as somewhere to sit.

Cable and charging management

Teens have more devices than anyone in the house.

  • A cable tray under the desk
  • A power strip mounted underneath, not on the carpet
  • A charging drawer in the bedside table
  • Velcro ties on every run

Ten minutes of work that makes the room look twice as tidy.

Blackout and sleep

Teenagers genuinely need more sleep than they get, and their body clocks shift later naturally.

A blackout blind plus curtains helps. So does keeping the LED strips warm rather than blue after dark, and having a bedside light so the overhead can go off earlier.

What to let go of

Two things worth accepting:

The room will not stay tidy to your standard. Aim for “floor clear, door closes” rather than perfection.

Their taste will not be yours. The reason to keep paint and furniture neutral isn’t to control the look — it’s so that when their taste changes in two years, only the cheap layer needs replacing.

Priorities in order for a small teen room:

  1. A real desk, properly sized
  2. A bed that includes storage or raises off the floor
  3. Three lighting sources
  4. Wardrobe to the ceiling
  5. Somewhere other than the bed to sit
  6. Walls they control
  7. Blackout at the window

Bedroom Ideas for Small Spaces That Feel Bigger

Small bedroom ideas that genuinely make a room feel bigger — bed sizes, clearances, sightlines, colour and the layout rules that create space you can feel.

Elena Marsh/August 12, 2026/4 min read

The short version

  • The clearances cannot be cheated: 24 inches beside the bed, 36 in front of a wardrobe, 30 to pull a drawer out.
  • Dropping one bed size frees more usable floor than any decorating trick.
  • Clear the longest diagonal in the room — an uninterrupted sightline does more than any colour choice, and costs nothing.
  • Furniture on legs lets you see floor underneath, so the room reads larger than the same pieces sitting flat.
  • Hang curtains 4-6 inches below the ceiling and 6-10 inches past each side; it is the cheapest transformation in a small bedroom.

Most advice about small bedrooms is about tricking the eye. Some of that works. But the biggest gains come from layout — from clearing floor and creating one long sightline.

Here’s both, starting with the measurements.

The clearances you actually need

You can’t cheat these, and knowing them tells you what will fit:

  • 24 inches of walkway beside a bed — the absolute minimum to walk past comfortably
  • 36 inches in front of a wardrobe to open doors and stand
  • 30 inches in front of a chest of drawers to pull a drawer out
  • 30 inches behind a desk chair to push back and stand

Bed sizes for reference:

Bed Size
Single 38 x 75 inches
Small double 48 x 75 inches
Double 54 x 75 inches
Queen 60 x 80 inches

In a 9 x 10 foot room, a double bed leaves you about 30 inches on one side and 24 on the other. A queen leaves you almost nothing. Dropping one bed size frees more usable space than any decorating trick.

Push the bed into a corner

The single biggest layout change in a small bedroom. A bed against two walls instead of floating with space on both sides can free up 20 square feet.

You lose easy access to one side — worth it in a child’s or single person’s room, less so for a couple.

Create one long sightline

A room feels bigger when you can see across it uninterrupted. Look at the longest diagonal in the room — usually from the door to the opposite corner — and clear it.

Nothing tall in that line. No wardrobe blocking it, no chest of drawers halfway along.

This does more than any colour choice, and it costs nothing but rearranging.

Go vertical with storage

Floor space is what you don’t have. Wall space above 60 inches is almost always empty.

  • Wardrobe to the ceiling — a full-height wardrobe holds far more and looks intentional; a short one with boxes on top looks cluttered
  • Floating shelves above the bed, above the door, in the corners
  • A shelf running the full length of a wall at 72 inches, above head height
  • Over-door storage
  • Wall hooks instead of a chair for clothes

Choose furniture with legs

Furniture that sits directly on the floor blocks it visually. Furniture on legs lets you see floor underneath, and the room reads as larger.

This applies to the bed frame, the bedside table, the dresser — everything. A bed with visible legs makes a noticeable difference compared to a divan base.

Floating bedside shelves

Bedside tables eat about 3 square feet each. A wall-mounted floating shelf at 26 inches does the same job with clear floor underneath.

In a really tight room, a single shelf plus a wall-mounted light frees up the entire footprint.

Under-bed storage

The space under a bed is roughly 15 square feet of storage doing nothing. Use it:

  • Drawers on castors
  • Vacuum bags for out-of-season bedding
  • A bed frame with built-in drawers
  • An ottoman bed if you need serious capacity

Fill this and you may not need a chest of drawers at all — which is 6 square feet back.

Colour and light

Warm, light walls reflect more light: cream, oat, warm white, a pale greige. Cool grey absorbs and flattens.

Same colour on the ceiling removes the contrast line and makes the room read taller.

A mirror opposite the window — reflecting light, not a blank wall.

Layered lighting rather than one overhead source. A room with light in three places feels larger than one with a single bright fixture, because the corners aren’t dark.

Curtains hung high and wide

Rod 4–6 inches below the ceiling. Extending 6–10 inches past each side of the window. Floor length, just kissing the floor.

This makes the window look larger and the wall taller. It’s the cheapest transformation in a small bedroom and almost everyone gets it wrong.

The rug rule

A rug that’s too small makes a room feel smaller. It fragments the floor.

For a bed, the rug should extend at least 18 inches beyond the sides and foot. If that’s not possible, run a large rug under the bottom two-thirds of the bed instead — or skip the rug and use two small runners at the sides.

Fewer, larger things

Counterintuitive but reliable: one large piece of art makes a small room feel bigger. Six small frames make it feel busy.

Same with furniture, plants, cushions and objects. In a small room, fewer and larger always wins.

What to remove

Small rooms improve more from subtraction than addition:

  • The chair that holds clothes
  • The second bedside table if only one person uses the bed
  • Anything stored on top of the wardrobe
  • Furniture you walk around rather than to
  • Small decorative objects on every surface

Doors and swings

If a door swings into the room and blocks usable space, consider rehanging it to swing the other way, or fitting a sliding or bifold door. Wardrobe doors especially — sliding doors reclaim the 36 inches a hinged door needs.

The four changes with the biggest effect:

  1. Move the bed to a corner and clear the longest sightline
  2. Take storage to the ceiling and under the bed
  3. Rehang the curtains near the ceiling, floor-length
  4. Remove one piece of furniture entirely

None of them require paint, and together they’ll change how the room feels more than any colour scheme.

Still wondering

Common questions

How much space do you need to walk around a bed?

24 inches is the minimum walkway beside a bed. You also need 36 inches in front of a wardrobe to open the doors and stand, and 30 inches in front of a chest of drawers to pull one out. These cannot be cheated, and they tell you what will genuinely fit.

What size bed fits in a small bedroom?

In a 9 by 10 foot room a double leaves roughly 30 inches on one side and 24 on the other; a queen leaves almost nothing. Dropping one bed size frees more usable floor than any decorating trick you could apply instead.

Should the bed go in the corner of a small bedroom?

It is the single biggest layout gain — a bed against two walls rather than floating can free around 20 square feet. You lose easy access to one side, so it works well in a child's or single person's room and less well for a couple.

What colour makes a small bedroom look bigger?

Warm, light walls — cream, oat, warm white, a pale greige — reflect more light than cool grey, which absorbs and flattens. Carrying the same colour onto the ceiling removes the contrast line at the top of the wall and makes the room read taller.

How should curtains be hung in a small bedroom?

Rod 4 to 6 inches below the ceiling, extending 6 to 10 inches past each side of the window, curtains floor length and just kissing the floor. It makes the window look larger and the wall taller, and almost everyone hangs them too low and too narrow.

What size rug works in a small bedroom?

One extending at least 18 inches beyond the sides and foot of the bed. If that is not possible, run a large rug under the bottom two-thirds of the bed instead, or use two runners at the sides. A rug that is too small fragments the floor and shrinks the room.

Bedroom Lighting: Why the Ceiling Light Is Ruining Your Room

One overhead bulb flattens a bedroom and wrecks your sleep. Here is the three-source layering method, plus the bulb specs that actually matter.

The short version

  • Three separately switchable sources at different heights is the point where a room stops having a light and starts having lighting.
  • 2700K is the bedroom number; 4000K and above belongs in a garage.
  • Swing-arm sconces sit 90-100cm above the mattress and about 20cm out from the bed, which frees the nightstand entirely.
  • Buy CRI 90+ where you can find it — below 80, wood goes grey and every textile in the room looks wrong.
  • If a fitting cannot dim, it can only ever be right at one time of day.

  2. 02The three-source rule

A single bright bulb in the middle of the ceiling is the worst possible way to light a bedroom, and it is how roughly every rented flat in the world is lit. It flattens every surface, throws hard shadows under everything, and — because of what it does to your melatonin — actively works against the room’s only real job.

Fixing it is cheap. You do not need an electrician, and in most cases you do not need to touch the ceiling at all.

Why overhead light fails

Light from directly above hits horizontal surfaces hard and vertical surfaces barely at all. Your bed, the floor and the top of the dresser get blasted; the walls, the headboard and your face fall into shadow. The room reads as flat and slightly clinical, because that is exactly how an operating theatre is lit.

Worse, most builder-grade ceiling fittings take a cool bulb — 4000K or higher — which is close enough to daylight that it suppresses melatonin production for a good while after you switch it off. A bedroom lit like an office does not feel restful, and that is not only in your head.

Good bedroom lighting comes from the sides, sits low, and gets warmer as the evening goes on.

The three-source rule

Every bedroom wants at least three separate, independently switchable light sources at different heights. Three is the number at which a room stops having “a light” and starts having lighting.

1. Ambient — the soft wash

This is your general fill. Options, roughly in order of quality:

  • Wall sconces on a dimmer, angled up
  • A floor lamp in the corner with an opaque shade throwing light at the ceiling
  • The ceiling fitting itself, but dimmed hard and fitted with a warm bulb
  • A plug-in wall light, if you cannot drill

The point is to lift the overall level slightly so the room is not a series of isolated pools. It should be the least noticeable layer.

2. Task — the reading light

One per sleeping side, ideally at a height where the bottom of the shade sits near shoulder height when you are propped up. Too high and it shines in your eyes; too low and it lights the sheets rather than the page.

Wall-mounted swing-arm sconces are the best answer here: they free the nightstand entirely and can be aimed. If you are renting, plug-in versions of the same thing exist and cost a fraction.

3. Accent — the low glow

The layer everyone skips and the one that does the most for atmosphere. A small lamp on a dresser, a picture light, a strip tucked behind the headboard, or a table lamp on a chest across the room. Keep it under about 25cm tall and very dim. It should read as a warm point of light, not as illumination.

At night, this is often the only thing you want on.

Bulb specifications that matter

Three numbers on the box, and only three.

Colour temperature (K). For a bedroom: 2700K. That is standard warm white — the colour of an old incandescent. 3000K is acceptable for a task light. Anything at 4000K or above belongs in a garage.

For the accent layer, 2200K — sometimes sold as “extra warm” or “amber” — is worth seeking out. It is close to candlelight and the difference at 10pm is dramatic.

Brightness (lumens). Forget watts. Rough targets per fitting:

  • Ambient: 400–800 lumens, dimmable
  • Reading: 400–600 lumens, directed
  • Accent: 100–250 lumens

Total ambient output for a typical 12–14m² bedroom sits around 1500–2000 lumens with everything on — and you should almost never have everything on.

Colour rendering (CRI). Buy 90+ if you can find it. Below about 80, wood goes grey, skin goes sallow and every textile in the room looks slightly wrong. It is the cheapest upgrade in lighting and it is printed on maybe half of packaging.

Get everything dimmable

If a fitting cannot dim, it can only ever be right at one time of day. Smart bulbs are the easiest route in a rental — they dim from a phone or a small stick-on remote and take no wiring. Just check that the bulb is dimmable and, if you are using a wall dimmer, that the dimmer is rated for LED. Mismatched pairs are the usual cause of flicker and buzz.

Placement, in centimetres

  • Swing-arm sconces: 90–100cm above the mattress top, roughly 20cm out from the edge of the bed on each side.
  • Table lamps: the bottom of the shade should sit at seated shoulder height — usually a lamp 60–70cm tall on a 60cm nightstand.
  • Floor lamp: in the corner furthest from the door, so the light pulls your eye across the room and makes it read as deeper.
  • Nothing directly above the pillows. Lying down should never mean looking into a bulb.

The evening sequence

The reason to wire three layers separately is so you can step down through them.

  • Evening: ambient plus one reading light
  • Winding down: reading light only, dimmed
  • Last thirty minutes: accent glow only

This is not fussiness — dropping both the intensity and the colour temperature as the evening goes on is roughly what daylight does, and the room feels progressively calmer for it.

The rental-friendly version

No drilling, nothing hard-wired, about £120 all in:

  • One plug-in swing-arm sconce per side, hung on a picture hook, cord clipped down the wall
  • One corner floor lamp with a linen shade, on a smart plug
  • One small ceramic lamp on the dresser with a 2200K bulb
  • Warm dimmable smart bulbs throughout, grouped into one “bedtime” scene

Leave the ceiling fitting switched off permanently. You will not miss it.

Pair this with the layering method in our guide to making a bed properly — soft side-light is what makes those fabric folds read.

Common questions

What colour temperature is best for bedroom lighting?

2700K — standard warm white, the colour of an old incandescent bulb. 3000K is acceptable for a reading light. Anything at 4000K or above suppresses melatonin for a good while after you switch it off, which is the opposite of what a bedroom is for.

How many light sources does a bedroom need?

At least three, independently switchable, at different heights: an ambient wash, a reading light on each sleeping side, and a low accent glow under about 25cm tall. Three is the number at which a room stops being one flat pool of light.

How high should bedside wall lights be mounted?

Swing-arm sconces go 90 to 100cm above the top of the mattress, roughly 20cm out from the edge of the bed. The bottom of the shade should land near shoulder height when you are propped up — higher shines in your eyes, lower lights the sheets rather than the page.

How many lumens do I need in a bedroom?

Roughly 400-800 dimmable lumens for ambient, 400-600 directed for reading, and 100-250 for accent. A typical 12-14m² bedroom totals around 1500-2000 lumens with everything on — and you should almost never have everything on.

Can I fix bedroom lighting in a rental?

Yes, with no drilling and nothing hard-wired. A plug-in swing-arm sconce per side hung on a picture hook, a corner floor lamp on a smart plug, a small dresser lamp with a 2200K bulb, and warm dimmable smart bulbs grouped into one bedtime scene. Then leave the ceiling fitting off permanently.

What does CRI mean on a light bulb?

Colour rendering index — how accurately the light shows colour. Buy 90 or above where you can find it. Below about 80, wood goes grey, skin looks sallow and every textile in the room reads slightly wrong. It is the cheapest upgrade in lighting.

Classic Duos

1. Thelma and Louise

Two women in 1990s road trip outfits — jeans, a bandana, sunglasses, and a determined expression. This is a classic, empowering duo costume that suits two women with a strong friendship.

Sandy in a poodle skirt and a white blouse, Danny in a leather jacket and jeans. Or both in the final scene outfits — Sandy in black leather, Danny in a letterman jacket.

The final scene outfits are more recognizable than the opening scene ones.

3. Bonnie and Clyde

1930s outfits — a beret, a midi skirt, and a toy gun for Bonnie; a suit, a flat cap, and a toy gun for Clyde. This is a classic, stylish duo costume.

The flat cap and the beret are the two most important elements.

4. Sherlock Holmes and Watson

Sherlock in a deerstalker hat, a pipe, and a magnifying glass; Watson in a bowler hat and a military uniform. This is a classic literary duo costume.

The deerstalker hat is the most important element for Sherlock.

5. Batman and Robin

Batman in a black costume with a bat symbol; Robin in a red and green costume with an “R” symbol. This is a classic superhero duo costume that suits two friends with a clear dynamic.

The masks are the most important elements for both costumes.

Common questions

What are the best Halloween costumes for best friends?

The best duo costumes are the ones that are instantly recognizable as a pair and reflect the friendship. Classic pairings like Thelma and Louise, Sandy and Danny from Grease, or a devil and an angel are perennially popular. Punny pairings like salt and pepper or peanut butter and jelly are reliably funny and easy to execute.

How do you coordinate best friend Halloween costumes?

Agree on the theme first, then divide the specific costumes. Make sure both costumes are at the same level of elaborateness — one person in a full costume and one in a half-hearted version looks unbalanced. Plan the costumes together and shop or make them at the same time.

How to Layer a Bed So It Actually Looks Like the Photographs

Hotel beds look better than yours for five specific reasons. Here is the layering order, the sizing rules and the pillow maths that fix it.

The short version

  • Buy the duvet one size larger than the mattress — it is the single highest-leverage change to how a bed looks.
  • Layer in order so each layer reveals a strip of the one behind it; those horizontal bands are what the eye reads as made properly.
  • Match pillow count to bed width rather than ambition: a double takes three, a king takes six.
  • Choose warm whites or cool whites and stay there — mixing the two reads as dirt.
  • Thread count above roughly 400 is marketing; weave and fibre length matter far more.

Every well-photographed bed you have ever envied is doing the same five things. None of them are expensive, and none of them require the bedding to match. What they require is order — literally, the order in which things go onto the bed — and a willingness to size up.

Here is the whole method.

The layering order, top to bottom

Work in this sequence. Skipping a layer is fine; reordering is not, because each layer is sized to sit slightly differently from the one beneath it.

  1. Fitted sheet. Deep-pocket, in your quietest neutral.
  2. Flat sheet, folded back over the duvet by about 25cm at the head.
  3. Duvet or quilt, the primary block of colour.
  4. Coverlet or blanket, folded in thirds across the lower third of the bed.
  5. Sleeping pillows, standing up against the headboard.
  6. Euro shams in front of them, if the bed is wide enough.
  7. Two decorative cushions. Two. Not six.
  8. Throw, draped asymmetrically across one corner.

The visual logic is simple: each layer should reveal a strip of the one behind it. That series of horizontal bands is what your eye reads as “made properly.”

Size up your duvet

This is the single biggest gap between a real bed and a magazine bed, and almost everyone gets it wrong.

Buy the duvet one size larger than your mattress. A queen mattress takes a king duvet. A king takes a super king. The standard-size duvet is cut to cover a mattress, which means it stops at the edge and hangs in a stiff, mean little lip.

An oversized duvet drapes. It falls past the side of the mattress, pools slightly, and creates the soft vertical folds that make a bed look inviting rather than made-up. It costs perhaps 15% more and it is the highest-leverage change in this entire article.

A bed reads as luxurious when the fabric has somewhere to fall. Undersized bedding has nowhere to go, so it looks tight, and tight reads as cheap.

The pillow maths

Pillows are where beds go wrong in the other direction — too many, in too many sizes, in a wall that has to be dismantled every night.

The formula that works, by bed width:

  • Single / twin: 1 sleeping pillow + 1 cushion
  • Double / full: 2 sleeping pillows + 1 lumbar cushion
  • Queen: 2 sleeping pillows + 2 euro shams + 1 lumbar
  • King: 3 sleeping pillows (or 2 king pillows) + 2 euro shams + 1 lumbar

Note that the count goes up with width, not with ambition. A double bed with six cushions looks smothered; a king with two looks under-dressed. Match the count to the frame.

Keep the decorative cushions in the same tonal family as the duvet, and vary the texture rather than the colour — a linen next to a boucle next to a fine cotton reads as considered. Three different patterns reads as a sale rail.

Choose fabrics by how they crease

Bedding is one of the few places where a fabric’s flaws are the point.

Linen creases immediately and permanently. That is the entire aesthetic — it looks lived-in the moment you put it on, and it gets softer for years. It is the easiest fabric to make look good with the least effort, which is why every stylist reaches for it. Buy it stonewashed.

Cotton percale is crisp, cool and matte. It creases sharply rather than softly, so it wants a bit of ironing to look right, but the hotel-crisp finish is genuinely lovely if you like a tidier bed.

Cotton sateen is smooth and slightly lustrous. It drapes beautifully and photographs well, but it shows every wrinkle as a shine line, so it is the least forgiving of the three.

Avoid microfibre on a bed you want to look good. It does not crease, which sounds like an advantage until you realise it also does not drape — it sits on the bed like a sheet of plastic and reflects light flatly.

A note on thread count

Thread count above roughly 400 is largely marketing. Weave and fibre quality matter far more than the number on the packet. A 200-thread-count long-staple cotton percale will outperform a 1000-thread-count short-staple sateen on every measure that matters.

Colour: pick a temperature and stay there

The quickest way to make a bed look chaotic is to mix warm whites with cool whites. They fight, and the eye reads the difference as dirt.

Choose one:

  • Warm scheme — cream, oatmeal, warm white, camel, terracotta, soft clay
  • Cool scheme — pure white, pale grey, slate, soft blue, sage

Then build the whole bed inside it. If you want a second colour, take it from the room, not from the shop — pull it out of a rug, a piece of art or the curtains, so the bed connects to something.

For a small room, keeping the bed close to the wall colour makes the bed recede and the room feel larger. We go into this properly in our guide to maximalist small bedrooms, where the opposite approach is also made to work.

The throw, and how to drape it

A throw draped straight across the foot of the bed, parallel to the footboard, looks like a hotel that has given up. Instead:

  • Fold it in half lengthways
  • Lay it diagonally across one bottom corner
  • Let one end fall to the floor, or nearly
  • Do not straighten it

The asymmetry is doing real work. A perfectly symmetrical bed looks staged; one deliberate imbalance makes the whole arrangement read as casual.

Making it survive real life

The version above takes about ninety seconds a morning once you are used to it. If that is ninety seconds you do not have, cut the euro shams and the coverlet. You will still get most of the effect from an oversized duvet, two pillows and a well-draped throw.

Bedding also needs to be washed, so buy two full sets from the start. Rotating them halves the wear on each and means the bed is never stripped and waiting.

The final check: stand in the doorway. If you can see at least three distinct horizontal bands of fabric and one thing that is deliberately not straight, you have got it.

Still wondering

Common questions

What size duvet should I buy for my bed?

One size larger than the mattress. A queen mattress takes a king duvet; a king takes a super king. Standard sizing stops at the mattress edge and hangs in a stiff lip, while an oversized duvet drapes past the side and creates the soft folds that make a bed look inviting.

How many pillows should be on a bed?

Match the count to the width. Single: one sleeping pillow and one cushion. Double: two pillows and a lumbar. Queen: two pillows, two euro shams, one lumbar. King: three pillows, two euro shams, one lumbar. Two decorative cushions is the ceiling, not the starting point.

Is linen or cotton better for bedding?

Linen if you want the lived-in look for the least effort — it creases immediately and softens for years. Cotton percale if you prefer crisp and tidy, though it wants ironing. Avoid microfibre: it does not crease, but it does not drape either, so it sits flat.

Does thread count actually matter?

Above roughly 400 it is largely marketing. Weave and fibre length matter far more. A 200-thread-count long-staple cotton percale will outperform a 1000-thread-count short-staple sateen on softness, durability and the way it falls over the edge of the bed.

How should I drape a throw on a bed?

Fold it in half lengthways, lay it diagonally across one bottom corner, and let one end fall to or near the floor. Do not straighten it. Straight across the footboard reads as a hotel that has given up; the deliberate asymmetry is what makes the bed look casual.

What order do you layer a bed in?

Fitted sheet, flat sheet folded back about 25cm at the head, duvet or quilt, coverlet folded across the lower third, sleeping pillows against the headboard, euro shams in front, two decorative cushions, then a throw. Skipping a layer is fine; reordering is not.

  • Floating shelves add storage without taking up any floor space.
  • A wardrobe organizer can double the usable space inside an existing wardrobe.
  • Closed storage always looks tidier than open storage in a small room.

Storage in a small bedroom works best when it uses space that would otherwise be wasted — under the bed, on the walls, behind doors, and inside existing furniture. Buying more storage furniture is rarely the answer in a room where floor space is already limited.

These ideas focus on the approaches that add the most storage with the least impact on the room’s sense of space.

1. Use Under-Bed Storage

The space under the bed is the most underused storage area in most bedrooms. Flat storage boxes, drawer beds, or vacuum storage bags can hold extra bedding, seasonal clothes, shoes, or sports gear.

Measure the under-bed clearance before buying — low bed frames often have less space than expected.

2. Add a Drawer Bed or Ottoman Bed

A drawer bed or ottoman bed replaces a separate chest of drawers in a very small room. The storage is hidden, the floor stays clear, and the room looks tidier.

Ottoman beds need clearance at the foot to lift — measure before buying.

3. Mount Floating Shelves Above the Bed

Floating shelves above the bed use wall space that is otherwise empty. Use them for books, small plants, a lamp, and a few personal objects. Keep them uncluttered — three to five items per shelf.

Mount them at a height that does not feel oppressive when lying in bed.

4. Use a Wardrobe Organizer

A wardrobe organizer — hanging shelves, drawer inserts, and shoe racks — can double the usable space inside an existing wardrobe without buying a new one. This is one of the most cost-effective storage upgrades in a small bedroom.

Measure the wardrobe interior before buying an organizer.

5. Add Hooks Behind the Door

The back of the bedroom door holds bags, belts, scarves, dressing gowns, and light jackets without using any floor or wall space. Use over-door hooks for a no-drill option.

Choose low-profile hooks so the door can still open and close fully.

6. Use a Tall Narrow Bookcase

A tall narrow bookcase uses vertical space efficiently and takes up a small floor footprint. Use it for books, folded clothes, baskets, and small accessories.

Secure it to the wall with a furniture strap — tall narrow bookcases can tip.

7. Add a Storage Ottoman at the Foot of the Bed

A storage ottoman at the foot of the bed holds extra blankets, pillows, or seasonal items and doubles as a seat. Choose one that is roughly the same width as the bed.

Avoid a large ottoman in a very small room — it can block the walking path.

8. Use Baskets on Open Shelves

Baskets on open shelves hide small items and make the shelves look tidy. Use matching baskets in a consistent size for the most cohesive look.

Label the baskets so items go back in the right place.

9. Mount a Pegboard on One Wall

A pegboard holds bags, accessories, jewelry, and small items on hooks and small shelves. It is flexible — hooks and shelves can be moved as needs change.

Paint the pegboard the same color as the wall for a subtle look.

10. Use the Space Above the Wardrobe

The space above a wardrobe is often wasted. Add a shelf or use matching storage boxes to hold seasonal items, spare bedding, or luggage.

Use a step stool to access this area safely — do not climb on the wardrobe.

11. Add a Slim Chest of Drawers

A slim chest of drawers — 12–14 inches deep — fits into spaces where a standard chest will not. Use it beside the wardrobe, in a corner, or as a bedside table with storage.

Measure the available space carefully — slim chests vary significantly in depth.

12. Use Vacuum Storage Bags for Seasonal Items

Vacuum storage bags compress bulky items — duvets, winter coats, extra pillows — to a fraction of their normal size. Store them under the bed or on the top shelf of the wardrobe.

Label the bags so you know what is inside without opening them.

13. Add a Wall-Mounted Jewelry Organizer

A wall-mounted jewelry organizer keeps necklaces, earrings, and bracelets visible and untangled without using any drawer or surface space. Mount it inside the wardrobe door or on a small section of wall.

Choose one with a mirror for a dual-purpose piece.

14. Use a Bedside Caddy

A bedside caddy — a fabric organizer that hangs over the side of the mattress — holds a phone, book, glasses, and small items without needing a bedside table. This is useful in very small rooms where a table is not practical.

Choose one with a firm back panel so it holds its shape.

15. Store Shoes in Clear Boxes

Clear shoe boxes stack neatly and make it easy to find a pair without opening every box. They also protect shoes from dust and keep the wardrobe floor tidy.

Label the end of each box with a photo or description.

16. Use a Corner Shelf Unit

A corner shelf unit uses the least useful part of the room for storage. Use it for books, plants, and small accessories that would otherwise clutter a surface.

A corner unit with a mix of open shelves and closed doors is the most versatile option.

17. Declutter Before Adding Storage

The most effective storage upgrade in a small bedroom is removing items that do not belong there. A bedroom that holds only bedroom items — clothes, bedding, books, and personal care — is always easier to organize than one that has become a general storage room.

Review the room every season and remove anything that has not been used.

Final Thoughts

Small bedroom storage works best when it uses existing space more efficiently rather than adding more furniture. Start with under-bed storage and a wardrobe organizer — those two changes alone can add significant capacity without affecting the room’s sense of space.

15 Bedroom Wall Decor Ideas Above the Bed

Fill the wall above your bed with 15 decor ideas including gallery walls, large art, mirrors, shelves, and textile hangings that make the room feel finished.

The short version

  • Hang art with its center at 57 inches from the floor — the standard gallery height.
  • The arrangement above the bed should be roughly two-thirds the width of the headboard.
  • One large piece always looks more considered than several small unrelated ones.
  • Hang art 6–10 inches above the headboard so it reads as connected to the bed.

The wall above the bed is the most visible surface in the bedroom. It is what you see when you walk in, and it is what makes the room feel finished or unfinished. A blank wall above the bed is the most common reason a bedroom looks like a showroom.

These ideas cover the approaches that work consistently — from a single large print to a layered gallery wall — with practical guidance on sizing and placement.

1. Hang One Large Piece of Art

A single large canvas or framed print centered above the bed is the simplest and most effective approach. The art should be roughly two-thirds the width of the bed — about 40 inches for a double, 50 inches for a king.

Hang it 6–10 inches above the headboard with the center at 57 inches from the floor.

2. Create a Symmetrical Gallery Wall

Two or three matching frames arranged symmetrically above the bed create a clean, hotel-like look. Use the same frame style and a consistent color palette for the prints inside.

Measure and mark the positions with painter’s tape before drilling.

3. Use an Asymmetric Gallery Arrangement

An asymmetric arrangement of different-sized frames feels more personal and relaxed than a symmetrical one. Mix prints, photographs, and small objects in frames of different sizes.

Lay the arrangement out on the floor first to find a composition that works before hanging anything.

4. Mount a Large Mirror

A large mirror above the bed reflects light and makes the room feel larger. Use a mirror with a simple frame in a material that suits the room — wood, metal, or rattan.

Ensure the mirror is securely fixed to wall studs — a large mirror above a bed must be properly anchored.

5. Add a Textile Wall Hanging

A woven wall hanging, a macramé piece, or a large piece of fabric adds texture and warmth that framed art cannot. It is also lighter than a framed canvas and easier to hang.

Choose a piece that is roughly the same width as the headboard.

6. Use a Picture Ledge

A picture ledge mounted above the bed lets you lean prints and small objects without drilling multiple holes. It also makes it easy to swap art without redecorating.

Use two ledges at different heights for a layered effect.

7. Add a Set of Three Prints

Three prints in matching frames, hung in a horizontal row, create a clean and balanced arrangement. Use prints with a consistent color palette — the same two or three colors across all three.

Space them evenly — about 2–3 inches between frames.

8. Mount a Decorative Plate Collection

A collection of decorative plates in complementary colors and patterns creates an organic, layered arrangement. Mix sizes and hang them in a loose cluster rather than a rigid grid.

Use plate hangers rated for the weight of each plate.

9. Use a Large Botanical Print

A large botanical print — a single oversized leaf, a floral illustration, or a pressed plant print — adds a natural, calm quality to the bedroom. Use a simple frame that does not compete with the print.

Black frames on white walls and natural wood frames on warm walls are the most versatile combinations.

10. Add Floating Shelves With Objects

Two floating shelves above the bed — one slightly wider than the other — create a layered display area for small plants, candles, books, and objects. This adds depth that flat art cannot.

Keep the shelves light and uncluttered — three to five objects per shelf is usually enough.

11. Use a Neon or LED Sign

A neon or LED sign above the bed adds a personal, playful element. Choose a word, phrase, or simple shape. Use warm white or soft amber rather than a bright primary color for a bedroom.

This works best in a room with a simple, neutral palette where the sign can be the focal point.

12. Create a Pressed Flower or Botanical Display

A series of small frames containing pressed flowers or botanical specimens creates a delicate, personal display. Use matching frames and arrange them in a loose grid.

This works particularly well in a bedroom with a natural or earthy color palette.

13. Add a Wicker or Rattan Wall Hanging

A large wicker or rattan wall hanging adds texture and a natural quality. It works well in bedrooms with a coastal, boho, or earthy aesthetic.

Choose a piece that is at least 24 inches wide so it reads clearly above the bed.

14. Use a Tapestry

A large tapestry hung above the bed adds color, pattern, and texture in one piece. It is one of the most affordable ways to fill a large wall area.

Use a curtain rod or a wooden dowel to hang it so it lies flat against the wall.

15. Leave the Wall Intentionally Minimal

In a room with strong color, pattern, or texture elsewhere, a blank wall above the bed can be the right choice. A single small object — one framed print, one small shelf — is sometimes more effective than a full arrangement.

The goal is always a room that feels considered, not a wall that is simply filled.

Final Thoughts

The wall above the bed works best when the arrangement feels connected to the bed rather than floating above it. Start with the sizing — two-thirds the width of the headboard — and the height — 6–10 inches above the headboard. Everything else follows from those two decisions.

Black and white is the most striking bedroom palette and the easiest to get cold. Done badly it looks like a showroom nobody sleeps in. Done well it’s the most timeless scheme there is.

The difference comes down to three things: the ratio, the exact shades, and the third material you add.

Get the ratio right

The mistake is a 50/50 split. Equal black and white is harsh and busy.

Use 70/20/10:

  • 70% white or off-white — walls, bedding, the majority of surfaces
  • 20% black — one large element plus the smaller details
  • 10% a warm third element — wood, brass, leather, or a natural texture

Flip it for a dramatic version: 70% black walls, 20% white bedding and trim, 10% warm wood. That works too, but it needs good natural light.

What doesn’t work is half and half.

Choose warm whites and soft blacks

This is the detail that separates a beautiful black-and-white room from a stark one.

Whites: use a warm off-white, not brilliant white. Brilliant white beside black is clinical.

Look at: White Dove and Chantilly Lace (Benjamin Moore), Pointing and Wimborne White (Farrow & Ball), Alabaster (Sherwin-Williams).

Blacks: almost never use pure black on walls. Use a soft or brown-black.

Look at: Railings and Off-Black (Farrow & Ball), Black Beauty and Soot (Benjamin Moore), Tricorn Black (Sherwin-Williams).

Pure black is fine for small metal details — a lamp base, a curtain rod, a frame.

The third element is essential

A room with only black and white feels unfinished. Add one warm material and it comes alive.

Wood — the easiest and most reliable. Oak, walnut or a warm mid-tone. A wooden bedside table or bed frame does most of the work.

Brass or gold — light fittings, hardware, a mirror frame. Adds warmth without adding colour.

Leather or tan — a leather bench at the foot of the bed, tan cushions.

Natural texture — jute rug, rattan, linen, a woven basket.

Greenery — a single large plant is often all a black-and-white room needs.

Pick one and repeat it three or four times around the room.

Where to put the black

Black works best as one large gesture plus small repeats, rather than scattered evenly.

Options for the large gesture:

  • One black accent wall, behind the bed
  • Black bed frame
  • Black curtains
  • A black wardrobe or dresser
  • Black window frames

Then repeat it small: picture frames, a lamp base, curtain rod, drawer handles, a cushion, the legs on a chair.

That repetition is what makes the scheme read as deliberate rather than accidental.
