Bunk beds are the single most space-efficient thing you can put in a shared boys’ room. They also come with more measurements and safety rules than any other piece of furniture in a house, and most articles skip all of them.

Here’s the practical version.

Check your ceiling height first

This is the thing to measure before you shop.

You need at least 30 inches between the top mattress surface and the ceiling. Less than that and a child sitting up in the top bunk hits his head.

Work it out:

  • Standard bunk top mattress sits about 60 inches off the floor
  • Add a 6-inch mattress → top surface at 66 inches
  • Add 30 inches clearance → you need 96 inches (8 feet) of ceiling

Standard ceilings are 8 feet, so most rooms just work. Rooms with sloped ceilings, ceiling fans or low soffits need checking carefully.

Never put a bunk bed under a ceiling fan.

Safety rules that actually matter

  • Top bunk: age 6 and up. This is the standard guidance and worth following.
  • Guardrails on both sides of the top bunk, even against a wall. Mattresses shift.
  • Guardrail height: at least 5 inches above the top of the mattress. If you buy a thicker mattress than the bed was designed for, you lose this margin.
  • Mattress thickness: never exceed the maximum stated by the manufacturer, usually 6 inches for a top bunk.
  • Ladder: angled ladders are considerably safer and more comfortable than vertical ones. Look for flat, wide steps rather than round rungs.
  • No hanging anything from the guardrails — ropes, belts, bags. This is a genuine strangulation risk and the reason the rule exists.

Layout options

Standard stacked bunk

Two beds directly above one another. Smallest footprint — roughly 42 x 80 inches. Best for genuinely tight rooms.

L-shaped bunk

Top bunk over a lower bed set at a right angle. Uses more floor but creates a natural nook underneath the top bunk for a desk, reading corner or storage. Excellent in a square room.

Bunk with desk underneath

The top bunk stays, the bottom becomes a workspace. Ideal for one older boy rather than two sharing. Gives you a bed and a home office in about 42 x 80 inches.

Triple bunk or trundle

A trundle that rolls out from under the bottom bunk gives you a third sleeping spot for sleepovers without a third permanent bed.

Clearances to leave

  • 30 inches of clear floor in front of the ladder for climbing down
  • 24 inches minimum walkway on the open side
  • Door swing must not hit the bed — check this before assembly, not after

Storage built into the bunk

This is where bunks earn their keep beyond just saving floor space.

Under-bed drawers — most bunk frames offer them as an add-on. Two large drawers replace an entire dresser.

Stair storage — bunks with staircases instead of ladders often have drawers built into each step. More expensive, considerably more storage, and safer for younger children.

End-of-bed shelving — some frames have built-in bookcases at the foot.

Bunk shelf or caddy — a small clip-on shelf for each bunk holds a phone, book, water and glasses. This is the cheapest upgrade and the one kids appreciate most.

Lighting for each bunk

Both boys need their own light. Without it, one child’s bedtime reading is the other’s problem.

  • Clip-on LED reading lights on each guardrail
  • Wall-mounted sconces if you can wire them — better light, no clutter
  • Battery puck lights stuck to the underside of the top bunk for the bottom sleeper
  • A dimmable strip along the inside of each bunk

Warm light, and make sure the top bunk’s light doesn’t shine down into the bottom bunk.

Giving each boy his own space

The main complaint in a shared room is having no privacy. A bunk makes that worse unless you plan for it.

  • A curtain rail on each bunk with a fabric panel — the single most requested feature by kids
  • Different bedding colours so each bunk is visibly his
  • A pinboard or pegboard per bunk at each child’s eye level
  • Separate storage — his own drawer, his own bin, clearly divided

Small territorial markers reduce arguments more than you’d expect.

Styling a bunk bed room

Bunk beds are visually heavy — a big rectangle of frame dominating the room. Ways to lighten it:

  • Paint the frame the same colour as the wall so it recedes
  • Metal frames read lighter than solid wood
  • Keep bedding simple — busy patterns on two stacked beds is a lot
  • One accent colour across both bunks, with each boy’s cushions and throw differing
  • Wall decals or art beside each bunk rather than one large piece behind

Making the bed — the honest bit

Making a top bunk is genuinely awkward. Two things help:

Use a duvet with no top sheet. One layer to pull up instead of three.

Fitted sheets with deep pockets stay on better and are easier to wrestle onto a mattress you can’t walk around.

Teach them to do it themselves from about seven. It’ll be badly made and that’s fine.

When a bunk bed isn’t the answer

If the ceiling is under 8 feet, if either child is under six and would take the top, or if the room is long and narrow rather than square, consider two singles placed head-to-head along one wall, or a mid-sleeper each.

A bunk that doesn’t fit the room properly causes more problems than the floor space it saves.

Measurement Requirement
Ceiling height 96 inches minimum
Top mattress to ceiling 30 inches minimum
Guardrail above mattress 5 inches minimum
Top mattress thickness 6 inches max (check manufacturer)

17 Boys Gaming Bedroom Ideas With Smart Desk Setups

Build a boys gaming bedroom that works for play and sleep with 17 ideas covering desk setups, cable management, lighting, and storage for gear.

The short version

  • Position the desk against a wall with the monitor at eye level to reduce neck strain.
  • Use a monitor arm and cable management tray to keep the desk surface clear.
  • Separate the sleep zone from the gaming zone with lighting and furniture placement.
  • Choose closed storage for controllers, headsets, and cables to keep the room tidy.

A boys gaming bedroom works best when the gaming setup and the sleeping area feel like two distinct zones. When everything is crammed together, the room looks cluttered and the sleep quality suffers.

These ideas focus on practical desk setups, smart storage, and lighting choices that make the room comfortable for both gaming and rest.

1. Position the Desk Against a Wall

A desk against a wall gives the monitor a neutral background, reduces glare, and keeps the gaming area contained. Leave enough depth for the monitor, keyboard, and a small amount of desk space on each side.

Avoid placing the desk directly facing a bright window, which creates screen glare.

2. Use a Monitor Arm

A monitor arm frees up the entire desk surface below the screen. It also makes it easy to adjust the monitor height and angle, which reduces neck and eye strain during long sessions.

Measure the desk thickness before buying — most arms clamp to the back edge.

3. Manage Cables From the Start

A cable management tray under the desk, a few velcro ties, and a power strip with a long lead keep cables off the floor and out of sight. This is the single biggest visual improvement to any desk setup.

Run cables along the back of the desk before adding anything else.

4. Choose a Chair With Lumbar Support

A chair with adjustable height and lumbar support is more important than an expensive gaming chair. The priority is that the feet rest flat on the floor and the screen is at eye level.

A good office chair often costs less than a branded gaming chair and lasts longer.

5. Add a Headset Stand

A headset stand on the desk keeps the headset off the surface and within easy reach. It also prevents the cable from tangling with the keyboard and mouse.

A simple hook on the side of the desk works just as well if space is tight.

6. Use a Pegboard Behind the Desk

A pegboard on the wall behind the desk holds controllers, headsets, small accessories, and even a small shelf for a lamp or plant. It keeps the desk surface clear and makes the setup look intentional.

Paint the pegboard the same color as the wall to keep it subtle.

7. Separate the Sleep Zone With Lighting

Use warm, dimmable lighting near the bed and brighter task lighting at the desk. This creates a visual separation between the two zones and makes it easier to wind down after gaming.

A smart bulb in the bedside lamp makes it easy to switch between modes.

8. Add LED Strip Lighting Behind the Desk

LED strip lights behind the monitor or under the desk reduce eye strain by adding ambient light behind the screen. Use a warm white or soft color rather than a bright primary color for everyday use.

Keep the brightness low — the goal is ambient fill, not a light show.

9. Use a Deep Desk for Dual Monitors

If a second monitor is planned, choose a desk at least 55 inches wide and 24 inches deep. A shallow desk with two monitors feels cramped and makes cable management harder.

Measure the room before buying — a large desk in a small room leaves no floor space.

10. Store Controllers in a Drawer or Charging Station

A charging station or small drawer keeps controllers off the desk and charged. This prevents the desk from becoming a dumping ground for accessories.

A two-controller charging dock takes up less space than a drawer and keeps everything visible.

11. Use Closed Storage for Games and Accessories

A small cabinet or drawer unit beside the desk keeps game cases, cables, and accessories out of sight. Open shelving for games looks tidy only when the collection is small and well-organized.

Label drawers so items go back in the right place.

12. Add a Small Shelf Above the Desk

A floating shelf above the desk holds a lamp, a small plant, or a few display items without using any desk space. Keep it at a height that does not block the monitor or require ducking.

One shelf is usually enough — more than two starts to feel cluttered.

13. Choose Dark or Neutral Wall Colors

Dark navy, charcoal, forest green, or warm grey work well in a gaming bedroom. They reduce glare on the screen and make the room feel more immersive without being oppressive.

Use a lighter color on the ceiling to keep the room from feeling too enclosed.

14. Use Blackout Curtains

Blackout curtains improve sleep quality and reduce screen glare during daytime gaming. Hang them high and wide — rod 4–6 inches above the frame, extending 6–10 inches past each side.

A blackout lining added to existing curtains is a cheaper alternative.

15. Keep the Bed Simple

A plain duvet in a neutral or dark color keeps the sleep zone calm. Avoid themed bedding that competes with the gaming setup — the desk area will already have enough visual interest.

One throw and two pillows is enough for a teenage bedroom.

16. Add a Small Bin Under the Desk

A small bin under the desk prevents wrappers, packaging, and cables from accumulating on the floor. It is one of the easiest ways to keep the gaming area tidy.

Empty it regularly — a full bin under a desk looks worse than no bin at all.

17. Leave Floor Space for Movement

Resist the urge to fill every corner with furniture or storage. A clear floor area beside the desk makes the room easier to move around in and prevents the gaming setup from dominating the entire space.

The best gaming bedrooms feel like a room that happens to have a great desk, not a desk that happens to have a room around it.

Final Thoughts

A boys gaming bedroom works when the desk setup is functional, the cables are managed, and the sleep zone is kept separate. Start with the desk position and lighting, then add storage and personal details. A well-organized setup always looks better than an expensive one.

Dark hair is an asset for Halloween costumes. Many of the most iconic, most striking, and most recognizable Halloween characters are canonically brunette — which means you can wear them without a wig and look more authentic than someone who has to cover their natural hair.

The ideas below are organized by style. All of them work with dark brown or black hair.

Gothic and Witchy

1. Wednesday Addams

A black dress with a white collar, two braids, and a deadpan expression. Wednesday has dark hair — this is one of the most authentic brunette Halloween costumes. The key is the expression: Wednesday never smiles.

A black dress with a white Peter Pan collar is the most accurate version.

2. Morticia Addams

A long black dress, pale skin, dark lips, and long dark hair worn loose. Morticia’s long, dark hair is one of her most defining features. This is an elegant, sophisticated costume that suits a brunette perfectly.

A long, form-fitting black dress is the most important piece.

3. The Wicked Witch of the West

A black dress, a pointed hat, green face paint, and dark hair. The Wicked Witch has dark hair — this is an authentic brunette costume. The green face paint is the most important element.

Use theatrical face paint rather than craft paint for the green skin.

4. Maleficent

A black dress, dramatic horns, pale makeup, dark lips, and dark hair. Maleficent’s dark hair is one of her most defining features. This is a striking, dramatic costume.

The horns are the most important piece — choose a quality pair that stays on securely.

5. The Evil Queen (Snow White)

A black and purple gown, a crown, pale makeup, dark lips, and dark hair. The Evil Queen has dark hair — this is an authentic brunette costume.

The crown and the dark lips are the two most important elements.

Still wondering

Common questions

What Halloween costumes look best on brunettes?

Characters who are canonically brunette — Wednesday Addams, Morticia Addams, Snow White, Moana, Hermione Granger, Katniss Everdeen — look most authentic when played by someone with dark hair. Gothic, witchy, and villain costumes also tend to suit dark hair because the contrast between dark hair and pale or dramatic makeup is striking.

Can brunettes wear blonde character costumes?

Yes, with a wig. A quality wig is always an option. But a costume that works with your natural hair is more comfortable, more convincing, and requires less maintenance throughout the evening. If you love a blonde character, invest in a good wig rather than a cheap one — the difference is significant.

The entryway is the first thing anyone sees at Christmas, and it’s also the space with the least room to spare. Coats, boots and bags multiply in December exactly when you want to decorate.

Here’s how to do it without blocking the door.

The rule for a small entry

Decorate the walls and vertical surfaces. Leave the floor alone.

A small entry can’t afford a floor-standing tree, a basket of pinecones and a nutcracker beside the door. Everything goes up.

Keep 30 inches of clear walkway. If people are stepping around your decorations while carrying shopping, they’ll get knocked over.

Wreath sizing

The wreath on the door is the main event.

Standard front door (36 inches wide): a 24-inch wreath. This is the size most people should buy and most people buy smaller.

Narrow door (30 inches): 20–22 inches.

Double doors: two 18–20 inch wreaths, one per door.

Rule of thumb: the wreath should be about two-thirds the door’s width.

Position: centred, with the top at about eye level — roughly 55–60 inches from the ground, or centred in the upper half of the door.

Hanging: an over-door wreath hanger, a suction hook on glass, or a ribbon looped over the top of the door. No holes needed.

Garland lengths

Garland is sold by the foot and people always underestimate.

Around a door frame: measure both sides plus the top, then add 50% for the drape and swag. A standard 36 x 80 inch door frame needs about 16 feet of garland to look full rather than stretched.

On a stair rail: the length of the rail plus 50–100% depending on how deep you want the swags.

On a console or shelf: the length plus a foot for the trailing ends.

Stretched, sparse garland is the most common Christmas decorating mistake. Buy more than you think.

The console or entry table

The one surface you have. Use the same formula as year-round styling — three heights — with seasonal contents.

Tall: branches with fairy lights, a small potted tree, tall brass candlesticks Medium: a garland laid along the surface, a lantern, a stack of books Low: a bowl of baubles, a tray of candles, dried oranges

Keep the key tray. It still has to function as an entryway.

One-third of the surface stays clear.

Lighting

An entry is often the darkest space in a house, and December is dark.

  • Warm white fairy lights — always warm, never cool white
  • Battery-operated lights in a garland, so no cable across the walkway
  • A lantern with a candle or an LED candle on the console
  • A small lamp if there’s a socket

Battery or plug-in with a timer. Six hours on, eighteen off, so you don’t think about it.

Small-space Christmas trees

If you want a tree in the entry:

  • A slim or pencil tree — 6 feet tall but only 24 inches wide
  • A tabletop tree on the console
  • A potted rosemary or bay clipped into a cone — real, useful afterwards, and it looks lovely
  • A wall tree — branches or lights arranged in a tree shape on the wall, taking zero floor space

Natural materials

The most reliable way to look elegant rather than plastic:

  • Fresh eucalyptus and pine
  • Dried orange slices
  • Cinnamon sticks tied with twine
  • Pinecones
  • Bay and rosemary sprigs
  • Cranberries or seeded eucalyptus for red

Fresh greenery lasts about three weeks indoors. Mist it and keep it away from radiators.

Colour schemes that look considered

Pick one and stick to it:

  • Green, brass and cream — classic, warm, works with any interior
  • Green, white and silver — cool and crisp
  • Green, rust and dried orange — warm and natural
  • All white and green — Scandinavian, calm
  • Traditional red and green, but muted rather than bright

Two colours plus greenery is plenty for a small space.

The practical December problem

Coats and boots double in winter. Decorating an entry that’s already overflowing makes it worse.

Before you decorate:

  • Move out-of-season coats elsewhere
  • Add a boot tray if you don’t have one
  • Add temporary hooks if guests will need somewhere for coats
  • Clear the drop zone

An entry that’s beautifully decorated and impassable isn’t a success.

Doormat and step

  • A seasonal doormat — the cheapest festive change there is
  • A lantern or a small potted evergreen beside the door, if there’s outdoor space
  • Lights around the door frame outside

Scent

The entry is where people form their first impression. A cedar, pine or orange-clove candle just inside the door, or a simmer pot in the kitchen that carries through.

A complete small entry, in order:

  1. 24-inch wreath on the door, centred at eye level
  2. 16 feet of garland around the door frame, with battery fairy lights
  3. Console styled in three heights, one-third clear
  4. A lantern with an LED candle
  5. A seasonal doormat
  6. Clear the coats and add a boot tray

Nothing on the floor, nothing blocking the door, and it’s the first thing anyone sees.

20 Classy Halloween Costumes That Are Elegant and Memorable

Look stunning this Halloween with 20 classy costume ideas that are sophisticated, elegant, and memorable. From gothic glamour to timeless literary characters.

The short version

  • A classy Halloween costume uses quality materials and restrained styling rather than cheap props.
  • The makeup and hair do more for an elegant costume than the outfit itself.
  • Choose a character whose aesthetic you genuinely admire — it shows in the execution.
  • A single statement piece — a quality gown, a real piece of jewelry, a professional wig — elevates any costume.

A classy Halloween costume is one that makes people say “you look amazing” before they say “what are you?” The ideas below are chosen for their elegance, their wearability, and their potential to look genuinely beautiful rather than just recognizable.

Quality materials and specific character references are what distinguish a classy costume from a cheap one.

Gothic Glamour

1. Morticia Addams

A long, form-fitting black dress, pale skin, dark lips, and long dark hair worn loose. Morticia is the gold standard of elegant Halloween costumes — she is instantly recognizable, inherently beautiful, and requires no props.

A long, form-fitting black dress is the most important piece. Everything else follows from it.

2. Elvira

A long black dress with a plunging neckline, big black hair, and dramatic makeup. Elvira is a classic Halloween character whose look is inherently glamorous.

A black wig with volume is the most important piece.

3. The Bride of Frankenstein

A white dress with a tall, streaked wig, pale makeup, and dramatic eye makeup. The Bride’s look is theatrical and striking — it photographs beautifully.

The tall, streaked wig is the most important piece.

4. A Victorian Ghost

A white or ivory Victorian dress, pale makeup, dark circles under the eyes, and an ethereal expression. This is a beautiful, atmospheric costume that suits a woman who wants to look haunting rather than scary.

A genuine vintage or vintage-inspired dress elevates this costume significantly.

5. The Black Swan

A black tutu or a black dress with feather details, dramatic black and white makeup, and a feather headpiece. This is a striking, theatrical costume inspired by the film.

The dramatic makeup — black and white with red accents — is the most important element.

6. Audrey Hepburn in Breakfast at Tiffany’s

A little black dress, long gloves, a pearl necklace, an updo, and a cigarette holder prop. This is one of the most elegant Halloween costumes — it is beautiful, recognizable, and requires no face paint or prosthetics.

The updo and the long gloves are the two most important elements.

7. Cleopatra

A white or gold dress, a black wig with a blunt fringe, a gold headpiece, and dramatic eye makeup. Cleopatra is a timeless Halloween character whose look is inherently regal.

The dramatic eye makeup — thick black liner and gold eyeshadow — is the most important element.

8. Marie Antoinette

A pastel ball gown, a powdered wig, beauty marks, and an elaborate updo. Marie Antoinette’s look is theatrical and opulent — it is one of the most visually striking Halloween costumes.

The powdered wig and the pastel ball gown are the two most important elements.

9. Josephine Baker

A 1920s-inspired outfit — a beaded dress, a feather boa, a headband with a feather, and a confident expression. Josephine Baker’s look is glamorous and distinctive.

The feather boa and the beaded dress are the two most important elements.

10. Frida Kahlo

A colorful embroidered blouse, a long skirt, flowers in the hair, and drawn-on connected eyebrows. Frida Kahlo’s look is artistic and distinctive — it is one of the most recognizable and most beautiful Halloween costumes.

The flowers in the hair and the connected eyebrows are the two most important elements.

11. Maleficent

A black dress, dramatic horns, pale makeup, dark lips, and dark hair. Maleficent’s look is inherently elegant — she is a villain who takes her appearance seriously.

The horns are the most important piece — choose a quality pair that stays on securely.

12. Cruella de Vil

A black and white outfit, dramatic makeup, and a fur coat or stole. The key is the hair — half black, half white. This is a striking, theatrical costume.

A dramatic smoky eye and a bold red lip complete the look.

13. The Evil Queen (Snow White)

A black and purple gown, a crown, pale makeup, dark lips, and dark hair. The Evil Queen’s look is regal and theatrical.

The crown and the dark lips are the two most important elements.

14. Ursula (The Little Mermaid)

A black and purple dress, dramatic makeup, white hair, and tentacle details. Ursula is a theatrical villain whose look is inherently dramatic.

The white hair and the dramatic makeup are the two most important elements.

15. Lady Tremaine (Cinderella)

A grey or purple gown, grey hair in an elegant updo, and a cold, imperious expression. Lady Tremaine’s look is sophisticated and understated — she is a villain who relies on elegance rather than theatrics.

The grey updo and the cold expression are the two most important elements.

16. Medusa

A green dress, snakes woven into the hair, and dramatic makeup. Medusa is a mythological character whose look is inherently striking.

17. Athena

A white or gold dress, a helmet or a laurel wreath, a shield prop, and a wise, composed expression. Athena is a mythological character whose look is inherently regal.

The helmet or laurel wreath is the most important element.

18. The Phantom’s Christine (Phantom of the Opera)

A white dress with a flower in the hair, pale makeup, and an expression of wonder. Christine’s look is romantic and ethereal.

The white dress and the flower in the hair are the two most important elements.

19. Titania (A Midsummer Night’s Dream)

A flowing, ethereal dress in white or pale green, a flower crown, and fairy wings. Titania is a literary character whose look is inherently beautiful.

The flower crown and the flowing dress are the two most important elements.

20. The Lady of Shalott

A white dress, long flowing hair, and a slightly tragic expression. The Lady of Shalott is a Pre-Raphaelite literary character whose look is hauntingly beautiful.

A genuine white or ivory dress elevates this costume significantly.

Final Thoughts

The best classy Halloween costumes are the ones that make you feel beautiful and confident. Choose a character whose aesthetic you genuinely admire, invest in one quality piece — a dress, a wig, a piece of jewelry — and focus on the makeup and hair. A costume that makes you feel good is always the right choice.

24 College Halloween Costume Ideas That Are Actually Creative

Stand out at every college Halloween party with 24 costume ideas that go beyond the basics. Clever, funny, and pop culture options at every budget.

Elena Marsh/October 2, 2026/8 min read

In this article

  1. 01Clever and Punny
  2. 02Pop Culture
  3. 03Thrift Store Finds
  4. 04Group Options for College
  5. 05Final Thoughts

The short version

  • The best college costumes are specific — a generic witch is forgettable, a specific character is memorable.
  • A costume built from thrift store finds is almost always better than a cheap costume kit.
  • Clever and punny costumes get more attention at college parties than scary ones.
  • Plan the costume at least a week in advance — last-minute costumes are always disappointing.

In this article

  1. 01Clever and Punny

  5. 05Final Thoughts

College Halloween is competitive. Everyone is trying to be clever, and the bar for “good costume” is higher than it is at a family trick-or-treat. The ideas below are chosen for their specificity and their conversation-starting potential.

A costume built from thrift store finds and one specific accessory is almost always better than a cheap costume kit.

Clever and Punny

1. Error 404: Costume Not Found

A plain outfit with a printed sign that says “Error 404: Costume Not Found.” This is the laziest Halloween costume on the list, but it is also one of the funniest at a tech-savvy college party.

Use a large, readable font on the sign.

2. Ceiling Fan

A plain outfit with a sign that says “Go Ceilings!” Respond to every “What are you?” with enthusiastic ceiling cheering.

The commitment to the bit is what makes this costume funny.

3. Freudian Slip

A slip dress with the word “Freudian” written on it, or a slip dress with Freud’s face printed on it. This is a clever, slightly intellectual pun that suits a college party.

The label needs to be large and readable — the pun only works if people can read it.

4. Identity Theft

A plain outfit covered in “Hello My Name Is” stickers with different names on each one. This is a clever, topical pun that suits a college party.

Use as many name tags as possible — the more, the funnier.

5. A Formal Apology

A formal suit or dress with a sign that says “I’m Sorry.” This is a clever pun that works on two levels — the formal outfit and the apology.

Apologize to everyone you meet throughout the evening for extra effect.

6. A Participation Trophy

A plain outfit with a large “Participation Trophy” ribbon and a sign that says “You Tried.” This is a funny, slightly self-deprecating costume that suits a college student with a good sense of humor.

The ribbon needs to be large and clearly readable.

7. A Nudist on Strike

Regular clothes with a sign that says “Nudist on Strike.” This is the most minimal funny Halloween costume and one of the most reliably funny at a college party.

Use a large, readable font on the sign.

Pop Culture

8. Walter White

A white hazmat suit or a yellow one, a bald cap or a shaved head, glasses, and a bag of blue rock candy labeled “Blue Sky.” This is a recognizable pop culture costume that suits a college student with a sense of humor.

The bald cap and the glasses are the two most important elements.

9. The Dude (The Big Lebowski)

A bathrobe, a white t-shirt, jeans, sunglasses, and a White Russian drink. This is a comfortable, recognizable costume that suits a college student who wants to be comfortable.

The bathrobe is the most important element — choose a white or cream one.

10. Michael Scott

A suit with a “World’s Best Boss” mug, a tie, and a slightly desperate expression. This is a recognizable pop culture costume that suits a college student who is a fan of The Office.

The “World’s Best Boss” mug is the most important prop.

11. Dwight Schrute

A mustard yellow shirt, a brown tie, glasses, and a beet prop. This is a recognizable pop culture costume that suits a college student who is a fan of The Office.

The mustard yellow shirt and the glasses are the two most important elements.

12. Wednesday Addams

A black dress with a white collar, two braids, and a deadpan expression. This is a perennially popular college Halloween costume that suits a student with dark hair.

The deadpan expression is the most important element — Wednesday never smiles.

13. Eleven (Stranger Things)

A pink dress, a blonde wig, a bloody nose, and a box of Eggo waffles. This is a recognizable pop culture costume that suits a college student who is a fan of Stranger Things.

The bloody nose makeup and the Eggo waffles are the two most important elements.

14. Ken (from Barbie)

A pink outfit — pink polo shirt, pink shorts or trousers — with a “Ken” name tag. This is a topical, funny costume that suits a college student with a sense of humor.

The more pink, the better.

Thrift Store Finds

15. A Specific Decade

Choose a specific decade — the 1970s, the 1980s, the 1990s — and dress in the most exaggerated version of that decade’s fashion. Thrift stores are full of decade-appropriate clothing.

The more exaggerated, the better — subtlety does not work for decade costumes.

16. A Specific Profession

Choose a specific profession — a 1950s housewife, a 1980s stockbroker, a 1990s aerobics instructor — and dress in the most exaggerated version of that profession’s uniform. Thrift stores are the best source for profession-specific clothing.

The more specific the profession, the funnier the costume.

17. A Thrift Store Painting

Find a thrift store painting of a person and dress as the person in the painting — matching the outfit, the hairstyle, and the expression as closely as possible. Carry the painting with you for comparison.

The closer the match between the costume and the painting, the funnier the costume.

18. A Specific Movie Character from a Specific Scene

Choose a very specific scene from a movie — not just “Indiana Jones” but “Indiana Jones in the opening scene of Raiders of the Lost Ark” — and dress as the character in that specific scene. The specificity is what makes it funny.

The more specific the scene, the more impressive the costume.

Group Options for College

Shop this costume makeup 42-Color Costume Makeup Kit See details & availability Check current price On Amazon · Opens in a new tab

19. The Office Cast

Assign each person a specific Office character — Michael, Dwight, Jim, Pam, Kevin, Angela, Ryan. The group is recognizable as a set because of the specific character details.

The “World’s Best Boss” mug is the most important prop for Michael.

20. Vine References

Each person dresses as a specific Vine reference — “It is Wednesday, my dudes,” “Road work ahead,” “I can’t believe you’ve done this.” This is a funny, nostalgic group costume for a college crowd.

The more obscure the Vine reference, the more impressive the costume.

21. A Group Chat

Each person wears a name tag with their group chat nickname and carries a printed phone screen showing a funny message exchange. This is a personal, inside-joke costume that suits a close friend group.

The funnier the message exchange, the better the costume.

22. Different Versions of the Same Person

Each person dresses as a different version of the same person — Monday morning version, Friday night version, exam week version, summer break version. This is a funny, relatable group costume for a college crowd.

The contrast between the different versions is the joke.

23. A Zoom Class

Each person wears a business outfit on top and pajamas on the bottom, with a name tag showing their Zoom display name. This is a relatable, post-pandemic group costume for a college crowd.

The contrast between the top and bottom halves is the joke.

24. The Stages of a College Night Out

Each person represents a different stage of a college night out — “Pre-drinks,” “First bar,” “Second bar,” “3am kebab,” “Next morning.” This is a funny, relatable group costume for a college crowd.

The more specific and accurate the stages, the funnier the costume.

Final Thoughts

The best college Halloween costumes are the ones that are specific, committed, and executed with confidence. Start with what you already own, add one specific accessory, and commit to the character for the whole evening. A simple costume worn with genuine enthusiasm is always more memorable than an elaborate one worn half-heartedly.

What are the best Halloween costumes for college students?

The best college Halloween costumes are specific, clever, and executed with commitment. Pop culture references, punny concepts, and group costumes with friends are the most popular options. A costume built from thrift store finds and one or two specific accessories is almost always better than a cheap costume kit from a party store.

The best couple Halloween costumes are the ones that tell a story. Each costume should be recognizable on its own, but together they create something more interesting than either one alone.

Classic and Timeless

1. Gomez and Morticia Addams

Gomez in a pinstripe suit with slicked-back hair and a thin mustache; Morticia in a long black dress with pale skin and dark lips. This is the most iconic couple costume and suits a couple with a dramatic, romantic dynamic.

2. Sandy and Danny (Grease)

Sandy in a poodle skirt and a white blouse, Danny in a leather jacket and jeans. Or both in the final scene outfits — Sandy in black leather, Danny in a letterman jacket.

17 Cozy Bedroom Lighting Ideas for a Warm Evening Look

Create a warm, layered bedroom atmosphere with 17 lighting ideas covering bedside lamps, fairy lights, dimmers, candles, and smart bulbs for a cozy evening look.

The short version

  • Use bulbs at 2700K or lower for the warmest, most relaxing bedroom light.
  • A dimmer switch on the overhead light is the single most impactful bedroom lighting upgrade.

Most bedrooms have one overhead light and nothing else. That single source flattens the room, casts unflattering shadows, and makes it impossible to create a warm evening atmosphere.

Cozy bedroom lighting comes from layering multiple sources at different heights. These ideas cover the specific changes that make the biggest difference — from a dimmer switch to a string of fairy lights.

1. Add a Dimmer Switch to the Overhead Light

A dimmer switch on the overhead light is the single most impactful bedroom lighting upgrade. It costs very little and takes an hour to install. Being able to lower the overhead light in the evening changes the entire mood of the room.

Use a smart dimmer if you want to control it from your phone or set schedules.

2. Use Warm Bulbs at 2700K

Swap any cool white bulbs for warm white ones at 2700K or lower. This single change makes a bedroom feel significantly warmer and more relaxing. Cool white light (4000K and above) makes a bedroom feel like a bathroom.

Check the bulb packaging — the color temperature is always listed in Kelvin.

3. Add a Bedside Lamp on Each Side

A bedside lamp on each side of the bed creates symmetry and gives each person their own reading light. Use matching lamps for a cohesive look, or complementary styles in the same material.

Choose a lamp with a shade that diffuses the light rather than directing it — a fabric shade is warmer than a metal one.

4. Use a Floor Lamp in a Dark Corner

A floor lamp in a corner that the overhead light does not reach adds a warm pool of light that makes the room feel larger and more layered. This is the third light source that most bedrooms are missing.

Position it behind a chair, beside a plant, or in the corner furthest from the bed.

5. Add Fairy Lights Along a Shelf or Headboard

A single strand of warm white fairy lights along a shelf, draped over a headboard, or tucked behind a mirror adds a soft, ambient glow. Use battery-powered lights to avoid visible cords.

Warm white (2200–2700K) fairy lights look far more atmospheric than cool white ones.

6. Use a Table Lamp on a Dresser or Desk

A small table lamp on a dresser or desk adds a light source at a different height from the bedside lamps. It also makes the dresser or desk feel like a considered part of the room rather than just a functional surface.

Use a lamp with a warm bulb and a shade that casts light downward and outward.

7. Add a Wall Sconce Above the Bed

A wall-mounted sconce above each side of the bed frees up the bedside table surface and creates a cleaner look. Plug-in sconces are available for rooms where hardwiring is not practical.

Position the sconce so the light falls on the book or phone rather than directly in the eyes.

8. Use a Salt Lamp for Ambient Glow

A Himalayan salt lamp emits a warm, amber glow that is too dim for reading but perfect as a night light or ambient accent. It works well on a bedside table or dresser.

Salt lamps absorb moisture — keep them away from humid areas and wipe them down occasionally.

9. Add LED Strip Lights Behind the Headboard

LED strip lights mounted behind the headboard or along the back of a floating shelf create a warm halo effect. Use warm white strips rather than color-changing ones for a bedroom.

Conceal the power cable behind the headboard or along the baseboard.

10. Use a Pendant Light Instead of a Ceiling Fixture

A pendant light hung from the ceiling — especially one with a fabric shade — creates a warmer, more intimate feel than a standard ceiling fixture. It also adds visual interest to the ceiling.

Hang it low enough to be effective but high enough not to be a hazard.

11. Add Candles for the Warmest Light

Real candles produce the warmest, most flattering light of any source. A few pillar candles on a tray or a cluster of tea lights on the dresser create an atmosphere that no electric light can replicate.

Use flameless LED candles in bedrooms where open flames are not practical.

12. Use a Clip-On Reading Light

A clip-on reading light attached to the headboard or bedside table provides focused task light without disturbing a partner. Choose one with a warm bulb and an adjustable arm.

This is a good solution for bedrooms where wall sconces are not practical.

13. Add a Lantern on the Floor

A floor lantern — a glass lantern with a candle or LED inside — adds a warm, low light source that creates atmosphere without taking up surface space. Place it beside the bed, in a corner, or on the floor beside a plant.

Use a battery-powered LED candle inside for a safe, low-maintenance option.

14. Use a Smart Bulb for Scene Control

A smart bulb in the bedside lamp lets you set a warm, dim scene for evenings and a brighter scene for mornings. Most smart bulbs can be controlled by voice or phone and set to change automatically at a scheduled time.

Start with one smart bulb in the most-used lamp before investing in a full system.

15. Add a Neon or LED Sign for Accent Light

A small neon or LED sign adds a warm accent light and a personal touch. Use warm white or amber rather than a bright color for a bedroom. Position it on a shelf or wall where it adds light to a dark area.

Keep it on a timer so it turns off automatically at night.

16. Use a Lava Lamp or Novelty Light for a Relaxed Mood

A lava lamp or a novelty light — a moon lamp, a cloud light, or a star projector — adds a playful, relaxed quality to a bedroom. These work particularly well in children’s and teenage bedrooms.

Use them as accent lights rather than primary sources.

17. Layer All Three Sources Every Evening

The goal is always three layers: overhead (dimmed low), bedside (warm and soft), and a third source (floor lamp, fairy lights, or candles). When all three are on at low levels, the room feels warm, layered, and genuinely cozy.

Turn off the overhead light first and see how the room feels with just the lower sources.

Final Thoughts

Cozy bedroom lighting is not about buying expensive fixtures. It is about layering multiple warm sources at different heights and keeping the overhead light low in the evenings. Start with a dimmer switch and a warm bulb in the bedside lamp — those two changes alone will transform the room.

If you are looking for cozy Christmas living room ideas, the best place to start is with function rather than decoration. A room feels better when the layout is easy to use, storage has a clear purpose, and the styling supports everyday life instead of getting in the way.

The ideas below are designed to be practical for real homes. You do not need to use every idea. Choose the changes that suit your space and your normal decor first, then build from there.

1. Start With the Tree Placement

Decide where the tree will go before adding any other decorations. Position it where it can be seen from the main seating area without blocking a walkway or door.

Choose pieces that are easy to store and that work with your normal decor.

2. Use Warm White Lights

Warm white lights throughout the room — on the tree, in garlands, and in lanterns — create a consistent, cozy atmosphere. Avoid mixing warm and cool white lights in the same space.

For cozy rooms, warm-white bulbs around 2700K are a useful starting point.

3. Layer Greenery Across One Main Surface

A garland of real or faux greenery across the mantel, console, or coffee table creates a strong seasonal impression before you add a single ornament.

Group a small number of items together and leave visible empty space so the surface can still do its real job.

4. Add a Basket of Holiday Throws

A large basket beside the sofa holds extra blankets and adds natural texture. It is useful decor rather than purely decorative decor.

Use labels only where they genuinely help.

5. Choose a Simple Holiday Color Palette

Red and green, gold and cream, or silver and white are classic combinations. Choose one and repeat it through the whole room rather than mixing multiple holiday color schemes.

A common mistake is introducing a different strong color in every object.

6. Start With Warm String Lights

String lights draped over a bookcase, around a window, or along a mantel add warmth and atmosphere before any other decoration is added.

For cozy rooms, warm-white bulbs around 2700K are a useful starting point.

7. Add Greenery Before Ornaments

Layer greenery first — garlands, wreaths, and branches — then add ornaments and decorative objects on top. This creates a more natural, layered look.

Choose pieces that are easy to store and that work with your normal decor.

8. Use a Few Meaningful Decorations

A handful of meaningful ornaments or decorations creates more atmosphere than a room full of generic seasonal products. Choose pieces with personal significance or that you genuinely love.

Choose pieces that are easy to store and that work with your normal decor.

9. Layer Cozy Throws and Cushions

Swapping cushion covers for holiday versions and adding a warm throw to the sofa is one of the fastest ways to make a living room feel festive.

Choose washable or easy-care materials in high-use areas.

10. Add a Small Wreath

A wreath on the wall, above the fireplace, or on a door adds a classic seasonal note without taking up any surface space.

Choose pieces that are easy to store and that work with your normal decor.

11. Style One Main Surface

Choose one surface — the mantel, coffee table, or console — and style it as the seasonal focal point. Keep the rest of the room calm.

Group a small number of items together and leave visible empty space so the surface can still do its real job.

12. Use Natural Wood and Woven Texture

Wood trays, woven baskets, and natural fiber textiles add warmth and texture without looking overtly themed. They also transition easily into January decor.

Choose washable or easy-care materials in high-use areas.

13. Add Candles or Flameless Candles

Candles add movement and warm light, especially on darker evenings. Use a stable tray and keep flames away from greenery, throws, and children or pets.

Flameless LED candles are a good alternative when open flames are not practical.

14. Use Ribbon to Update Existing Decor

A length of velvet or satin ribbon tied around a vase, lamp base, or picture frame adds a seasonal touch without buying new decorations.

Choose pieces that are easy to store and that work with your normal decor.

15. Create a Small Holiday Tray

A tray containing a candle, a small ornament, and a sprig of greenery keeps the seasonal display contained and easy to move.

A tray is useful because the whole group can be moved at once.

16. Add Mini Trees in Tight Spaces

A small tabletop tree on a side table, bookcase, or windowsill adds a festive note in a space too small for a full-size tree.

Choose pieces that are easy to store and that work with your normal decor.

17. Use Garland Without Overfilling the Room

A single garland on the mantel or staircase is usually enough. Adding garland to every surface can make the room feel cluttered rather than festive.

Choose pieces that are easy to store and that work with your normal decor.

18. Add One Festive Artwork Print

A framed holiday print swapped into an existing frame adds a seasonal note without buying new decor. Choose a simple design that suits your existing color palette.

Choose pieces that are easy to store and that work with your normal decor.

19. Bring in Pinecones or Dried Orange

A bowl of pinecones or dried orange slices adds natural texture and a subtle seasonal scent. Both are inexpensive and easy to store between seasons.

Choose pieces that are easy to store and that work with your normal decor.

20. Keep the Main Walkway Clear

Seasonal decorations should never block the main walkway through the living room. Keep the path between the entrance and the main seating area clear.

Choose pieces that are easy to store and that work with your normal decor.

21. Use Vertical Space for Decor

Tall arrangements, wall-mounted wreaths, and hanging ornaments use vertical space rather than surface space. This is especially useful in a small living room.

Measure the wall before drilling or ordering storage.

Final Thoughts

The strongest cozy Christmas living room ideas are the ones that make the room feel warm and inviting, not simply more decorated. Start with lighting and greenery, choose one focal point, and keep enough empty space for the room to feel comfortable. Small, deliberate improvements are usually more successful than changing everything at once.

15 Cream Bedroom Ideas for a Soft, Calm Look

Create a soft, calm bedroom with 15 cream bedroom ideas covering paint, bedding, furniture, texture, and accent colors that keep the room warm and inviting.

The short version

  • Cream works best when paired with warm wood, natural linen, and soft textures.
  • Use different shades of cream across walls, bedding, and furniture to add depth.
  • Warm lighting at 2700K prevents cream from looking yellow or flat.
  • Add one or two accent colors — dusty rose, sage, or terracotta — to prevent the room from feeling bland.

A cream bedroom is one of the most versatile and enduring choices in interior design. It is warm without being yellow, neutral without being cold, and it works with almost every accent color and material.

The challenge is making it feel layered and interesting rather than flat and bland. These ideas show how to use cream effectively across walls, bedding, furniture, and accessories.

1. Use Warm Cream on the Walls

Choose a warm cream with a yellow or pink undertone rather than a cool cream with a grey undertone. Cool creams can look clinical under artificial light. Test the paint in the room before committing — cream shades vary significantly between brands.

Apply the paint in the room’s natural light and check it at different times of day.

2. Layer Different Shades of Cream

Using the same shade of cream on every surface makes the room look flat. Layer slightly different shades — a warmer cream on the walls, a cooler linen on the bedding, a natural cotton on the curtains — to add depth.

The variation between shades creates visual interest without introducing a new color.

3. Add Warm Wood Furniture

Warm wood — oak, pine, or walnut — is the natural partner for cream. It adds warmth and a natural quality that prevents the room from feeling sterile. A wooden bed frame, wooden bedside tables, or a wooden dresser all work well.

Avoid mixing too many wood tones — choose one and repeat it.

4. Use Linen Bedding

Linen bedding in a natural or undyed cream is the most effective way to add texture to a cream bedroom. Linen has a slightly rumpled, relaxed quality that suits the softness of cream walls.

Linen softens with every wash — it looks better after a few months than it does when new.

5. Add a Textured Throw

A chunky knit, waffle-weave, or boucle throw in cream, oatmeal, or a soft accent color adds texture and warmth to the bed. Drape it loosely over the foot of the bed rather than folding it flat.

A throw in a slightly different shade of cream adds depth without introducing a new color.

6. Use Warm Lighting

Cream walls look their best under warm lighting at 2700K. Cool white light makes cream look yellow and flat. Use warm bulbs in every light source in the room.

A dimmer switch on the overhead light lets you adjust the warmth of the room in the evening.

7. Add a Dusty Rose or Terracotta Accent

A single accent color — dusty rose, terracotta, sage, or warm rust — prevents a cream bedroom from feeling bland. Use it in cushions, a throw, a lamp shade, or a piece of art.

Keep the accent to 10% of the room’s color — one or two pieces is enough.

8. Use Cream Curtains With Texture

Cream linen or cotton curtains add softness and warmth to the window area. Choose a fabric with a slight texture — a loose weave or a subtle pattern — rather than a flat, shiny fabric.

Hang them high and wide — rod 4–6 inches above the frame, extending 6–10 inches past each side.

9. Add a Natural Fiber Rug

A jute, sisal, or wool rug in a natural or cream tone adds texture to the floor and grounds the room. Choose a rug that extends at least 18 inches beyond the sides and foot of the bed.

Natural fiber rugs are durable and improve with age.

10. Use Rattan or Wicker Accessories

Rattan and wicker accessories — a lamp base, a mirror frame, a small basket — add a natural, organic quality that suits a cream bedroom. They also add texture without introducing a strong color.

One or two rattan pieces are enough — more can start to feel like a beach house.

11. Add Dried Flowers or Pampas Grass

Dried flowers, pampas grass, or dried seed heads in a simple vase add a natural, textural element that suits a cream bedroom. They last for months and require no maintenance.

Use a ceramic or terracotta vase rather than a glass one for a warmer look.

12. Keep the Ceiling Cream or White

A cream ceiling in a slightly lighter shade than the walls creates a seamless, enveloping effect. A white ceiling on cream walls creates a clean contrast that makes the ceiling feel higher.

Avoid a dark ceiling in a cream bedroom — it works against the softness of the palette.

13. Use Cream and White Together

Cream and white work well together when the shades are clearly different. Use white for trim, skirting boards, and door frames, and cream for the walls. This creates a clean, layered look.

Avoid using cream and white in shades that are too similar — the difference will look like a mistake rather than a choice.

14. Add a Soft Sage or Olive Green Plant

A plant in a soft sage or olive green adds a natural accent color that suits cream perfectly. A snake plant, a pothos, or a small olive tree all work well in a cream bedroom.

Use a simple ceramic pot in cream, white, or terracotta.

15. Keep the Room Uncluttered

A cream bedroom looks its best when the surfaces are clear and the room is uncluttered. Cream is a color that shows mess more than darker colors — a few well-chosen objects look far better than a crowded surface.

Edit the room regularly and remove anything that does not contribute to the calm, soft quality of the space.

Final Thoughts

A cream bedroom works when the shades are layered, the textures are varied, and the lighting is warm. Start with the wall color and the bedding, then add wood, linen, and one or two accent colors. The goal is a room that feels soft and inviting rather than plain and empty.

DIY outdoor Halloween decor does not require a workshop or a large budget. Most of the ideas below use materials from the craft store, the garden, or the recycling bin, and the majority can be finished in an afternoon.

Start with one or two projects rather than attempting everything at once. A few well-made pieces look better than a yard full of rushed ones.

1. Make Paper Bag Luminaries

Fill brown paper bags with a few inches of sand or gravel, cut simple shapes into the sides — a jack-o-lantern face, a bat, a moon — and drop a battery tea light inside. Line them along a path or porch steps.

Use battery tea lights rather than real candles to avoid fire risk.

2. Hang Cheesecloth Ghosts from a Tree

Cut cheesecloth into large squares, drape over a foam ball or crumpled newspaper, tie at the neck, and hang from a tree branch with fishing line. The fabric moves in the breeze, which adds to the effect.

Use white or off-white cheesecloth — it photographs better than bright white.

3. Spray-Paint Dollar-Store Skulls

Foam or plastic skulls from the dollar store look far more convincing after a coat of matte black or aged-bronze spray paint. Arrange them in a cluster on the porch steps or along a garden wall.

Apply a second coat of dark brown in the eye sockets for depth.

4. Bundle Dried Corn Stalks

Tie bundles of dried corn stalks to porch posts or fence posts with twine. Add a few dried gourds at the base. This is one of the most traditional outdoor Halloween looks and costs almost nothing if you have a garden center nearby.

Secure the bundles tightly — they catch wind easily.

5. Make a Stuffed Scarecrow

Stuff old clothes with newspaper or plastic bags, add a carved pumpkin or paper-mache head, and prop it in a chair on the porch. A hat and a pair of boots complete the look.

Use clothes you were going to donate rather than buying new ones.

6. Paint Rocks as Pumpkins

Collect smooth rocks and paint them orange with black jack-o-lantern faces. Arrange them along a path, in a planter, or on porch steps. They are weatherproof, reusable, and cost almost nothing.

Seal with outdoor matte varnish so the paint lasts through rain.

7. Make a Witch Hat Pathway

Cut large witch hat shapes from black foam board or cardboard, seal with outdoor spray paint, and stake them into the lawn along the path to the front door. Space them evenly for the most graphic effect.

Reinforce the base with a wooden skewer pushed through the foam.

8. Create a Graveyard with Foam Headstones

Cut headstone shapes from foam insulation board, paint them grey, add names and dates with black paint, and stake them into the lawn. A small graveyard of five or six stones is enough — more starts to look cluttered.

Use a serrated knife to cut foam insulation board cleanly.

9. Hang a Bat Swarm on the Fence

Cut bat shapes from black card or foam sheet, punch a hole in each, and hang them from a fence or trellis with black thread at different heights. A swarm of twenty or thirty bats costs almost nothing and photographs well.

Vary the sizes for a more natural look.

10. Make a Hay Bale Display

Stack two or three hay bales near the front door and arrange pumpkins, gourds, and a scarecrow on top. Hay bales are inexpensive at garden centers in autumn and can be composted after the season.

Place a tarp underneath to protect the porch surface.

11. Wrap Trees in Orange Fairy Lights

Wrap the trunk and lower branches of a tree or large shrub in orange or warm amber fairy lights. Use solar-powered or battery-powered lights to avoid running extension cords across the yard.

Solar lights need a few hours of direct sun to charge fully.

12. Make a Cauldron Centerpiece

Paint a large plastic pot or bucket black, add a few dry ice pellets or a battery-powered fog machine insert, and surround it with pumpkins and dark branches. It works as a porch centerpiece or a yard focal point.

Handle dry ice with gloves — it burns skin on contact.

13. Carve a Pumpkin Totem Pole

Stack three carved pumpkins of decreasing size on a wooden stake driven into the ground. Each pumpkin gets a different face. The totem pole shape is more graphic than a single pumpkin and takes up very little ground space.

Use a long wooden dowel or a piece of rebar as the stake.

14. Make a Spider Web from Yarn

Stretch black yarn between two fence posts or porch columns in a web pattern, securing each strand with a small nail or staple. Add a few plastic spiders. A large web is one of the most dramatic outdoor Halloween effects for the cost.

Use outdoor-rated staples or small cup hooks to avoid rust marks.

15. Create a Mummy Door

Wrap the front door in white crepe paper or strips of white fabric in a mummy pattern, leaving a gap for the peephole. Add two large googly eyes cut from card. It takes about twenty minutes and costs almost nothing.

Use painter’s tape to attach the strips so the door paint is not damaged.

16. Line the Path with Glowing Jars

Fill glass jars with battery fairy lights or glow sticks and line them along the path to the front door. Use orange, green, or white lights depending on the look you want. The jars can be reused for other seasonal displays.

Seal the lids loosely so the battery pack can be accessed easily.

Final Thoughts

The best DIY outdoor Halloween decor is the kind that looks intentional rather than rushed. Start with one or two projects, use materials you already have where possible, and seal anything painted so it survives the weather. A few well-made pieces always outperform a yard full of cheap store-bought props.

Still wondering

Common questions

What are the easiest DIY outdoor Halloween decorations for beginners?

Paper bag luminaries, cheesecloth ghosts hung from a tree, and painted pumpkins are the easiest starting points. Each takes under an hour, costs under five dollars, and requires no special tools. They also pack flat, which makes storage simple at the end of the season.

How do you make outdoor Halloween decorations that survive rain?

Seal painted surfaces with an outdoor matte varnish spray. Use plastic or foam bases rather than paper for anything left out overnight. Battery-powered lights in a sealed compartment handle light rain. Bring paper luminaries and fabric ghosts inside if heavy rain is forecast.

Ceramic Planters Without the Kiln (Or The Price Tag)

Designer ceramic planters run $40-$150 each, and they’re everywhere right now. But here’s what nobody tells you: you can make versions nearly indistinguishable from the real thing with air-dry clay and basic tools.

This project costs about $8-12 per planter and takes 2-3 hours start to finish (including drying time). Let’s make some.

What You’ll Need

Materials:

  • Air-dry clay (we use Faber-Castell because it’s fine-textured)
  • Water in a spray bottle
  • Ceramic glaze or acrylic sealer
  • Acrylic paint (optional, for color variations)
  • Drainage insert or small plastic pot to fit inside

Tools:

  • Rolling pin or dowel
  • Cutting mat or ceramic board
  • Butter knife or modeling knife
  • Sponge
  • Ruler
  • Thumbprint texture tool (optional; a real ceramic thumb works too)

Pro tip: You don’t need a pottery wheel. Modern ceramic aesthetic is all about the handmade imperfections anyway.

Method 1: Hand-Pinch Pot (Best For Beginners)

This is the fastest route and works great for small-to-medium planters.

Step 1: The Ball

Roll out a ball of clay about 3 inches in diameter. Make it smooth and even.

Step 2: The Hole

Push your thumb into the center of the ball, leaving about 1/2-inch at the base for drainage to sit.

Step 3: Pinch and Rotate

Gently pinch the walls between thumb (inside) and fingers (outside). Rotate the ball as you pinch so the walls get thinner and taller evenly. This should take 5-7 minutes per planter. Your walls should be about 1/4-inch thick.

Step 4: The Rim

When you’ve reached your desired height (usually 3-4 inches), smooth the rim with wet fingers. This is a detail that separates DIY from designer.

Step 5: Texture (Optional)

Press your thumbprint or a texture tool around the exterior if you want that hand-thrown look. Planters with thumbprint patterns are having a moment, and for good reason—they hide minor imperfections.

Step 6: Drying

Place your planter upside-down on parchment paper (prevents cracking). Air-dry for 48 hours.

Method 2: Coil-Built Modern (Best For Larger Planters)

If you want to make a statement planter 6+ inches tall, coil-building is your move.

Step 1: Roll Coils

Roll out “snakes” of clay about 1/2-inch thick and 6-8 inches long. You’ll need 5-8 coils depending on height.

Step 2: Build the Base

Flatten a disk of clay (about 4 inches diameter) to be your base. Score the top with a fork—this helps the first coil stick.

Step 3: Stack and Blend

Attach the first coil around the edge of your base, overlapping slightly. Blend the inner seams with your fingers (leave outer seams for texture if you like). Add coils on top, spiraling up.

Step 4: Shape and Smooth

As you stack, gently shape the walls to angle inward (for a planted flower pot look) or outward (for a modern vase). Smooth the exterior with a wet sponge.

Step 5: The Finish

Craft an intentional rim: smooth, or slightly flared, or with a subtle lip. Details matter.

Step 6: Drying

Again, upside-down on parchment for 48 hours.

Finishing & Sealing

After 48 hours, your planters are bone-dry. Now the fun part.

Option A: Glaze Finish (Looks Most Like Ceramic)

Use a matte ceramic glaze designed for air-dry clay. Brush on 2-3 thin coats, sanding lightly between coats. This creates a subtle, sophisticated finish.

Our favorite glazes:

  • Cool Ash Gray (contemporary, goes with everything)
  • Warm Terracotta (earthy, timeless)
  • Soft Sage (trend-proof)

Option B: Acrylic + Sealer (More Control)

Paint your air-dry pot with acrylic paint (great for solid colors or subtle patterns), then seal with matte polyurethane or polycrylic. This is also cheaper and safer for homes with kids/pets who might chew on plants.

Drainage

Before sealing, drill a small hole (1/4-inch) in the base if your clay is thick enough. Use a ceramic bit and go slow. Or, place a small plastic nursery pot inside your planter and rest your actual plant on top—zero drainage headaches, and it looks seamless.

Displaying Your Collection

Three planters of different heights, staggered on a shelf or window ledge, look curated. Plant them with:

  • Snake plants (trendy, low-maintenance)
  • Pothos (cascading, dramatic)
  • Monstera cuttings propagating in water (Instagram gold)

A grouping of handmade planters with living plants is the aesthetic equivalent of a Scandinavian pottery gallery. And nobody has to know you made them.

Troubleshooting

Cracking during drying? Air-dry clay sometimes stress-cracks. This is normal. Sand the crack smooth after it’s fully dry, paint over it, and seal. It adds to the handmade charm.

Walls are uneven? This is not a flaw; it’s texture. The irregular thickness is what makes them look genuine.

Paint looks too flat? Layer two colors. Paint the first coat, let it dry, then dry-brush a second shade over highlights. This creates depth and looks expensive.

Cost Breakdown

  • Air-dry clay (enough for 3-4 planters): $6
  • Glazes or paint: $4
  • Tools (one-time): $15
  • Sealant: $8

Per planter cost: $8.25 Retail equivalent: $60-80

That’s about a 75% savings on premium ceramic planters. And they’re 100% unique because you made them.

DIY Floating Shelves That Hold Real Weight

Most floating shelf tutorials skip the part that matters: the bracket and the fixing. Here is how to build shelves that carry books, not just candles.

A floating shelf is a simple object with one hard problem: everything about how it holds itself up is hidden, so the failure mode is a shelf full of books ending up on the floor at 3am. Most tutorials online show you a lovely piece of oak and gloss over the two things that determine whether it stays on the wall — the bracket and the fixing.

This is the version that holds. Two shelves, about £45 in materials, a Saturday.

Understand the load first

A floating shelf is a cantilever. All the downward force on the shelf becomes a rotating force trying to pull the top of the bracket out of the wall and push the bottom into it. Two consequences follow:

  • Depth is the enemy. Doubling the shelf depth roughly doubles the leverage on your fixings. A 20cm shelf is trivial to support; a 40cm shelf is four times the problem it looks like.
  • The top fixing does the work. It is in pure tension — being pulled straight out of the wall. That is the fixing that fails.

Practical limits, for a shelf on a solid bracket into a sound wall:

Depth Realistic load per 1m of shelf
15cm 25–30kg
20cm 18–22kg
25cm 12–15kg
30cm+ Use a supported shelf instead

For reference, a metre of paperbacks is about 15kg; a metre of hardbacks is 25–30kg. If you want a metre of hardbacks, you want a 15–20cm shelf and very good fixings.

Materials

For two shelves, 90cm × 20cm:

  • 1 length of 20mm oak or pine board, 90cm × 20cm × 2 — around £25
  • 1 length of 44×20mm softwood batten for the cleats
  • Wood screws, 5×80mm
  • Fixings appropriate to your wall (see below) — this is not the place to economise
  • Wood glue, 120- and 180-grit paper, finishing oil or wax

Tools: drill/driver, spirit level, stud detector, tape, saw, countersink bit, pencil.

Choose the right fixing for your wall

This is the step that decides everything. Knock on the wall: a dull thud is masonry, a hollow sound is plasterboard.

Into masonry (brick, block, concrete): an 8mm masonry bit and a good nylon plug with a 5×80mm screw. Drill into the brick, not the mortar — mortar crumbles under tension. Easily strong enough for anything on the table above.

Into timber studs behind plasterboard: the best case. Find the studs with a detector, confirm with a small pilot hole, and screw straight into the timber with a 5×80mm screw. Studs are usually at 400mm or 600mm centres, so a 90cm shelf will catch two.

Into plasterboard with no stud: this is where shelves fail. Plastic wall anchors are not adequate. Use either:

  • Metal toggle fixings (Grip-It, Snaptoggle) — genuinely strong, roughly 20–30kg each in 12.5mm board
  • Heavy-duty spring toggles — strong, but need a large hole

Never hang a book shelf on plasterboard fixings alone if you can reach a stud instead. If you cannot, halve the load figures in the table.

If you take one thing from this: find the studs. A £12 detector is the difference between a shelf that holds books and a shelf that holds a candle.

Build the cleat

The cleat is a batten fixed to the wall that the hollow shelf slides over. For a solid-board shelf like this one, we use a simpler L-cleat and route a groove — or, easier, screw up through the cleat into the underside of the board.

Method (simple, strong, beginner-friendly):

  1. Cut the cleat to 4cm shorter than the shelf, so it stays invisible from the sides.
  2. Mark your line. Measure up from the floor at both ends — never assume the floor is level — then draw the line with a spirit level and check it twice. A shelf 3mm out of level is visible from across the room.
  3. Mark fixing points on the line at your stud positions, or at 30cm intervals into masonry. Minimum three fixings on a 90cm shelf.
  4. Drill the cleat with clearance holes and countersink them.
  5. Drill the wall, plug if needed, and fix the cleat. Check level again before the last screw goes fully in.
  6. Test it. Hang your full body weight off the cleat. Seriously — better it fails now than loaded with your books.

Fit the shelf

  1. Sand the board — 120 grit, then 180, always with the grain. Ease the front edge and the corners slightly; a sharp arris looks unfinished and chips.
  2. Finish before fitting. Two coats of hardwax oil, thin, with a light 240-grit sand between. Doing this off the wall is far easier and gives a better result.
  3. Sit the board on the cleat, push it back flush to the wall.
  4. Fix from underneath: three 40mm screws up through the cleat into the underside of the shelf. Invisible, and stops the shelf lifting or sliding.
  5. Optional: a bead of wood glue along the top of the cleat before fitting, if you never intend to remove it.

Getting the spacing right

Two shelves need a considered gap or they look like an accident.

  • Between shelves: 30–35cm for books, 40cm if you want to stand things on the lower one
  • Above a sofa: the lowest shelf at least 25cm above the sofa back, so heads do not meet it
  • Above a desk: 45–50cm above the desktop
  • Length: shelves look best either matching the width of the furniture below, or clearly wider — never 10cm wider, which reads as a mistake

Styling them so they do not look cluttered

The same rules from our open shelving guide apply: cluster in odd groups, leave roughly a third of the run empty, vary the height.

The quick version for a two-shelf run:

  • Books stacked horizontally in one place, upright in another — the horizontal stack doubles as a plinth
  • One object taller than everything else, positioned off-centre
  • One trailing plant, at the end, so it breaks the horizontal line
  • Genuine empty space at one end of each shelf

Troubleshooting

The shelf sags in the middle. The board is too thin or the span too long. 20mm board should not exceed about 90cm unsupported; beyond that, go to 27mm or add a fixing.

It tips forward at the front edge. The cleat is too shallow relative to the shelf depth. The cleat should be at least half the shelf depth.

There is a gap between shelf and wall. The wall is not flat — very few are. Scribe the back edge of the board to the wall with a compass and plane it, or run a thin bead of decorator’s caulk and paint it in.

The screws spin without biting. You are in mortar or a failed plasterboard hole. Move 5cm along and use a proper toggle. Do not fill the hole and re-drill the same spot.

Cost breakdown

  • Oak board (2 shelves): £25
  • Batten and screws: £6
  • Toggle fixings or masonry plugs: £8
  • Hardwax oil (enough for many projects): £14

Total: around £53, or roughly £26 per shelf. Comparable ready-made solid oak floating shelves run £45–£70 each — and most of them are veneered MDF.

Once they are up, the hard part is not filling them. Our open shelving styling guide covers the 70/30 rule that keeps a shelf looking curated.

17 Elegant Halloween Decor Ideas for a Sophisticated Home

Create a stylish seasonal display with 17 elegant Halloween decor ideas using muted palettes, matte pumpkins, taper candles, and restrained styling.

  • Choose a restrained palette of black, cream, and muted orange rather than bright primary colors.

  • Create one spooky focal point and keep the rest of the room calm.
  • Choose pieces that store flat and work with your normal decor to keep costs low.

Elegant Halloween decor is about restraint. A few well-chosen pieces in a limited palette create more atmosphere than a room covered in themed products. The goal is to bring in the season without making the space feel like a temporary display.

The ideas below are designed to be practical for real homes. You do not need to use every idea. Choose the changes that suit your space and your normal decor first, then build from there.

1. Use Black, Cream, and Muted Orange

A palette of black, cream, and muted orange reads as Halloween without the garish brightness of primary colors. Repeat these three tones through candles, pumpkins, textiles, and small accessories.

A common mistake is introducing a different strong color in every object. A limited palette usually feels larger, calmer, and easier to update later.

2. Choose Matte Pumpkins

Matte-finish pumpkins in cream, sage, charcoal, or terracotta suit a neutral interior far better than shiny orange ones. Group two or three together rather than spreading them across every surface.

Choose pieces that are easy to store and that work with your normal decor.

3. Use Taper Candles for Height

Black or cream taper candles in simple candlesticks add height and drama without taking up much surface area. Use a stable base and keep flames away from dried materials and textiles.

Flameless LED tapers are a good alternative when open flames are not practical.

4. Add One Moody Floral Arrangement

Dark dahlias, dried grasses, black-dyed stems, or deep burgundy flowers in a ceramic vase create a striking seasonal arrangement. Use one large arrangement rather than several small ones.

Choose pieces that are easy to store and that work with your normal decor.

5. Choose a Restrained Color Palette

Start with one calm base and repeat one or two accent colors through smaller items such as cushions, art, candles, or accessories. A common mistake is introducing a different strong color in every object.

In a small room, a limited palette usually feels larger, calmer, and easier to update later.

6. Use Pumpkins in Different Sizes

Grouping pumpkins of different heights and sizes creates a more natural, editorial look than a row of identical ones. Mix real, ceramic, and fabric pumpkins to reduce yearly waste.

Choose pieces that are easy to store and that work with your normal decor.

7. Add Black Candles or Flameless Candles

Black candles are one of the simplest ways to signal the season without adding themed products. Use them in existing candlesticks or lanterns you already own.

Choose pieces that are easy to store and that work with your normal decor.

8. Create One Spooky Focal Point

Rather than decorating every surface, choose one area — a mantel, console table, or dining table — and make it the seasonal focal point. Keep the rest of the room calm.

Repeat a few materials and colors instead of using many unrelated decorations.

9. Use Dried Branches in a Tall Vase

A few bare or dark-painted branches in a tall vase add height and a slightly eerie quality without any obvious Halloween imagery. They also last the entire season.

Choose pieces that are easy to store and that work with your normal decor.

10. Add a Simple Black Garland

A thin black garland of leaves, stars, or geometric shapes adds a subtle seasonal note to a mantel, shelf, or staircase without overwhelming the space.

Choose pieces that are easy to store and that work with your normal decor.

11. Decorate With Vintage-Inspired Prints

A framed vintage-style print of a moon, botanical skull, or dark landscape adds atmosphere without looking childish. Swap it into an existing frame you already own.

Choose pieces that are easy to store and that work with your normal decor.

12. Use Dark Linen or Velvet Textiles

Swapping a cushion cover or throw for a dark linen, velvet, or jacquard version adds seasonal depth without any obvious Halloween imagery. Choose charcoal, deep plum, or forest green.

Choose washable or easy-care materials in high-use areas.

13. Style a Coffee Table Tray

A tray containing a candle, a small pumpkin, and one or two dark objects keeps the seasonal display contained and easy to move. Leave enough empty surface for everyday use.

A tray is useful because the whole group can be moved at once.

14. Add Subtle Skeleton Details

A small ceramic skull, a skeleton hand holding a candle, or a single skeleton figurine adds a touch of Halloween without dominating the room. Use one or two pieces rather than a collection.

Choose pieces that are easy to store and that work with your normal decor.

15. Use Warm Amber Lighting

Warm amber bulbs or candles create a moody atmosphere that suits Halloween without any additional decoration. Swap a standard bulb for an amber one in a lamp you already own.

For cozy rooms, warm-white bulbs around 2700K are a useful starting point.

16. Decorate the Entryway First

The entryway is the first thing guests see and the last thing you see when you leave. A wreath, a pumpkin, and one candle lantern can create a strong seasonal impression without decorating the whole house.

Choose pieces that are easy to store and that work with your normal decor.

17. Add a Few Paper Bats to One Wall

Cut-paper or card bats arranged on one wall add a playful seasonal note that is easy to remove and costs almost nothing. Keep the arrangement loose and asymmetric for a more editorial look.

In rentals, removable adhesive strips mean no damage to walls.

Final Thoughts

The strongest elegant Halloween decor is the kind that makes the room feel atmospheric rather than themed. Start with a restrained palette, choose one focal point, and add a few well-chosen pieces that work with your existing decor. Small, deliberate choices are usually more successful than covering every surface.

Entryway Storage Ideas for Shoes, Coats and Keys

Practical entryway storage ideas that handle shoes, coats, bags and keys without cluttering a small hall — with real measurements and renter-friendly options.
