Entryway clutter isn’t a storage problem. It’s a landing problem — everyone walks in holding four things and there’s nowhere obvious to put any of them.

Good entryway storage gives each of those four things a home within arm’s reach of the door. Here’s how to build that, whether you own the place or you’re renting and can’t drill anything.

Start by counting what actually lands there

Before buying anything, stand at your door and list what you’re holding when you walk in. For most households it’s:

  • Shoes (the biggest space hog)
  • One coat or jacket per person
  • A bag, backpack or purse
  • Keys, phone, wallet
  • Mail and packages

Design for those five. Storing every coat you own in the entry is what makes entries fail.

Shoe storage that actually contains the mess

Tilt-out shoe cabinet — about 9 inches deep, holds 9–15 pairs, and the closed front is what makes it work. Nothing looks tidier than shoes you can’t see. Best option if you have 24+ inches of wall.

Two-tier open rack — cheap, holds 8 pairs, fits under most console tables. Open storage means it looks messy unless you’re disciplined about it.

Boot tray — a rimmed tray by the door for wet or muddy shoes. Costs almost nothing and stops half your floor cleaning problems.

Under-bench baskets — if you have a bench, two woven baskets underneath hold shoes out of sight and look intentional.

One rule that matters more than which you pick: set a capacity and stick to it. When the shoe storage is full, shoes go to the bedroom. Storage that expands infinitely becomes a pile.

Coat storage without a closet

Most small entries have no coat closet. Hooks solve it better than a rack.

Hook height matters. Mount adult hooks at 60–66 inches from the floor. Kid hooks at 40 inches so children actually use them instead of dropping coats.

Space hooks 8–10 inches apart. Closer than that and coats bunch into one lump.

Two rows beat one long row in a narrow hall — a rail at 66 inches for coats and a second at 44 inches for bags and kids’ things.

For renters: adhesive hooks rated for 5+ lbs handle a jacket fine but not a wet winter coat. A freestanding coat rack with a weighted base, or an over-the-door hook rail, gives you real capacity with no holes.

The key and mail drop zone

This is the smallest piece of the puzzle and the one that fails most often, because keys need to land immediately — not two steps into the room.

Mount a small shelf, bowl or wall pocket within one arm’s reach of the door handle. That’s the whole trick. Anything further away and people carry their keys into the kitchen.

A wall-mounted mail sorter beside it handles post. Give it a rule: sorted every Sunday, nothing lives there longer than a week.

Bag and backpack storage

Bags are heavy and awkward and they end up on the floor. Two things fix it:

Heavy-duty hooks at 44 inches — low enough that a loaded backpack doesn’t need lifting, rated for 15+ lbs.

A bench with a cubby — one cubby per person. School bags go in, not on the floor. This single change transforms weekday mornings in a house with kids.

Storage furniture worth the money

Storage bench — seating plus a lift-top or cubbies underneath. Needs about 40 inches of wall. The most useful single piece for an entry.

Hall tree — hooks, bench and shoe storage in one unit. Great for a wall with nothing else on it, but check the depth; many are 16+ inches and will crowd a narrow hall.

Narrow console with drawers — drawers for keys, gloves and dog leads, open shelf below for baskets. Look for 10–12 inch depth.

Slim cabinet — closed storage hides everything. Best choice if visual calm matters more to you than grab-and-go speed.

Renter-friendly options

If you can’t drill:

  • Freestanding shoe cabinet — no mounting needed
  • Over-the-door hook rail — instant coat storage
  • Command-style hooks — fine for light jackets and keys, not for heavy coats
  • Tension rod inside a nook with hanging baskets
  • Leaning ladder shelf for baskets and bags
  • Rolling cart tucked beside the door

None of these leave a mark, and all of them come with you when you move.

Small entry, no wall space?

If your door opens straight into the living room with no dedicated wall at all:

  • Use the back of the door itself — over-door organisers hold shoes, scarves and gloves
  • Put a slim cabinet on the wall behind the door swing
  • Use the first 18 inches of the adjacent wall, even if it feels like part of another room
  • A basket beside the sofa arm nearest the door works better than nothing

The maintenance habit that keeps it working

Every storage system in an entryway degrades in about three weeks without one habit: a weekly reset.

Once a week, take back the shoes that don’t belong, clear the mail, empty the drop bowl. Five minutes. Without it, even the best-designed entry silts up.

Measurements to remember:

Item Height / depth
Adult coat hooks 60–66 inches
Kid coat hooks 40 inches
Bag hooks 44 inches
Hook spacing 8–10 inches apart
Narrow console depth 10–12 inches
Shoe cabinet depth 9–10 inches
Bench wall space 40 inches minimum

Entryway Table Decor Ideas

How to style an entryway table so it looks finished and still works — layouts, height rules, seasonal swaps and what to keep off the surface.

An entryway table is the first surface anyone sees in your home, and it’s also where keys, post and receipts go to die. Styling one is really about balancing those two jobs.

The good news is there’s a formula, and once you know it you can restyle the table in ten minutes for any season.

The basic formula that always works

Three elements, three heights:

  1. Something tall — a lamp, a vase with branches, a tall piece of art leaning against the wall
  2. Something medium — a stack of books, a small plant, a sculptural object
  3. Something low and functional — a tray or bowl for keys

Group them so they form a rough triangle rather than a straight line. Uneven numbers look more natural than even ones.

That’s it. Everything below is variation on that.

Get the proportions right

This is where most entryway tables go wrong.

The art or mirror above should be about two-thirds the width of the table. Wider than the table looks unbalanced; much narrower looks lost.

Leave 6–10 inches between the top of the table and the bottom of the art.

The tallest object on the table should reach roughly one-third to one-half the height of the art above it. A tall lamp beside a small mirror fights for attention.

Keep one-third of the surface clear. This is the rule people skip, and it’s the reason some tables look styled and others look cluttered.

Layout 1: Lamp on one side

The most reliable arrangement. Lamp at one end, a stack of two or three books with a small object on top at the other, a bowl for keys in the middle-front.

Works because the lamp gives you height on one side and the eye naturally balances it against the grouping on the other.

The lamp does double duty — warm light at eye level is what makes an entry feel welcoming when you walk in at night.

Layout 2: Symmetrical pair

Two matching lamps or two matching vases at either end, one object in the centre. Formal, calm, works well in traditional homes and under a large mirror.

Downside: it leaves less room for the functional stuff, so add a drawer or a basket below for keys and post.

Layout 3: Asymmetric with a tall vase

A large vase with tall dried stems — pampas, eucalyptus, cherry blossom branches — set to one side, with a low tray and a small stack of books to the other.

This is the most Pinterest-friendly look and the easiest to swap seasonally. Change the stems, change the season.

What to put in the tray

A tray or shallow bowl is the piece that makes an entryway table work in real life. It contains the daily clutter instead of letting it spread.

Put in it: keys, sunglasses, the small things that arrive in pockets.

Keep out of it: post, receipts, coins, anything that accumulates. Those need their own home or they’ll take over.

A tray with a raised edge works better than a flat one — things stay put.

Seasonal swaps that take five minutes

The framework stays; only two elements change.

Spring — tulips or cherry blossom branches, a light linen runner, pastel candle Summer — greenery in a clear vase, a shell or coral object, brighter tray Autumn — dried grasses, small pumpkins, amber glass, a wooden bowl Winter — evergreen sprigs, brass candlesticks, a bowl of pinecones, warm textured throw over a basket below

Keep the lamp and the tray in place year-round. Swap the vase contents and one small object. That’s the whole seasonal refresh.

Things worth styling with

  • Books — hardcovers with the dust jackets removed look better; stack two or three
  • A small plant — pothos, small snake plant, or a faux one if there’s no light
  • Candles — a single pillar or a pair of tapers in brass holders
  • A small sculpture or object — something with an interesting shape
  • A basket underneath, not on top, for slippers or extra blankets
  • Framed photo — one, not a collection

Things that make it look cluttered

  • More than five objects on the surface
  • Everything the same height
  • Objects lined up in a row, evenly spaced
  • Small items scattered rather than grouped
  • Mail, chargers, and daily clutter left out
  • Too many competing patterns and textures

The most common mistake is quantity. A table with three well-chosen objects beats a table with eight.

If your table has drawers

Use them for the ugly essentials — chargers, dog treats, spare keys, batteries, pens. Nothing decorative goes in a drawer.

This is what lets the top stay clear. A console with two drawers is worth paying more for.

If there’s space underneath

A basket for shoes, a small stool that tucks in, or two woven baskets side by side. The underneath is prime storage and most people leave it empty.

Just keep it visually calm — one or two large items, not five small ones.

No table? Use a floating shelf

A wall-mounted shelf styled the same way gives you the look without the floor space. Everything above applies: three heights, a tray, one-third clear.

The bonus is the clear floor underneath, which makes a small entry feel bigger.

The weekly reset

Whatever you build, it degrades in about a week without maintenance. Once a week: clear the post, put the strays away, wipe the surface.

Two minutes, and it’s the difference between a styled entry and a dumping ground.

Quick styling checklist:

  • Three objects, three different heights
  • Grouped in a triangle, not a line
  • Art two-thirds the table width, 6–10 inches above
  • A tray for keys
  • One-third of the surface left empty
  • A lamp if you can — warm bulb, 2700K

17 Fall Apartment Decor Ideas for a Cozy Seasonal Home

Bring autumn warmth into a small space with 17 fall apartment decor ideas using seasonal textiles, natural accents, warm lighting, and renter-friendly styling.

  • Use removable hooks and renter-friendly options to avoid wall damage.
  • Create one seasonal focal point rather than decorating every surface.
  • Layer textiles and warm lighting before adding any seasonal objects.

If you are looking for fall apartment decor ideas, the best place to start is with function rather than decoration. A space feels better when the layout is easy to use, storage has a clear purpose, and the styling supports everyday life instead of getting in the way.

The ideas below are designed to be practical for real homes. You do not need to use every idea. Choose the changes that suit your space and your normal decor first, then build from there.

1. Use Decor That Stores Flat

Prints, garlands, and fabric items store flat and take up almost no space between seasons. Choose pieces that are easy to store and that work with your normal decor.

This keeps seasonal decorating affordable and makes setup and cleanup much faster.

2. Choose One Seasonal Focal Point

Rather than decorating every surface, choose one area — a console table, coffee table, or windowsill — and make it the seasonal focal point. Keep the rest of the apartment calm.

Repeat a few materials and colors instead of using many unrelated decorations.

3. Decorate With Small Branches and Textiles

A few autumn branches in a vase and a warm throw on the sofa can transform a room without any obvious seasonal products. Both are easy to store and work with most existing decor.

Choose pieces that are easy to store and that work with your normal decor.

4. Use Removable Hooks for Rental Walls

Removable adhesive hooks let you hang wreaths, garlands, and lightweight decor without damaging walls. This is especially useful in rentals where drilling is not permitted.

In rentals, removable hooks or freestanding alternatives can achieve a similar result.

5. Create Clear Zones in One Room

Even in a small apartment, grouping activities together reduces clutter. Keep seasonal decor in one or two defined areas rather than spreading it through every room.

Choose pieces that are easy to store and that work with your normal decor.

6. Use Furniture With More Than One Job

A storage ottoman holds extra blankets while doubling as a coffee table. A bench near the door provides seating and storage for seasonal accessories.

Measure the furniture footprint and the path around it before buying.

7. Choose Storage That Goes Up, Not Out

In a small apartment, vertical storage keeps the floor open. Use tall shelves, wall-mounted hooks, and storage above doors for seasonal items.

Choose pieces that are easy to store and that work with your normal decor.

8. Use the Space Under the Bed

Store off-season decor in flat boxes under the bed. Group similar items together so the space does not become a hidden pile that is difficult to maintain.

Measure width, depth, and height before choosing containers.

9. Add Storage Above Doors

A shelf above an interior door holds seasonal baskets or boxes without using any floor space. Use it for items you reach for only occasionally.

Measure the wall before drilling or ordering storage.

10. Use Baskets on Open Shelves

Baskets on open shelving hide small seasonal items while keeping the shelf looking calm. Use a consistent basket size and style so the shelves look intentional.

Matching baskets can make open storage look calmer.

11. Choose a Slim Console

A narrow console table near the entrance gives you a surface for a seasonal arrangement without blocking the walkway. Keep it simple: one vase, one candle, one small object.

Keep walking paths, doors, drawers, and frequently used surfaces easy to access.

12. Create a Drop Zone Near the Door

A hook rail and small tray near the entrance stops bags, keys, and coats from spreading through the apartment. Keep only current-season items here.

Start with what you already own, then make one small change at a time.

13. Use the Back of Doors

Over-door organizers and hooks turn the back of every door into useful storage for seasonal accessories, bags, and lightweight items.

Before buying anything, measure the available area and think about how the item will be used every day.

14. Try a Storage Ottoman

A storage ottoman in the living area holds extra blankets and seasonal cushion covers while doubling as a coffee table or extra seating.

Measure the furniture footprint and the path around it before buying.

15. Add a Tall Bookcase

A tall bookcase uses vertical space efficiently and can hold seasonal decor on upper shelves while keeping everyday items at an easy height.

A slightly slimmer piece that leaves breathing room often looks better than a larger item with more storage but poor circulation.

16. Keep Large Surfaces Visually Clear

Countertops and dining tables work better when they are not covered in seasonal objects. Group a small number of items together and leave visible empty space.

A tray is useful because the whole group can be moved at once.

17. Use Matching Containers

Matching baskets or bins for seasonal storage reduce visual clutter and make the apartment look intentional rather than cluttered.

Use labels only where they genuinely help.

Final Thoughts

The strongest fall apartment decor ideas are the ones that make the space feel warmer and more inviting, not simply more decorated. Start with textiles and lighting, choose one focal point, and keep enough empty space for the apartment to feel comfortable. Small, deliberate improvements are usually more successful than changing everything at once.

22 Funny Halloween Costume Ideas That Will Actually Make People Laugh

Get genuine laughs this Halloween with 22 funny costume ideas including puns, pop culture jokes, and clever concepts. Solo, duo, and group options included.

The short version

  • The best funny costumes have one clear joke that is readable in under three seconds.
  • Pun costumes work best when the pun is visible on a sign — do not make people guess.
  • Commitment sells the joke — a funny costume worn half-heartedly is just a weird outfit.
  • Topical costumes are funny now but date quickly — a timeless pun lasts forever.

A funny Halloween costume has one job: make people laugh. The ideas below are chosen for their clarity — each one has a single, readable joke that lands in under three seconds.

Commitment is everything. A funny costume worn with confidence and commitment is always funnier than the same costume worn apologetically.

Pun Costumes

1. Ceiling Fan

A plain outfit with a sign that says “Go Ceilings!” This is one of the most reliably funny Halloween costumes because the pun is unexpected and the setup is so minimal.

Respond to every “What are you?” with enthusiastic ceiling cheering.

2. Error 404: Costume Not Found

A plain outfit with a printed sign that says “Error 404: Costume Not Found.” This is the laziest Halloween costume on the list, but it is also one of the funniest — especially at a tech-savvy party.

Use a large, readable font on the sign.

3. Formal Apology

A formal suit or dress with a sign that says “I’m Sorry.” This is a clever pun that works on two levels — the formal outfit and the apology.

Apologize to everyone you meet throughout the evening for extra effect.

4. Nudist on Strike

Regular clothes with a sign that says “Nudist on Strike.” This is the most minimal funny Halloween costume and one of the most reliably funny.

Use a large, readable font on the sign.

5. Deviled Egg

A white outfit with a yellow circle on the front and devil horns. This is a punny, unexpected costume that always gets a reaction.

The yellow circle needs to be large enough to be readable from across the room.

6. Holy Guacamole

An avocado costume with a halo. This is a food pun costume that suits someone who enjoys both avocados and wordplay.

The halo is the most important element — without it, it is just an avocado costume.

7. Freudian Slip

A slip dress with the word “Freudian” written on it, or a slip dress with Freud’s face printed on it. This is a clever, slightly intellectual pun that suits a party with a well-read crowd.

The label needs to be large and readable — the pun only works if people can read it.

8. Identity Theft

A plain outfit covered in “Hello My Name Is” stickers with different names on each one. This is a clever, topical pun that suits a party with a tech-savvy or security-conscious crowd.

Use as many name tags as possible — the more, the funnier.

9. A Piece of Gum Stuck to the Bottom of a Shoe

A grey outfit with a shoe print on the back. This is an unexpected, specific pun that suits someone who enjoys absurdist humor.

The shoe print needs to be large and clearly visible.

10. A Smartie Pants

Trousers covered in Smarties (or M&Ms) with a sign that says “Smartie Pants.” This is a sweet, literal pun that suits a family-friendly party.

Glue the Smarties to the trousers with a hot glue gun — they will not stay on with tape.

Pop Culture Jokes

11. Ken (from Barbie)

A pink outfit — pink polo shirt, pink shorts or trousers — with a “Ken” name tag. This is a topical, funny costume that suits a man with a sense of humor about gender expectations.

The more pink, the better.

12. Siri or Alexa

A white outfit with a printed logo, a headset, and a sign that says “Ask Me Anything.” Respond to every question with a robotic voice and a slightly unhelpful answer.

The robotic voice and the unhelpful answers are what make this costume funny.

13. A Netflix Loading Screen

A grey outfit with a spinning loading circle and the Netflix logo. This is a topical, relatable pun that suits a party with a streaming-savvy crowd.

The loading circle needs to be large and clearly visible.

14. A Zoom Call

A business outfit on top, pajamas on the bottom, with a sign that says “Zoom Call.” This is a relatable, post-pandemic pun that suits almost any party.

The contrast between the top and bottom halves is the joke — make it obvious.

15. A Spam Email

A plain outfit covered in printed spam email subject lines — “You’ve Won a Million Dollars,” “Nigerian Prince Needs Your Help,” “Enlarge Your Vocabulary.” This is a clever, specific pun that suits a tech-savvy crowd.

Use as many subject lines as possible — the more, the funnier.

Subversive Costumes

16. A Responsible Adult

A sensible outfit with a sign that says “Responsible Adult.” This is a funny, self-aware costume that suits someone who is known for being the responsible one in their friend group.

The more sensible and boring the outfit, the funnier.

17. A Morning Person

A bright, cheerful outfit with a coffee cup and a sign that says “Morning Person.” This is a funny, relatable costume that suits someone who is definitively not a morning person.

The contrast between the cheerful costume and the wearer’s personality is the joke.

18. A Cat Person

A plain outfit with a cat on a leash (a stuffed cat or a cat toy). This is a literal interpretation of “cat person” that suits someone who is known for loving cats.

The stuffed cat needs to be large enough to be recognizable from across the room.

19. A Conspiracy Theorist

A plain outfit covered in printed conspiracy theory headlines, connected with red string. Add a tinfoil hat for extra effect.

The tinfoil hat is the most important element — it is the universal symbol of conspiracy theorists.

20. A Participation Trophy

A plain outfit with a large “Participation Trophy” ribbon and a sign that says “You Tried.” This is a funny, slightly self-deprecating costume that suits someone with a good sense of humor.

The ribbon needs to be large and clearly readable.

Group Funny Costumes

21. Rock, Paper, Scissors

Three people — one dressed as a rock (grey, rounded outfit), one as paper (flat, white outfit with lines), one as scissors (silver outfit with scissor blades). This is a classic punny group costume.

The props are the most important elements — make them large and clearly recognizable.

22. A Bag of Jelly Beans

Each person wears a different color outfit and a sign that says their jelly bean flavor. The group wears a large bag-shaped sign together. This is a funny, colorful group costume.

Use large, readable labels — the pun needs to be visible from across the room.

Final Thoughts

The best funny Halloween costumes are the ones with a single, clear joke that lands immediately. Choose a pun or a concept you find genuinely funny, commit to it completely, and be prepared to explain it to the people who do not get it — that is part of the fun. A costume that makes you laugh is always the right choice.

Still wondering

Common questions

What makes a Halloween costume actually funny?

A funny costume has one clear, specific joke that is immediately readable. The best funny costumes are either a clever pun, a subversion of expectations, or a very specific pop culture reference that the audience will recognize. Vague or overly complex jokes do not land in a crowded party — the simpler and more specific, the funnier.

What are the funniest Halloween costumes that are easy to make?

Pun costumes are the easiest funny costumes to make — a plain outfit with a printed sign. 'Error 404: Costume Not Found,' 'Ceiling Fan,' 'Formal Apology,' and 'Nudist on Strike' all require nothing more than a plain outfit and a printed sign. The joke is the costume.

  • Begin with a warm throw, textured cushion covers, and a small palette of autumn colors.
  • Layer table and floor lamps for a comfortable glow while keeping reading areas bright enough.
  • Bring in wood, woven baskets, and a few seasonal accents while leaving everyday surfaces usable.
  • Refresh what you already own and stop decorating while the room still has breathing space.

A cozy fall living room does not need to be covered in orange pumpkins. Often the biggest change comes from a few practical layers: softer textiles, warmer light, natural materials, and deeper accent colors.

Use these fall living room decor ideas as a menu rather than a shopping list. Choose the changes that suit your room, your storage space, and the way you actually use the living area.

1. Start With One Warm Throw

A throw blanket is one of the fastest seasonal changes because it adds both color and texture. Choose wool, a soft woven cotton, fleece, or a chunky knit depending on your climate.

Drape it over one sofa arm or fold it into a basket instead of covering the entire sofa.

2. Swap Cushion Covers, Not the Inserts

Changing only the covers is cheaper and requires less storage than buying complete seasonal cushions. Try rust, olive, camel, burgundy, chocolate, or warm beige.

Repeat two or three colors already present in the room so the seasonal update still feels connected to your normal decor.

3. Layer Texture Before Adding More Objects

Wool, boucle, velvet, linen, woven baskets, and natural wood create a cozy feeling without cluttering surfaces. This is especially useful in small living rooms where too many decorative objects can feel busy.

Use different textures within a limited color palette for a calmer result.

4. Bring in Warm Wood

A wood tray, side table, picture frame, bowl, or stool adds visual warmth. You do not need to replace furniture; one or two small wood elements are enough.

For a budget option, move wooden pieces from another room for the season rather than buying new decor.

5. Use Warm, Layered Lighting

Table lamps and floor lamps usually feel cozier than one bright ceiling light. Warm-white bulbs around 2700K are a good starting point for an inviting evening atmosphere.

Keep task areas bright enough to read comfortably, and use dimmers where possible rather than making the whole room too dark.

6. Keep the Coffee Table Practical

Use a tray to contain a candle, small vase, book, or one seasonal object. Leave enough empty surface for drinks and everyday use.

A common mistake is turning the table into a seasonal display that has to be moved every time someone sits down.

7. Use One Tall Arrangement of Autumn Branches

A few branches in a ceramic or glass vase can create more impact than many small decorations. They add height and natural color without using much surface area.

If using real branches, check for insects and avoid placing dry material too close to candles or heaters.

8. Choose a Few Pumpkins in Muted Colors

Cream, green, terracotta, and soft orange pumpkins can work with neutral interiors without feeling overly themed. Group two or three together rather than spreading small pumpkins across every shelf.

Reusable ceramic or fabric pumpkins reduce yearly waste if you enjoy the same look each season.

9. Add Candles Safely

Candles add movement and warm light, especially on darker evenings. Use a stable tray and keep flames away from curtains, dried leaves, throws, and children or pets.

Flameless LED candles are a good alternative when open flames are not practical.

10. Anchor the Seating Area With a Rug

A rug makes a living room feel softer underfoot and visually connects the seating area. Vintage-inspired, wool-look, or warm neutral rugs work well for fall.

If you are buying one, try to choose a size that allows at least the front legs of the main seating to sit on the rug; tiny floating rugs can make a room feel smaller.

11. Style the Mantel With Restraint

Choose one main focal point such as a mirror or artwork, then add a few supporting elements: candles, branches, or a small group of seasonal objects.

Leave some empty space. A crowded mantel can make the whole living room feel visually heavy.

For a closer look at arranging this focal point, see our autumn mantel styling guide.

12. Store Extra Throws in a Woven Basket

A large basket beside the sofa keeps blankets accessible while adding natural texture. It is useful decor rather than purely decorative decor.

Choose a basket with smooth edges so it does not snag delicate throws.

13. Introduce One Deeper Accent Color

Olive green, chocolate brown, rust, burgundy, or charcoal can make a neutral room feel more seasonal without repainting. Add the color through a cushion, throw, art print, or vase.

Repeating the accent in two places usually looks more intentional than using many unrelated dark colors.

14. Use Dried Flowers or Grasses

Dried hydrangeas, grasses, wheat, and eucalyptus suit the season and last longer than fresh flowers. Use one loose arrangement rather than several small ones.

Keep dried arrangements away from open flames because the material is highly flammable.

15. Create a Reading Corner

An unused corner can become a cozy seasonal feature with a comfortable chair, a small table, a lamp, and a throw. It adds function instead of simply adding more decor.

In a small room, use a compact chair or reposition an existing chair rather than buying an oversized accent chair.

16. Bring Books Into the Styling

Books add height and make a room feel lived-in. Use a small stack under a bowl or candle, or keep favorite books within reach on the coffee table.

Avoid building tall decorative stacks that make everyday surfaces harder to use.

17. Remove Bright Summer Pieces

Fall decorating can be as much about editing as adding. Put away highly summery colors or lightweight beach-themed objects if they clash with the warmer seasonal palette.

This is a free way to change the room and prevents seasonal decorating from becoming clutter accumulation.

18. Swap One Piece of Artwork

Changing a single framed print can shift the entire mood of a room. Try a warm landscape, vintage botanical, textured abstract, or moody photograph.

Use the same frame and change only the print to keep the update inexpensive and easy to store.

19. Decorate With Natural Materials

Wood, stone, clay, linen, jute, and woven fibers feel grounded and seasonal without being limited to fall. They also transition easily into winter decor.

Choose materials you would still like after the season ends; this reduces the need for short-lived decorative purchases.

20. Add a Subtle Seasonal Scent

Cedarwood, amber, apple, sandalwood, vanilla, or light spice can reinforce the cozy atmosphere. Use one scent source at a time so the room does not become overwhelming.

If anyone in the home is sensitive to fragrance, skip scented products and rely on lighting and textiles instead.

21. Stop Before Every Surface Is Decorated

The goal is warmth, not maximum seasonal coverage. Once the sofa feels layered, the lighting is comfortable, and one or two surfaces have fall accents, the room may already be finished.

Leaving empty space makes seasonal details more noticeable and keeps the living room easy to live in.

Keep the room feeling calm with the principles in our minimalist living room guide.

Final Thoughts

A warm fall living room is mostly about atmosphere. Layer textiles, soften the lighting, introduce a few natural materials, and then add seasonal details only where they improve the room. The most successful fall decor still feels like your home - just a little warmer and more inviting.

The short version

  • The best funny couple costumes have one clear joke that is readable in under three seconds.
  • Pun costumes work best when the pun is visible on a sign — do not make people guess.

A funny couple costume has one job: make people laugh. The best ones have a single, clear joke that lands the moment people see you together. The ideas below are chosen for their clarity and their commitment potential.

Food Puns

1. Deviled Egg and Angel Egg

One person in a white outfit with a yellow circle on the front and devil horns; the other in a white outfit with a yellow circle and angel wings and a halo. Together you are a deviled egg and an angel egg.

The yellow circles need to be large enough to be readable from across the room.

2. Salt and Pepper

One person in a white outfit labeled “Salt,” the other in a black outfit labeled “Pepper.” This is the most classic punny couple costume and always gets a reaction.

Use large, readable labels — the pun needs to be visible from across the room.

3. Ketchup and Mustard

One person in a red outfit labeled “Ketchup,” the other in a yellow outfit labeled “Mustard.” This is a simple, recognizable punny couple costume.

Use large, readable labels — the pun needs to be visible from across the room.

4. Peanut Butter and Jelly

One person in a brown outfit labeled “Peanut Butter,” the other in a purple outfit labeled “Jelly.” This is a cheerful, recognizable punny couple costume.

Use large, readable labels — the pun needs to be visible from across the room.

5. Fork and Spoon

One person in a silver outfit shaped like a fork (with a fork prop or a fork-shaped sign); the other in a silver outfit shaped like a spoon. Together you are a “fork and spoon” — or, if you are feeling cheeky, you are “spooning.”

The props are the most important elements — make them large and clearly recognizable.

6. Avocado and Toast

One person in a green avocado costume; the other in a beige outfit with brown squares as a piece of toast. Together you are avocado toast — the most millennial couple costume possible.

The avocado pit is the most important element for the avocado costume.

Tech and Pop Culture Puns

7. Plug and Socket

One person dressed as an electrical plug, the other as a socket. This is a clever, slightly cheeky punny couple costume that always gets a knowing laugh.

The props are the most important elements — make them large and readable.

8. Netflix and Chill

One person in a Netflix-branded outfit; the other in a blanket and pajamas with a remote control. This is a funny, relatable couple costume.

The Netflix logo needs to be large and clearly readable.

9. WiFi and Dead Zone

One person in an outfit covered in WiFi signal bars; the other in an outfit with a “No Signal” symbol. This is a clever, topical pun that suits a tech-savvy couple.

The signal bars and the no-signal symbol need to be large and clearly readable.

10. Siri and Alexa

One person in an Apple-branded outfit labeled “Siri”; the other in an Amazon-branded outfit labeled “Alexa.” Respond to every question in a robotic voice and give slightly unhelpful answers.

The robotic voices and the unhelpful answers are what make this costume funny.

11. Error 404 and Found

One person in a plain outfit with a sign that says “Error 404: Not Found”; the other in a bright outfit with a sign that says “Found!” This is a clever, tech-savvy pun that suits a couple with a sense of humor.

The contrast between the two signs is the joke.

Relationship Puns

12. Ceiling Fan and Floor Fan

One person in a plain outfit with a sign that says “Go Ceilings!”; the other in a plain outfit with a sign that says “Go Floors!” This is a punny, low-effort couple costume that always gets a laugh.

The signs need to be large and readable — the pun only works if people can read them.

13. Formal Apology and Formal Complaint

One person in a formal outfit with a sign that says “Formal Apology”; the other in a formal outfit with a sign that says “Formal Complaint.” This is a funny, slightly passive-aggressive couple costume.

The formal outfits are the most important element — the contrast between the formality and the message is the joke.

14. Swipe Right and Swipe Left

One person in an attractive outfit with a green “Swipe Right” sign; the other in a less attractive outfit with a red “Swipe Left” sign. This is a funny, dating-app-era couple costume.

The contrast between the two signs is the joke.

15. Introvert and Extrovert

One person in a quiet, understated outfit with a sign that says “Introvert”; the other in a loud, colorful outfit with a sign that says “Extrovert.” This is a funny, relatable couple costume that suits a couple with contrasting personalities.

The contrast between the two outfits is the joke.

Classic Funny Pairings

16. Shrek and Fiona

Shrek in a green bodysuit or green face paint with brown vest and boots; Fiona in a green dress with a red braid. This is a funny, recognizable couple costume that suits a couple with a sense of humor about their relationship.

The green face paint is the most important element for both characters.

17. Ken and Barbie (Reversed)

The woman in a “Ken” outfit — pink polo shirt, khakis, and a “Ken” name tag; the man in a “Barbie” outfit — a pink dress and a blonde wig. This is a funny, gender-swapped couple costume.

The gender swap is the joke — commit to it completely.

18. A Selfie

One person holds a large printed frame in front of them as if taking a selfie; the other stands behind the frame as the subject of the selfie. Add a printed phone prop for extra effect.

The frame needs to be large enough to frame the subject’s face clearly.

Final Thoughts

The best funny couple costumes are the ones where both partners are equally committed to the joke. Choose a concept you both find genuinely funny, make the pun readable from across the room, and commit to the characters for the whole evening. A couple that is clearly having fun with their costume is always funnier than a couple that is wearing a funny costume reluctantly.

Assign the baby and the dog the most comfortable and most adorable costumes, plan the group photo in advance, and commit to the theme for the whole evening. A well-executed family costume is one of the most memorable things you can do on Halloween.

What are the best funny Halloween costumes for families with young children?

The best family costumes for young children are the ones where the child's costume is comfortable and recognizable without being elaborate. A baby pumpkin, a toddler lion, and parents as farmers creates a complete farm scene. The child's comfort is the priority — a miserable child in a perfect costume makes for bad photos.

How do you include a baby in a family Halloween costume?

Assign the baby the simplest, most comfortable costume in the group — usually a onesie with a printed design or a soft hat. Build the family theme around what the baby can wear comfortably. A baby pumpkin with parents as farmers, a baby Yoda with parents as Jedi, or a baby shark with parents as scuba divers all work well.

Funny outdoor Halloween decorations work because they tell a story. A skeleton sitting in a lawn chair reading a newspaper is funny because it is specific and relatable. A pile of random props is not funny — it is just a pile of props.

The ideas below are organized around clear scenarios. Each one has a single joke that is readable from the street in a few seconds.

Witch Scenarios

1. Witch Crashed Into the Tree

Attach a pair of striped witch legs — stuffed tights with boots at the end — to a tree trunk, as if the witch flew into it at speed. Add a broomstick on the ground below. This is one of the most classic funny Halloween yard decorations and always gets a reaction.

Use tights in classic witch stripes — black and white or black and orange.

2. Witch Crashed Into the Fence

The same idea works on a fence panel — attach the legs horizontally as if the witch hit the fence at full speed. Add a bent broomstick and a witch hat on the ground.

Stuff the tights firmly so the legs hold their shape in wind.

3. Witch Parking Only Sign

A sign that reads “Witch Parking Only — All Others Will Be Toad” next to a broomstick leaning against the fence creates a punny, low-effort display that is readable from the street.

Print the sign on weatherproof card or seal it with outdoor varnish spray.

Seat a skeleton in a lawn chair with a newspaper, a cup of coffee, and a pair of reading glasses. Add a sign that says “Still Waiting for the Weekend.”

Use an old newspaper rather than a current one — the date does not matter.

6. Skeleton Sunbathing

Lay a skeleton on a sun lounger with sunglasses, a bottle of sunscreen, and a cocktail. Add a sign that says “I Waited All Summer For This.”

This works especially well in climates where October is still warm.

Prop a skeleton holding a leash attached to a plastic skeleton dog. Add a sign that says “He’s Friendly.” The specificity of the dog walker scenario is what makes it land.

Use a plastic dog skeleton from a pet costume store.

Animal Scenarios

13. Zombie Flamingos

Secure the cat to the post with a zip tie so it does not blow off in wind.

15. Crow Convention

Arrange a large number of plastic crows — twenty or thirty — on the fence, the roof, and the lawn, all facing the same direction. Add a sign that reads “Annual Crow Convention.” The sheer number of crows is what makes it funny.

17 Gothic Halloween Decor Ideas — Dark Botanical Aesthetic

Create a gothic Halloween atmosphere with 17 dark botanical decor ideas using dried flowers, taper candles, black foliage, antique prints, and a moody palette.

The short version

  • The dark botanical palette is black, deep burgundy, forest green, and aged cream.
  • Dried flowers in dark tones are the centrepiece of the gothic botanical aesthetic.
  • Taper candles in black or deep burgundy add height and drama to any surface.
  • The look works year-round — it does not need to be packed away after Halloween.

Gothic Halloween decor in the dark botanical style is one of the most sophisticated seasonal aesthetics available. It draws on Victorian mourning traditions, apothecary culture, and the natural world — dried flowers, bare branches, dark foliage, and candlelight — rather than plastic props and bright orange.

The result is a home that feels atmospheric and considered, and that transitions naturally into the rest of autumn and winter without needing to be dismantled.

The Palette

1. Black, Deep Burgundy, and Forest Green

The dark botanical palette is black, deep burgundy, forest green, and aged cream. These four colours work together across every material — textiles, botanicals, ceramics, and candles — and create a cohesive look without requiring everything to match exactly.

Avoid bright orange entirely. Muted terracotta is the closest acceptable warm tone.

Botanicals

2. Dried Flowers in Dark Tones

Dried dahlias, roses, and grasses in deep burgundy, black, and aged cream are the centrepiece of the dark botanical aesthetic. Arrange them in a ceramic or earthenware vase rather than glass. They last the entire season and look better as they dry further.

3. Black-Dyed Stems

Black-dyed dried flowers and grasses add a dramatic element that is specific to the gothic aesthetic. Mix them with natural dried stems for contrast. They are available from florists and craft suppliers.

4. Bare Branches

Bare branches in a tall vase — left natural or sprayed black — add height and a slightly eerie quality. They are free if you collect them from the garden and last the entire season.

Shop this Halloween decor Black Flameless Candles, Set of 9 See details & availability Check current price On Amazon · Opens in a new tab

5. Dark Foliage

Dark-leaved plants — black mondo grass, deep burgundy heuchera, or dark-leaved succulents — in ceramic pots add a living botanical element. They also work as year-round houseplants.

6. Dried Herb Bundles

Bundles of dried sage, lavender, or rosemary tied with dark ribbon add a witchy, apothecary quality. Hang them from a hook, lay them on a shelf, or tuck them into a botanical arrangement.

7. Moss and Lichen

Preserved moss and lichen add texture and a slightly wild, forest quality to a display. Use them as a base layer in a tray or bowl, with candles and objects placed on top.

Candles

8. Black Taper Candles

Black taper candles in brass, pewter, or verdigris candlesticks are the most recognisable element of the gothic aesthetic. Group three candlesticks of different heights together rather than spacing them evenly.

Use flameless tapers near dried materials.

Shop this Halloween decor 16-Piece Mini Pumpkin Decor Set See details & availability Check current price On Amazon · Opens in a new tab

9. Deep Burgundy Pillar Candles

Deep burgundy pillar candles on a wooden board or tray add warmth and depth. Group them with dried flowers and a few dark objects for a complete display.

10. Candelabra

A single candelabra — real or flameless — adds height, drama, and period authenticity. It is one of the most effective gothic props and works on a mantel, dining table, or console.

Objects and Props

11. Apothecary Bottles

Dark glass bottles, cork-stoppered vials, and small ceramic pots labelled with handwritten tags create an apothecary display. Fill them with dried herbs, dark sand, or leave them empty. Group them on a tray or shelf.

12. Ceramic Skulls

A ceramic skull in cream, black, or terracotta reads as gothic rather than cheap when the material is right. One well-chosen ceramic piece is worth more than ten plastic props. Place it among the botanicals for a natural, collected look.

Shop this Halloween lighting Halloween-Themed Fairy Lights See details & availability Check current price On Amazon · Opens in a new tab

13. Antique-Style Prints

Victorian botanical prints, moon phase charts, and dark landscape illustrations in antique-style frames add a period quality to the walls. Look for public domain images from the 1890s–1920s and print them at home.

14. Dark Mirrors

A dark-framed or slightly foxed mirror adds depth and a slightly unsettling quality. Lean it against a wall rather than hanging it for a more casual, collected look.

Textiles

15. Velvet and Lace

Deep burgundy or black velvet cushion covers, a lace table runner, or a velvet throw add the textile richness that defines the gothic aesthetic. Both materials photograph well in candlelight.

16. Dark Linen

A dark linen table runner or shelf liner in charcoal or deep navy creates a base for a display that feels aged and considered. Layer objects on top rather than placing them directly on a light surface.

Finishing Details

17. Wax Seal Details

Dark wax seals — in black, burgundy, or forest green — on envelopes, tags, or small cards add a period detail that is specific to the gothic aesthetic. Use a simple seal stamp and coloured wax sticks.

Final Thoughts

Gothic Halloween decor in the dark botanical style works because it treats the season as an aesthetic rather than a theme. The dried flowers, taper candles, and apothecary bottles create atmosphere without any obvious Halloween imagery. Start with the botanicals and the candles, add one or two ceramic objects, and let the palette do the rest. The result is a home that feels genuinely atmospheric — and that you will not want to pack away on 1 November.

The bathroom is one of the most overlooked rooms for Halloween decor, and one of the most effective. It is a small space, which means a few well-chosen objects create a strong impression. It is also a room every guest uses, which means the seasonal styling gets seen.

The ideas below keep the bathroom functional while adding genuine Halloween atmosphere.

The Mirror

1. String Lights Around the Mirror

Warm orange or amber string lights around the bathroom mirror create a vanity-style glow that suits the Halloween aesthetic. Use battery-powered lights to avoid water proximity issues.

2. Bat Window Clings on the Mirror

Removable bat or spider window clings applied to the mirror add a playful Halloween element that removes cleanly. Use them on the lower half of the mirror so they do not block the reflection.

3. Wreath on the Mirror

A small Halloween wreath — dried flowers, dark leaves, or a simple black and orange design — hung on or leaned against the bathroom mirror adds a seasonal focal point.

4. Framed Halloween Print

A framed vintage-style Halloween print — a moon, a botanical skull, a dark botanical illustration — swapped into an existing frame on the bathroom wall adds atmosphere without buying new decor.

7. Apothecary Bottles

Dark glass bottles or cork-stoppered vials on the counter — labelled with handwritten tags — add a witchy apothecary quality. Fill them with bath salts, cotton balls, or leave them empty.

8. Small Pumpkin

A single small pumpkin — real, ceramic, or faux — on the bathroom counter adds a seasonal note without taking up much space. Choose a matte finish in cream or terracotta rather than bright orange.

  • Repeat the palette in three places, such as the tree, doorway and table, instead of buying matching pieces for every surface.

Green Christmas decor does not have to mean buying a completely new set of emerald ornaments. The most convincing schemes let real or realistic foliage do much of the work, then repeat a few green details at different heights: a wreath by the door, ribbon on the tree and one small arrangement on the table.

These twenty ideas move from the biggest focal points to details you can make or reuse. The photographs show the specific styling move beside each idea; they are inspiration, not a claim that we made or tested the pictured projects. If you have a compact home, our small-space Christmas decor ideas offer a more space-first approach.

1. Let white ornaments brighten a green tree

White baubles and small floral accents are especially clear against deep needles. Start with the largest pale pieces, spread them across the front and sides, then add smaller ornaments between them. This creates contrast without hiding the tree’s natural color. Silver garland can add a little movement, but keep it light enough that the branches remain visible.

Photo: Irina Iriser on Pexels.

2. Thread ribbon into the branches, not around the outside

Short lengths of ribbon tucked into a tree feel softer than one tight spiral. Let each piece disappear behind a branch and reappear lower down; the needles and lights then break up the fabric naturally. The photographed tree mixes ribbon, pinecones and warm lights, a good reminder that texture matters as much as color.

Photo: Brett Sayles on Pexels.

3. Add one saturated green ornament among quieter finishes

An emerald bauble has more impact when it is surrounded by matte, clear or natural decorations. Put a few at eye level rather than scattering dozens across the tree. Against evergreen needles, a reflective green surface catches nearby light and gives a nearly monochrome palette some depth.

Photo: Connor Scott McManus on Pexels.

4. Make a miniature tree the whole tabletop display

For a narrow shelf or bedside table, a small tree can replace a collection of little decorations. Set it on a tray so the base, a tag and perhaps one ornament read as a single vignette. Leave clear space around it: miniature does not have to mean crowded.

Photo: Djordje Vezilic on Pexels.

5. Use a leafy wreath as the entryway’s main color

A green wreath with a small amount of red berry detail gives a door a clear focal point without needing matching floor decorations. On a wooden door, the foliage already has a warm backdrop. Measure the clear area between panels or hardware before buying so the wreath does not collide with the handle or door frame.

Photo: Qnula on Pexels.

6. Frame an entrance with garland

Greenery around a doorway can make the entrance feel decorated before a guest reaches the tree. The photograph shows a festive storefront, but the principle translates to a home: follow the frame, use a restrained ribbon color and make sure the door still swings freely. For an exterior door, choose a fastening method rated for the surface and weather rather than assuming indoor adhesive hooks will hold.

Photo: Lokman Sevim on Pexels.

7. Run greenery behind mantel stockings

The stockings are the repeated shapes; a low line of greenery connects them. Keep garland behind the stocking hooks so it does not interfere with how the stockings hang. If the fireplace is used, follow the fireplace manufacturer’s clearances and keep foliage, fabric and lights away from heat and flame.

Photo: cottonbro studio on Pexels.

8. Repeat gold and green along the staircase

A staircase has a natural rhythm: rail, post, rail, post. Let garland follow that line and repeat one metallic accent rather than attaching an ornament to every inch. Secure decorations to the outside or top of the rail so people can still grip it safely. Keep loose loops and trailing cords out of the walking path.

Photo: RDNE Stock project on Pexels.

9. Put a single pine stem in a clear bottle

A lone branch gives you the silhouette of a tree without the footprint. A clear bottle keeps the arrangement visually light on a desk, windowsill or console. Choose a vessel with a stable base, trim any branch that overbalances it and keep fresh greenery away from heaters or vents. University of Minnesota Extension specifically recommends cooler indoor spots for cut pine and cedar.

Photo: Tima Miroshnichenko on Pexels.

10. Turn clipped conifer stems into a small bouquet

A few short stems and two or three ornaments make a compact arrangement for a sideboard. Put the branches in water if the vessel and foliage allow it, and check them as the season progresses. The gold baubles in the photograph lift the green without turning the bouquet into a miniature imitation tree.

Photo: Максим Юрченко on Pexels.

11. Pair pine with dried citrus and natural wood

Green needles look fresh beside the warm brown and orange of dried fruit. Gather the pieces on a tray or a single tabletop area; that boundary stops small objects spreading across the whole room. A wood ornament or tree shape adds height without another saturated color. The photographed vignette shows how a few different textures can do more than a dozen matching trinkets.

Photo: Kaboompics on Pexels.

12. Use evergreen sprigs as the table’s repeating detail

At a dinner table, repeat small pieces of greenery near the center rather than building one tall arrangement that blocks conversation. Pale linens and a little gold make the foliage visible from across the room. Keep loose needles away from food, and leave room for serving dishes before deciding how much decor the table can hold.

Photo: Yan Krukau on Pexels.

13. Separate candlelight from real branches

Conifer and candlelight make a beautiful color combination, as the photograph shows, but do not copy a tight arrangement with lit candles near foliage. Use flameless candles among branches, or put real flames in sturdy holders well away from anything combustible. The NFPA candle-safety guidance recommends at least 12 inches between a lit candle and things that can burn.

Photo: aliona zueva on Pexels.

14. Scatter paper and bottle-brush trees down the table

Small trees can become a centerpiece that guests can see over. Mix a few heights but keep one clear green thread, such as a green candle or foliage stem. The pictured table uses paper and bottle-brush forms; their varied textures stop the repetition feeling too uniform. Move anything delicate before hot dishes arrive.

Photo: Jilly Noble on Pexels.

15. Make one green paper tree as a craft accent

Folded or rolled green paper can add a handmade note to a shelf or place setting. Work from a firm cone or folded base, build the layers evenly and let glue dry before moving it. The photograph is of a paper-tree craft in progress, so treat it as an approach rather than a finished-product pattern. Keep paper well away from candles and hot bulbs.

Photo: Leeloo The First on Pexels.

16. Make wrapped gifts part of the palette

Packages are visible under the tree for weeks, so their paper and ribbon count as decor. Use green on just some boxes, then balance it with plain brown or cream paper. The photographed set uses green ribbon against a green background; at home, vary the wrap finish so the packages remain distinguishable from one another.

Photo: hasan kurt on Pexels.

17. Save velvet ribbon for a few focal packages

Deep green velvet has a softer, darker finish than shiny plastic ribbon. Use it on the gifts displayed at the front of the tree or on a special package near the mantel; there is no need to wrap everything the same way. A simple knot keeps the fabric’s texture visible and makes the ribbon easier to reuse.

Photo: Nati on Pexels.

18. Give a plain garland one bold ornament color

A full garland already has texture. Instead of filling it with a mixture of tiny ornaments, repeat one striking bauble finish at intervals. The photographed green garland has colorful ornaments, which shows the spacing idea; narrowing those accents to one color is a simple way to create a quieter version for a shelf or interior doorway.

Photo: HOÀNG VŨ on Pexels.

19. Build a low Advent-style greenery vignette

A small wreath or ring of greenery looks especially good on a coffee table because it is low enough to see across. Put candles on a stable, nonflammable base separate from the foliage; flameless versions are the safer choice in a tight arrangement. Repeat the green in just one nearby cushion or book cover to connect the vignette to the room.

Photo: Nati on Pexels.

20. Finish with a soft garland above the bed

For a bedroom, a thin green garland over a canopy or headboard brings the color in without a second tree. The pictured canopy uses ribbon and berries for a gentle finish. Keep the arrangement securely fixed, away from light fittings and out of reach of anyone sleeping beneath it; skip heavy ornaments overhead. For more bedroom-specific styling, see our cozy Christmas bedroom ideas.

Photo: Alexander Mass on Pexels.

Green works best when it travels through a home in different forms rather than exactly matching everywhere. Choose the three spots you notice most—often the tree, the entrance and the table—and repeat a restrained palette there first. Everything else can stay as it is.

Still wondering

Common questions

What colors look good with green Christmas decor?

Warm white and brass let green foliage remain the focus. Red gives the scheme a traditional look, while brown paper, wood and dried citrus make it feel more natural. Pick one secondary color and repeat it so the tree, table and entryway look connected.

How do I decorate with green if my Christmas tree is already green?

Use texture and contrast. Pale ornaments stand out against dark branches, while green velvet ribbon, paper decorations and a few metallic pieces add depth. Leave some needles visible rather than covering every branch; the tree itself is part of the palette.

A Halloween centerpiece works best when it has a clear anchor, a limited palette, and at least three heights. The ideas below are designed for dining tables, coffee tables, and console tables — choose the scale that suits your space.

You do not need to use every idea. One strong centerpiece is more effective than small displays scattered across every surface.

1. The Classic Pumpkin Cluster

Group three pumpkins of different sizes and finishes — one real, one ceramic, one fabric — on a wooden board or tray. Add two taper candles in simple candlesticks and a handful of dried leaves. This is the most versatile Halloween centerpiece and works on any table.

Use odd numbers of objects — three or five — for the most natural arrangement.

2. Dark Floral Arrangement

Deep burgundy dahlias, black-dyed stems, dried grasses, and dark foliage in a ceramic or terracotta vase create a striking centerpiece that reads as both Halloween and autumn. Use one large arrangement rather than several small ones.

Dried stems last the entire season and cost less than fresh flowers.

3. Candle and Skull Tray

Arrange three pillar candles of different heights, a ceramic skull, and a few small pumpkins on a rectangular tray. The tray keeps the display contained and makes it easy to move when you need the table.

Use flameless candles if the table is used for meals — real flames and food do not mix well.

4. Apothecary Jar Display

Fill glass apothecary jars with black sand, dried beans, small plastic spiders, or candy corn. Arrange three jars of different heights together and add a label in a gothic font. This works well on a console or sideboard.

Print labels on kraft paper for a more vintage look.

5. Lantern Centerpiece

Place two or three lanterns of different sizes in the center of the table, each with a flameless candle inside. Surround the base with small pumpkins, dried leaves, and a few sprigs of dried eucalyptus.

Lanterns store easily and work for other seasonal displays throughout the year.

6. Bare Branch Arrangement

A few bare branches in a tall, heavy vase add height and a slightly eerie quality without any obvious Halloween imagery. Spray them black or leave them natural. Hang small paper bats or tiny pumpkins from the branches with thread.

Weight the vase with stones or sand so it does not tip.

7. Pumpkin Candleholder

Hollow out a medium pumpkin and place a pillar candle or a cluster of tea lights inside. Carve small stars or moon shapes rather than a face for a more sophisticated look. Surround it with smaller gourds and dried leaves.

Line the inside with foil to protect the pumpkin from heat.

8. Black and White Tablescape

Use a black table runner, white pumpkins, cream candles, and a single black vase with white dried flowers. This palette is striking, unusual, and works well for a dinner party where you want the food to be the focus.

Add a few silver or mercury glass votives for extra light.

9. Moss and Skull Terrarium

Fill a glass bowl or cloche with sheet moss, a ceramic skull, a few small pumpkins, and a battery tea light. The cloche keeps the display contained and adds a Victorian apothecary quality.

Use preserved moss rather than fresh — it lasts indefinitely without water.

10. Tiered Cake Stand Display

Use a two or three-tier cake stand to create a vertical centerpiece. Place small pumpkins, skulls, candles, and dark chocolates on each tier. The height makes it a strong focal point on a dining table.

A cake stand centerpiece doubles as a dessert display for a Halloween dinner party.

11. Pumpkin Vase

Cut the top off a large pumpkin, hollow it out, and use it as a vase for a dark floral arrangement. Deep red roses, black dahlias, and dried grasses work well. The pumpkin vase lasts about a week before it needs replacing.

Keep the arrangement in water using a plastic cup inside the pumpkin.

12. Witch Hat Centerpiece

Stack two or three witch hats of different sizes in the center of the table, surrounded by small pumpkins and a few scattered stars cut from black card. This is a playful option that works well for a family Halloween dinner.

Use craft-store hats rather than costume hats — they are stiffer and hold their shape better.

13. Candelabra with Dripping Wax

A tall candelabra with black or deep red taper candles, allowed to drip slightly, creates a dramatic centerpiece for a Halloween dinner party. Place it on a tray to catch the wax.

Use dripless candles if you want the effect without the mess.

14. Pumpkin and Book Stack

Stack two or three old hardcover books, place a small pumpkin on top, and add a candle and a few dried leaves. This works well on a coffee table or console and suits a home with a lot of books already.

Use books with dark or neutral spines for the most cohesive look.

Final Thoughts

The strongest Halloween centerpieces are the ones that look like they belong in the room rather than on top of it. Start with a tray or runner to anchor the display, vary the heights, and limit the palette to two or three colors. One well-styled centerpiece is always more effective than decorating every surface.

Still wondering

Common questions

What makes a good Halloween centerpiece for a dining table?

Height variation, a limited palette, and a clear anchor point. Use a tray or a runner to define the space, then build up with candlesticks, a tall vase, and low pumpkins. Three heights — tall, medium, low — create the most balanced look without requiring a florist's skill.

How do you make a Halloween centerpiece that works for both Halloween and autumn?

Stick to natural materials — dried grasses, gourds, terracotta pumpkins, and cream candles — rather than obviously themed products. A palette of rust, cream, and charcoal reads as autumn through November. Add one or two Halloween-specific pieces like a skull or black candles that can be removed after the 31st.

20 Halloween Bedroom Decor Ideas — Spooky But Still Cozy

Transform your bedroom for Halloween with 20 ideas using string lights, dark bedding, pumpkins, and moody accents that stay comfortable enough to sleep in.

The short version

  • Swap one cushion cover and add string lights — those two changes do most of the work.
  • Keep the bed itself comfortable and calm; put the Halloween detail on the surfaces around it.
  • Amber or warm orange string lights are the single most effective Halloween bedroom element.
  • A small pumpkin on the bedside table is enough — you do not need to decorate every surface.

A Halloween bedroom works best when it stays comfortable enough to actually sleep in. The goal is atmosphere — moody lighting, a few dark accents, and one or two seasonal objects — rather than a full themed transformation that makes the room feel like a display.

The ideas below are organised from the most impactful to the most subtle. Start with the lighting and build from there.

Lighting

1. Orange or Amber String Lights

Warm orange or amber string lights draped along the headboard, around a mirror, or along a shelf are the single most effective Halloween bedroom element. They change the entire mood of the room without adding a single object.

Use battery-powered lights to avoid visible cords.

2. Swap to a Warm Amber Bulb

Replacing a standard bedside lamp bulb with a warm amber one — around 2200K — creates a moody, candlelit quality that suits Halloween without any additional decoration. It is also the most reversible change on this list.

3. Add Candles or Flameless Candles

A group of two or three candles on the bedside table or dresser adds warmth and movement. Use a stable tray and keep flames away from bedding and curtains. Flameless LED candles are a good alternative for safety.

4. Fairy Lights in a Glass Jar

A handful of warm fairy lights stuffed into a glass jar creates a glowing lantern effect on a bedside table or shelf. It takes about thirty seconds and costs almost nothing.

Bedding and Textiles

5. Swap One Cushion Cover

A dark velvet cushion cover in charcoal, deep plum, or forest green adds seasonal depth without any obvious Halloween imagery. Swap it back in November and the cost is zero.

6. Add a Dark Throw

A chunky knit or faux-fur throw in charcoal, rust, or deep burgundy adds seasonal warmth and changes the mood of the bed without any other changes. Drape it loosely over one corner rather than folding it flat.

7. Dark Bedding for the Season

If you have dark bedding — charcoal, deep navy, or forest green — this is the time to use it. Dark sheets and a duvet cover create a moody base that makes every other Halloween element read more strongly.

8. Add a Seasonal Pillow

A single Halloween-themed pillow — a subtle bat, a moon, or a simple black cat — adds a seasonal note without committing the whole bed to a theme. One is enough.

Surfaces and Objects

9. Bedside Table Pumpkin

A small pumpkin — real, ceramic, or faux — on the bedside table is the simplest Halloween bedroom addition. Choose a matte finish in cream, terracotta, or muted orange rather than bright orange.

10. Dresser Vignette

A small tray on the dresser containing a candle, a small pumpkin, and one dark object — a ceramic skull, a small lantern, a dark stone — keeps the seasonal display contained and easy to remove.

11. Dried Flowers in a Dark Vase

Dried dahlias, roses, or grasses in deep burgundy or black in a ceramic vase add botanical texture and a slightly eerie quality. They last the entire season and require no maintenance.

12. Skull Candle Holder

A ceramic skull candle holder on the bedside table or dresser adds a Halloween reference without looking childish. Choose a matte finish in cream, black, or terracotta.

Walls and Vertical Space

13. Bat Wall Arrangement

Cut-paper or card bats arranged on the wall above the bed or beside the mirror add a playful seasonal note that is easy to remove and costs almost nothing. Keep the arrangement loose and asymmetric.

In rentals, removable adhesive strips mean no damage to walls.

14. Wreath on the Mirror

A small Halloween wreath — dried flowers, dark leaves, or a simple black and orange design — hung on or leaned against the bedroom mirror adds a seasonal focal point without using any surface space.

15. Framed Halloween Print

A framed vintage-style Halloween print — a moon, a botanical skull, a dark landscape — swapped into an existing frame adds atmosphere without buying new decor. Store it flat between seasons.

16. String Lights Around the Mirror

Warm string lights draped around a standing or wall mirror create a vanity-style glow that suits the Halloween aesthetic. Use battery-powered lights for flexibility.

Scent

17. A Seasonal Candle

A candle in a seasonal scent — pumpkin spice, dark amber, cedarwood, or black fig — adds an atmospheric layer that no visual decoration can replicate. One candle on the bedside table is enough.

18. Dried Herb Bundle

A bundle of dried sage or rosemary tied with dark ribbon and hung near the bed adds a subtle herbal scent and a slightly witchy quality. It also looks good on a hook or bedpost.

Finishing Details

19. Dark Ribbon on the Headboard

A length of dark velvet or satin ribbon tied loosely around the headboard or bedpost adds a seasonal detail that takes thirty seconds and costs almost nothing.

20. Seasonal Book Stack

A small stack of books with dark or Halloween-adjacent covers — gothic novels, a book of myths, anything with a dark spine — on the bedside table adds a subtle seasonal note that also looks intentional.

Final Thoughts

The strongest Halloween bedroom is the one that feels atmospheric rather than themed. Start with the lighting — swap the bulb and add string lights — then add one or two objects on the bedside table. Keep the bed itself comfortable and calm. The room should feel like a place you want to sleep in, not a display you have to dismantle before bed.

A Halloween boo basket is a small gift left anonymously on someone’s doorstep — the Halloween equivalent of a May Day basket. The tradition is to leave it, ring the bell, and run before you are seen.

The best boo baskets are personal rather than generic. The ideas below are organized by category so you can build a basket around what she actually likes.

Cozy Gifts

1. Fall Candle

A candle in a fall scent — pumpkin spice, apple cider, woodsmoke, or cinnamon — is the most universally appreciated boo basket item. Choose a quality candle in a glass jar she can reuse.

Look for candles with a burn time of at least 40 hours for the best value.

2. Cozy Socks

A pair of thick, cozy socks in a Halloween print — black cats, pumpkins, ghosts — or in a fall color — rust, mustard, forest green — is a practical gift that always gets used.

Choose a size that fits most adults — most cozy socks are one-size-fits-most.

3. Chunky Knit Mug

A chunky ceramic mug in a fall color — terracotta, sage, or cream — is a gift she will use every morning through the season. Fill it with a few hot chocolate sachets or tea bags.

Choose a mug with a handle large enough for a comfortable grip.

4. Cozy Blanket or Throw

A small throw blanket in a fall color or a Halloween print is a generous boo basket item that she will use all season. Choose a soft material — fleece, faux fur, or chunky knit.

Fold it neatly and place it at the bottom of the basket as the base layer.

5. Halloween Pajama Set

A Halloween-print pajama set — pumpkins, ghosts, or black cats — is a fun, cozy gift that suits the season. Choose a soft material and a relaxed fit.

Check the size before buying — pajamas are not one-size-fits-most.

6. Face Mask

A sheet mask or a clay mask in a Halloween-themed packaging — or simply a high-quality mask she would not buy herself — is a practical self-care gift. Add a pair of under-eye patches for extra points.

Choose a mask suited to her skin type if you know it.

7. Hand Cream

A rich hand cream in a fall scent — pumpkin, vanilla, or sandalwood — is a practical gift that gets used every day. Choose a tube rather than a jar for easier application.

A hand cream with SPF is a thoughtful upgrade.

8. Bath Bomb or Bath Salts

A Halloween-themed bath bomb or a jar of fall-scented bath salts is a luxurious self-care gift. Choose a scent she already likes rather than something unfamiliar.

Wrap the bath bomb in tissue paper so it does not crumble in the basket.

9. Nail Polish

A nail polish in a Halloween color — deep burgundy, matte black, dark plum, or burnt orange — is a small, personal gift. Choose a brand she already uses if you know it.

Add a nail file and a cuticle oil for a complete nail care set.

10. Lip Balm Set

A set of lip balms in fall flavors — pumpkin spice, apple cider, cinnamon — is a small, practical gift that fills the basket without taking up much space.

Choose a set with at least three flavors for variety.

11. Her Favorite Chocolate

A bar or box of her favorite chocolate is always the right choice. If you do not know her favorite, a high-quality dark chocolate bar is a safe bet.

Choose a chocolate with a Halloween-themed wrapper if available.

12. Halloween Candy Mix

A bag of mixed Halloween candy — candy corn, pumpkin-shaped chocolates, caramel apples — fills the basket and adds a festive touch. Choose a mix that includes her favorites.

Avoid candy she is allergic to — check before buying.

13. Spiced Nuts or Popcorn

A bag of spiced nuts or Halloween-flavored popcorn — caramel, cheddar, or kettle corn — is a savory option that balances the sweetness of the candy.

Choose a resealable bag so she can save some for later.

14. Hot Chocolate Mix

A jar or packet of premium hot chocolate mix — with marshmallows, or in a pumpkin spice or salted caramel flavor — is a cozy treat that suits the season.

Pair it with the chunky mug for a complete cozy gift set.

15. Pumpkin Spice Cookies or Biscuits

A box of pumpkin spice cookies, ginger snaps, or Halloween-shaped shortbread is a festive treat that looks impressive in the basket.

Choose a box with a clear window so the cookies are visible.

16. Halloween Earrings

A pair of small Halloween earrings — ghost studs, pumpkin hoops, or black cat drops — is a fun, wearable gift. Choose a style that suits her everyday jewelry rather than something overtly costume-like.

Sterling silver or gold-filled findings are worth the extra cost for sensitive ears.

A canvas tote bag with a Halloween print — a ghost, a pumpkin, or a spooky quote — is a practical gift she will use for grocery shopping or as a trick-or-treat bag.

Choose a bag with sturdy handles and a flat bottom.

18. Small Halloween Decoration

A small ceramic pumpkin, a skull candle holder, or a Halloween-print tea towel is a decorative gift she can use in her home. Choose something in a neutral palette — cream, terracotta, or black — rather than bright orange.

A Halloween-themed novel, a cozy mystery, or a book of ghost stories is a thoughtful gift for a reader. Choose a book she has not read rather than a classic she already owns.

Add a bookmark with a Halloween print for extra detail.

A set of scented wax melts in fall scents — pumpkin, cinnamon, apple — is a practical gift for someone who already owns a wax warmer. Choose a set with at least three different scents.

Check that she owns a wax warmer before buying wax melts.

Final Thoughts

The best boo basket is the one that feels personal rather than generic. Start with one item you know she will love — her favorite candle scent, her favorite chocolate, a cozy pair of socks — and build the rest of the basket around it. Presentation matters: a black or orange basket with tissue paper and a handwritten note makes even a modest collection of gifts feel special.

Common questions

What do you put in a Halloween boo basket for a woman?

The best boo baskets for women combine something cozy, something sweet, and something personal. A fall candle, her favorite chocolate, a face mask, a cozy pair of socks, and a small Halloween decoration cover all the bases. The best Halloween costumes for guys are the ones that are specific and committed. A generic vampire is forgettable. Dracula with the right cape, the right makeup, and the right accent is a conversation starter.

The ideas below are organized by style. Start with what you already own.

Classic and Timeless

1. Dracula

A black suit or tuxedo, a black cape, pale makeup, slicked-back hair, and theatrical fangs. The key is the commitment — Dracula speaks with an accent, moves with deliberate slowness, and never breaks character.

A quality cape is worth the investment — cheap ones look exactly like cheap capes.

2. Frankenstein’s Monster

Green face paint, a flat-top wig or hair styled upward, a dark suit with a white shirt, and bolts on the neck. This is a classic Halloween costume that is easy to execute and always recognizable.

The green face paint is the most important element — use theatrical face paint rather than craft paint.

3. Werewolf

Torn clothes, fur prosthetics or face paint, and a wild wig. The best werewolf costumes are mid-transformation — half human, half wolf — rather than fully transformed.

Prosthetic fur pieces from a costume store create the most convincing mid-transformation look.

4. Mummy

Wrap yourself in strips of white fabric or bandages, leaving gaps for the face and hands. Add grey and brown makeup to the exposed skin for a decayed look.

Use fabric strips rather than actual bandages — they are more comfortable and easier to move in.

5. Zombie

Torn, dirty clothes, pale and grey makeup, dark circles under the eyes, and fake blood. The best zombie costumes are specific — a zombie version of a specific character or profession.

Theatrical makeup is more convincing than face paint for zombie skin.

Pop Culture
