12. Witch Silhouette

A witch silhouette — a figure with a pointed hat, a broomstick, and a flowing cloak — cut into the pumpkin. Use a printed stencil for the most accurate result.

Cut the broomstick as a separate piece from the figure for a cleaner result.

13. Pumpkin Within a Pumpkin

Carve a small jack-o-lantern face into the surface of the pumpkin without cutting all the way through. The thin skin glows orange when lit, creating a pumpkin-within-a-pumpkin effect.

Use a linoleum carving tool for the shallow carving.

14. Constellation Map

Poke small holes in the pumpkin in the pattern of a constellation — Orion, the Big Dipper, or Cassiopeia. When lit, the holes create a star map effect. This is a beautiful, unusual design that suits an older child with an interest in astronomy.

Use a skewer or a thick needle to make the holes.

15. Portrait

Carve a portrait of a favorite character — a superhero, a movie character, or a family pet — into the pumpkin using a printed stencil. This is the most advanced design on the list and requires patience and steady hands.

Use a printed stencil and trace it onto the pumpkin with a toothpick before carving.

Finishing and Display

Once the pumpkin is carved, rub the cut edges with petroleum jelly to slow down drying and extend the pumpkin’s life. Light it with a battery tea light rather than a real candle — battery tea lights are safer, last longer, and can be left on all evening without supervision.

Display carved pumpkins in a cool, shaded spot during the day to extend their life. Bring them inside overnight if temperatures drop below freezing.

Final Thoughts

The best kid-friendly pumpkin carving experience is one where the child feels ownership over the design and the process. Let them choose the design, do as much of the carving as is safe for their age, and display the finished pumpkin prominently. The pride they feel in a pumpkin they made themselves is worth more than a perfectly executed design.

Still wondering

Common questions

What age can children start carving pumpkins?

Children can start scooping and painting pumpkins at any age. Supervised carving with child-safe plastic tools is appropriate from around age 6 or 7. Independent carving with adult supervision is suitable from around age 10 or 11, depending on the child's maturity and coordination.

What are the easiest pumpkin carving designs for beginners?

A classic triangle-eye, triangle-nose, and jagged-mouth jack-o-lantern is the easiest design. Simple geometric shapes — circles, squares, and triangles — are easier to carve cleanly than curved or detailed designs. Stencils help beginners achieve more complex designs without freehand drawing.

A kitchen corner can hide useful storage or become the place where pans and packets disappear. The right fix depends on whether the awkward space is inside a cabinet, on a counter, or along an unused wall. Start by measuring the space and deciding what should live there.

1. Add a Lazy Susan to a Corner Cabinet

A turntable makes oils, sauces, and jars at the back easier to reach. Measure the shelf and check that the tray clears the cabinet frame before choosing a size.

2. Install a Pull-Out Corner System

Swing-out or pull-out shelves bring the contents of a deep base cabinet toward you. Check the cabinet width, hinge position, and door opening; some systems need professional fitting.

3. Use a Two-Tier Turntable

Stacked rotating trays make use of vertical cabinet space for smaller items such as spice jars or tea boxes. Keep heavier bottles on the lower level.

4. Store Pots and Pans by Frequency

Keep the pans used every day near the front of a corner cabinet and move occasional baking dishes farther back. A simple grouping prevents the deepest space from becoming a random pile.

5. Add a Vertical Divider for Lids

A divider keeps pot lids, trays, and chopping boards standing upright. This makes each item visible and avoids lifting a stack to reach the one underneath.

6. Put a Shelf Riser in a Corner Cupboard

A low riser creates another level for cups, small bowls, or pantry jars. Choose a stable shelf that fits the cabinet depth and leaves enough headroom for the items above it.

7. Use a Corner Drawer Organizer

If the corner has a drawer, a fitted or adjustable organizer can separate utensils and small tools. Measure the drawer at its narrowest point because angled sides reduce usable space.

8. Create a Baking Zone

Keep mixing bowls, measuring cups, and baking ingredients together in one corner cabinet near the work surface. Grouping them by task saves steps and keeps the rest of the kitchen cabinets less crowded.

9. Put a Small Appliance on a Corner Shelf

A sturdy shelf can hold a lightweight appliance that is used regularly. Confirm the shelf’s load rating and keep cords away from the hob, sink, and hot surfaces.

10. Try an Appliance Garage

A countertop cabinet with a lift-up or roll-up door hides a toaster or coffee machine while keeping it plugged in. Check appliance ventilation requirements and leave room for heat to escape.

11. Use a Narrow Freestanding Corner Shelf

A small open shelf can fit into an unused wall corner for cookbooks, fruit, or a few everyday dishes. Keep its footprint out of the main path and secure tall furniture if children are in the home.

12. Hang a Rail on an Empty Wall Corner

A short rail with hooks can hold lightweight utensils or oven mitts. Before drilling, check for wiring and pipes, and choose fixings suited to the wall and the expected load.

13. Add Floating Shelves Above a Worktop

One or two shelves can make a bare corner useful for frequently used cups or small jars. Leave enough clearance below for appliances and avoid placing open food near steam or grease.

14. Store Dry Goods in Square Containers

Square containers make efficient use of straight-edged shelves and are easier to line up than round jars. Label the contents and keep the original use-by information accessible.

15. Make a Coffee or Tea Corner

Group mugs, tea, coffee, and a small tray in one corner so the routine has a defined home. Keep only daily supplies there; store refills elsewhere to prevent the area from spreading.

16. Use the Inside of a Cabinet Door

A shallow rack or a few hooks can hold lightweight measuring spoons, clips, or wraps. Check that the door still closes and that stored items do not hit the shelves.

17. Keep the Counter Corner Open for Prep

Not every corner needs an organizer. If it is part of the main preparation area, leave it clear or use one washable tray for the few items that belong there.

The best corner storage is easy to reach and sized for the things you actually use. Measure first, group items by task, and leave enough open space to cook and clean comfortably.

15 Kitchen Drawer Organization Ideas for Small Kitchens

Organize every kitchen drawer with 15 ideas covering cutlery trays, utensil dividers, spice drawers, junk drawer systems, and zone-based layouts for small kitchens.

The short version

  • Empty every drawer before organizing — start from a blank space.
  • Use adjustable dividers so the layout can change as needs change.
  • Group items by task — cooking tools together, baking tools together, serving tools together.
  • A dedicated junk drawer with a simple tray is better than letting clutter spread to every drawer.

Kitchen drawers become unusable when everything is mixed together. The fix is not more drawers — it is a clear system in the drawers you already have.

These ideas cover the specific approaches that make kitchen drawers faster to use and easier to maintain in a small kitchen.

1. Empty Every Drawer Before Organizing

Remove everything from every drawer before deciding what should live where. This prevents the habit of organizing around existing clutter and makes it easier to see what you actually have.

Wipe the drawers while they are empty.

2. Use Adjustable Dividers

Adjustable dividers let you customize the layout of each drawer to fit the items inside. They are more flexible than fixed inserts and can be repositioned as needs change.

Measure the drawer interior before buying — dividers vary in length and height.

3. Dedicate One Drawer to Cutlery

A cutlery tray in a dedicated drawer keeps knives, forks, and spoons separated and easy to find. Choose a tray that fits the drawer width exactly — a tray that slides around is harder to use.

Add a section for serving spoons and a small section for teaspoons if the drawer is large enough.

4. Group Utensils by Task

Group cooking utensils by task: stirring and flipping tools together, measuring tools together, and baking tools together. This makes it faster to find what you need when cooking.

Use a drawer divider to separate the groups clearly.

5. Use a Deep Drawer for Pots and Pans

If you have a deep drawer, use it for pots, pans, or lids rather than a cabinet. Drawers are easier to access than deep cabinets because you can see everything at once.

Add a non-slip liner to prevent items from sliding.

6. Create a Dedicated Spice Drawer

A shallow drawer with a spice insert — angled rows that hold jars label-up — makes it easy to find any spice at a glance. This is more practical than a spice rack on the counter or a cabinet shelf.

Label the top of each jar so the name is visible when the drawer is open.

7. Use a Knife Block Insert

A knife block insert in a drawer keeps knives safely stored and easily accessible. It is safer than a loose knife in a drawer and takes up less counter space than a freestanding knife block.

Choose an insert rated for the size of your knives.

8. Add a Foil and Wrap Organizer

A foil and wrap organizer in a drawer keeps cling film, foil, and baking paper in one place and makes it easy to tear off a sheet without the roll falling out.

A simple tension rod inside a cabinet door also works for this purpose.

9. Use a Junk Drawer With a Tray

Every kitchen needs a junk drawer. The key is to contain the junk with a simple tray or a few small bins. This prevents the clutter from spreading to other drawers.

Review the junk drawer every few months and remove anything that has found a permanent home elsewhere.

10. Store Batteries and Small Tools Together

A small section of the junk drawer — or a dedicated small drawer — for batteries, a tape measure, scissors, and a screwdriver keeps these items findable without a dedicated tool box.

Use a small bin or tray to keep these items grouped.

11. Use a Drawer for Tea and Coffee Supplies

A shallow drawer near the kettle for tea bags, coffee pods, and sweeteners keeps the counter clear and the supplies organized. Use a simple tray or a few small bins to separate the categories.

This works particularly well in a small kitchen where counter space is limited.

12. Add Non-Slip Liner to Every Drawer

A non-slip liner prevents items from sliding around when the drawer is opened and closed. It also protects the drawer base from scratches and makes it easier to clean.

Cut the liner to fit the drawer exactly.

13. Use a Drawer for Plastic Bags and Wraps

A dedicated drawer for plastic bags, reusable bags, and food wraps keeps these items out of sight and easy to find. Use a simple bag dispenser or a small bin to keep them organized.

Fold reusable bags neatly so they take up less space.

14. Label Every Drawer

Labels on the outside of drawers make it clear where things belong and reduce the time spent searching. Use simple text labels or small icons.

Labels are especially useful in a shared kitchen where different people put things away.

15. Review the System Regularly

A drawer organization system that works today may not work in six months as habits and needs change. Review each drawer regularly and adjust the arrangement as needed.

The goal is a system that makes cooking faster and easier, not one that looks perfect in a photograph.

Final Thoughts

Kitchen drawer organization works best when it starts with a clear-out, uses adjustable dividers, and groups items by task. Start with the cutlery drawer and the utensil drawer — those two changes alone make a significant difference to how the kitchen feels to use.

Minimalist Living Rooms: Less Is More

Create a serene, clutter-free living room that prioritizes calm, function, and timeless beauty. A complete guide to minimalist design principles.

The Philosophy Behind Minimalist Living

Minimalism isn’t about having nothing. It’s about having only what serves you. A minimalist living room is a space stripped of excess, where every piece has purpose and intentionality. The result? A room that feels calm, spacious, and paradoxically, more inviting.

Recent studies show that visual clutter increases cortisol (stress hormone) production. By embracing minimalism, you’re literally designing for better mental health.

The Three Pillars of Minimalist Design

1. Simplicity Strip away ornament and decoration. A minimalist room celebrates clean lines, open space, and the beauty of emptiness. This doesn’t mean austere or cold—it means thoughtful curation.

2. Function Every item earns its place. A chair must be comfortable to sit in. A side table must hold what you actually use. Decoration without purpose is clutter in disguise.

3. Quality Over Quantity One beautiful, well-made sofa beats five mediocre ones. Invest in pieces that last, that feel good to use, and that age beautifully. This is how minimalism becomes sustainable.

The Color Palette

Minimalist rooms typically lean on neutral bases because they’re restful. But “neutral” doesn’t mean boring.

The Core Palette:

  • One soft base color (off-white, soft gray, warm beige) for walls and large surfaces
  • A secondary neutral for contrast (slightly darker shade of the same family)
  • One accent color—just one—for depth and character

Ratios that Work:

  • 70% base neutral
  • 25% secondary neutral
  • 5% accent color (used in a single piece of art, a throw, a plant pot)

The accent color is your only permission to break the minimalist code. Use it wisely.

Furniture: The Essentials

You need four things in a living room: something to sit on, something to rest your feet, something to rest drinks on, and storage for life’s necessities.

The Sofa: Choose a neutral-colored sofa in a natural fabric (linen, cotton, wool). Two-seater or three-seater? Whatever fits your space without dominating it. Avoid sectionals unless your room is genuinely large—they tend to fill space and reduce flexibility.

Seating: One accent chair in your base neutral, or a pair of simple wooden chairs. No more. Minimalism means hosting one friend at a time instead of entertaining a crowd, and that’s okay.

The Table: A simple wooden coffee table or a marble-top side table. Keep the legs visible (this makes a room feel less heavy) and choose a finish that will develop character with age—natural wood is perfect.

Storage: A single credenza or shelving unit. This is where your minimalism actually lives—behind closed doors or on floating shelves that look intentional, not cluttered. Floating shelves should hold objects spaced out with breathing room between them.

The Walls

Minimalist walls are quiet. Very quiet.

Option A: Blank Canvas Pure white or soft gray walls with zero decoration. This creates a truly meditative space. It sounds austere until you’re sitting in it—the emptiness becomes your decoration.

Option B: One Statement Piece A single large artwork (abstract, photography, or a minimal landscape). Let it breathe. One piece per wall, maximum. The negative space around it is as important as the artwork itself.

Option C: Texture Over Pattern A subtle linen wallpaper, or walls painted in a matte finish that catches light softly. No pattern, no busy-ness. The texture is barely noticeable—it just makes the room feel less flat.

Never use wallpaper with pattern in minimalist spaces. Pattern competes with emptiness.

Lighting Design

Lighting is your secret weapon in minimalist design. It creates mood without adding clutter.

  • One ceiling fixture (recessed or a simple flush mount)
  • One floor lamp with a minimal silhouette
  • No table lamps, no string lights, no “mood lighting”

Lamps should have simple cylindrical or conical shades in white or off-white linen. Brass or matte black bases add a touch of elegance without fuss.

The Art of Strategic Emptiness

Here’s where minimalism becomes design. The empty spaces are as curated as the filled ones.

Wall Space Above Furniture: Leave it blank. Resist the urge to “fill” it. That emptiness makes your room feel bigger and calmer.

Shelf Space: If you have five shelves, style three of them and leave two bare. Sounds wrong? It feels right. Group objects in threes, leave breathing room, and don’t fill every inch.

Floor Space: Area rug should not cover the entire floor. Let hardwood or natural flooring show around the edges. This keeps the room feeling light and spacious.

Plants: The Exception to Minimalism

Plants are acceptable—even encouraged—in minimalist spaces. They’re alive, they serve a function (air purification), and they add subtle warmth without clutter. But follow the rule: 2-3 plants, maximum. Choose tall varieties (fiddle leaf fig, snake plant) that draw the eye upward, making rooms feel more spacious.

Pots should be in white, soft gray, or natural ceramic. All the same material and color family for cohesion.

Styling Your Minimalist Living Room

When styling is complete, your room should pass this test: Can you describe it in one sentence?

“A neutral living room with a linen sofa, one artwork, and a single potted plant.”

If you need three sentences to describe your “minimalist” room, there’s too much happening.

The Honest Assessment

Minimalism requires discipline. Every time you bring something home, something else must leave. Every time you decorate for a holiday, it must be removed (minimal holiday decor = white lights and one gold accent).

But the payoff is real. Minimalist rooms are cheaper to furnish (quality over quantity), easier to clean, more restful to inhabit, and they age beautifully—there’s nothing trendy to go out of style.

Your minimalist living room is a practice, not a destination. Start with the essentials, add only what sparks joy, and embrace the freedom of empty space.

The Kitchen Island: Clearance, Overhang and What Goes on Top

Islands fail on measurements long before they fail on styling. The clearances, seating overhangs and the three-object rule for a surface you actually use.

In this article

  2. 02Seating overhang

  6. 06Making it survive real life
  7. 07When a trolley beats an island

An island is the most expensive thing in most kitchen renovations and the easiest to get wrong, because the mistakes are dimensional and therefore permanent. A beautiful island with 85cm of walkway behind it will irritate you every single day, and no amount of styling fixes it.

So: measurements first, objects second.

The clearances, in centimetres

These are the numbers to design around. They are not aspirational — below them, the kitchen genuinely does not work.

Walkway around the island:

  • 100cm minimum on any side you walk down
  • 110–120cm on the working side, between the island and the run with the hob or sink — you need room to turn with an open oven door
  • 120cm+ if two people cook at once, or if a dishwasher and an oven door both open into the same aisle
  • 90cm is the absolute floor, and only on a side nobody works on

The commonest error is designing to 90cm all round because it fits. It fits until someone opens the dishwasher.

Island size:

  • Minimum useful: 100cm × 60cm. Below this it is a table, not an island.
  • Comfortable: 180–240cm × 90–100cm
  • Depth over 120cm means you cannot reach the middle from either side — anything you put there is lost.

Check the room can take it: island width + 100cm + 110cm of aisle. A 240cm island needs a room at least 450cm wide. If your kitchen is under 370cm wide, you probably want a peninsula or a trolley rather than an island.

If the numbers do not work, the honest answer is no island. A cramped island makes a kitchen worse than no island at all, and a good galley layout beats a bad island layout every time.

Seating overhang

If people are going to sit at it, the worktop has to overhang far enough for knees.

  • Standard height (90cm worktop, 65cm stool): 30cm overhang
  • Bar height (105cm worktop, 75cm stool): 25cm overhang
  • Table height (75cm, dining chair): 40cm overhang

Width per seat: 60cm. So a 180cm island seats three comfortably, or two with elbow room. Squeezing four onto 180cm means nobody can cut anything up.

An overhang beyond about 25cm on stone needs support — steel corbels or a hidden bracket set into the cabinetry. Unsupported granite or quartz will crack, usually when someone leans on the edge.

Where the services go

Decide early, because these need routing through the floor.

Sink in the island: good for sociability — you face the room while washing up. Costs you the largest run of uninterrupted worktop, and you will look at dirty dishes from the sofa.

Hob in the island: dramatic, and needs extraction. A ceiling hood over an island is expensive and visually dominant; a downdraft extractor is neater and less effective. Also consider that spitting oil now has a 360° audience.

Neither: the best answer for most kitchens. An uninterrupted island is enormously useful for prep, homework, laying out food and everything else, and you keep the sink under the window where it belongs.

Whatever you choose, put at least two double sockets in the island ends. Everyone forgets, everyone regrets it.

Overhead lighting

Pendants over an island are the single most-photographed and most-miscalculated element in a kitchen.

  • Height: the bottom of the pendant sits 75–85cm above the worktop. Higher and it stops lighting the surface; lower and you cannot see the person opposite.
  • How many: two large ones, or three small ones, on an island up to 240cm. Even numbers of large fittings and odd numbers of small ones both look deliberate; three large fittings usually look crowded.
  • Spacing: centre the group on the island, then space them so the outermost pendants sit at least 30cm in from the island ends.
  • Bulbs: 2700–3000K, and get them dimmable. An island is a prep surface at 6pm and a wine table at 10pm.

What goes on top

Now the styling — and the rule is restraint, because the island’s value is its emptiness. A clear metre of worktop is worth more than any object you could put on it.

The three-object rule: at most three groupings on the island, occupying no more than a third of the surface, clustered towards one end.

A reliable trio:

  1. Something living — a herb in a good pot, or a bowl of fruit. Real, and used.
  2. Something practical — a wooden board leaning or lying flat, a stone mortar, a crock of utensils.
  3. Something low — a shallow bowl, a stack of two linen napkins, a small dish of salt.

Cluster them at one end. The other two-thirds stays empty and available. That empty run is what makes a kitchen feel calm and expensive, and it is exactly what gets lost when the island becomes a landing strip for post and car keys.

The material story

Keep the island’s objects in the same material family as the rest of the kitchen. If your shelves are ceramic-and-wood, the island is ceramic-and-wood — the same logic we set out in our open shelving guide. Mixing chrome, brass, plastic and stone on one surface reads as unresolved.

Making it survive real life

The island is where everything lands. Two habits keep it clear:

  • Give the landing pile a home elsewhere — a tray, a drawer or a hook by the door. The island cannot be the default surface if something else is closer to the entrance.
  • Reset it when you finish cooking, not before you next cook. Wiping down while the oven cools takes ninety seconds; doing it the next morning takes ten minutes and a scraper.

If you have children, accept that a third of the island belongs to homework and craft between four and six. Design the seating end for that and keep the working end clear.

When a trolley beats an island

If your kitchen cannot make the clearance numbers, a butcher’s block on castors gives you most of the benefit:

  • Extra prep surface where you need it
  • Moves out of the way for a full clear floor
  • A tenth of the cost
  • No services, no structural work

Get one with a solid top, locking castors and a shelf underneath. It is not a compromise so much as a different, often better, answer for a room under 370cm wide.

Working out the surfaces around it? Our open shelving guide covers the 70/30 rule for everything on display.

The Open Shelving Question: Beautiful or Chaotic?

Open shelving has been a divisive trend for five years now. The Scandinavian minimalist crowd loves it. The “I actually cook” crowd? Less sure.

The truth: open shelving works brilliantly when you commit to the styling and accept that it requires maintenance. It’s not for everyone, but when it’s done right, it looks like you have your life together (even if your chaos is just behind closed doors below).

The No-Stress Open Shelving Formula

Step 1: Choose Your Material Vocabulary

Everything on your open shelves should speak the same visual language. Pick two material families:

Option A (Warm & Natural):

  • Ceramic in warm whites and creams
  • Wood items (wooden spoons, cutting boards)
  • Linen towels
  • Glass
  • Brass or warm metal accents

Option B (Cool & Minimal):

  • White or pale gray ceramics
  • Stainless steel
  • Clear glass
  • Soft gray linen
  • Minimal metal (black or brushed chrome)

Option C (Eclectic Maximalist):

  • One accent color (sage, terracotta, or blue)
  • Mix of materials but unified by color
  • Patterned bowls and mugs in the same palette
  • Texture variation (matte, glossy, ceramic, wood)

Do not mix material families. A shelf with both brass and stainless steel and warm wood and cool ceramics reads as unmotivated.

The Math of Open Shelf Styling

Designers use a formula, and once you understand it, styling becomes system-based instead of chaotic.

The 70-30 Rule

  • 70%: Functional items (bowls, plates, glasses, cooking tools)
  • 30%: Decorative items (small plants, books standing up, a framed recipe, a pretty pitcher)

This keeps your shelves looking collected rather than cluttered. If you go over 30% decorative, it starts feeling like a shelf in a gift shop. Below 30%, it feels cold and under-styled.

The Height + Weight Distribution

Top shelf: Keep it light visually. Stack 2-3 lightweight items (bowls stacked, a small plant, a single cookbook standing up). Leave 60% of the shelf empty.

Middle shelf(s): This is your feature shelf. This is where heavier visual weight lives. A large serving bowl, stacked plates, a small pitcher, a few mugs hung on a rail.

Bottom shelf: Repeat the top shelf’s lightness. Heavy items (cast iron, canned goods) belong below eye level in a cabinet.

The Grouping Rule

Never dot items across the entire shelf. Group things in clusters of 3-5, leaving gaps. This looks intentional. Spreading items across the full shelf reads as “I had nothing to put here.”

Example arrangement for a 36-inch shelf:

  • Left cluster: 3 stacked bowls, one small plant
  • Center gap: 12 inches of empty shelf
  • Right cluster: 4 coffee mugs on hooks, one glass pitcher

Styling by Category

Ceramics & Dishware

Stack plates to save space and add height variation. Group bowls by color if you have them, or by size if you’re working with white-on-white.

Hang mugs on small brass hooks for visual interest. Pro move: hang 3-5 mugs, not 12. Shows intentionality.

Glassware

Group drinking glasses together in one area. Let them breathe—no need to cram them in. The negative space around glass actually makes it look more luxe.

Drink-ware should be your most neutral zone. No patterned drinking glasses on view shelves; save those for the cabinet.

Cookbooks

Display 2-4 books standing upright (spines out if they’re beautiful, or facing out if the cover is stunning). Lay one flat if it’s oversized. This adds visual depth.

Small Appliances

A sleek coffee maker or stand mixer is fine on open shelves if it’s an appliance you actually use and love the look of. A cluttered toaster oven? Cabinet time.

A freestanding rack can make a separate appliance and coffee zone so your wall shelves stay easier to style and use.

Plants

A single small potted plant per shelf, never more. Trailing plants (pothos, string of pearls) add lovely visual movement. Tall plants steal height real estate.

The Maintenance Reality

Open shelving needs tidying once a week minimum, more if you cook heavily. Dust settles on everything. Grease builds up if you cook with high heat.

The honest maintenance schedule:

  • Weekly wipe-down: Takes 10 minutes with a microfiber cloth
  • Monthly deep clean: Remove everything, wipe shelves, replace items
  • Seasonal styling refresh: Swap seasonal items (winter whites for spring pastels, etc.)

If you’re not willing to do this, open shelving will drive you crazy.

Common Open Shelving Mistakes (And How to Fix Them)

Mistake #1: Too Many Mugs Fix: Keep 4-6 mugs on display. Everything else lives in a cabinet.

Mistake #2: Dusty, Cluttered Look Fix: Reduce items by 30%, increase spacing, commit to weekly dusting.

Mistake #3: Looks Like A Gift Shop Fix: Remove decorative items. Keep to 20% instead of 30%, and make sure they have function (a pretty bowl you use, a cookbook you actually cook from).

Mistake #4: Too Matchy-Matchy Fix: All-white shelves are pure minimalist, but they can read sterile. Add one accent color (one terracotta bowl, one sage bowl) to warm it up.

Mistake #5: Uneven Shelves Visually Fix: If your shelves are physically uneven, this is on your contractor. If they’re even but look uneven, you’re clustering too much on one side. Mirror your arrangement: if you have heavy weight on the left, balance it with something on the right.

The Hybrid Approach (Best For Real Humans)

Open shelves look great, but not everyone has 30 minutes a week for styling maintenance. Consider this:

  • Top shelf: Open, fully styled (decorative items + one functional thing)
  • Middle shelf: Open, 50-50 functional/decorative
  • Bottom shelf: Closed cabinet doors (or the shelf below is cabinets)

This gives you the look of open shelving without the full commitment.

When Open Shelving Actually Saves Time

Yes, really. If you use your kitchen actively, open shelving accelerates your workflow:

  • Grab mugs, bowls, plates without opening doors (faster in the morning)
  • You see what you have (less forgotten condiments)
  • Kids can reach (if shelves are low enough)
  • No cabinet door slams in the morning

The styling maintenance is a trade-off for functional efficiency.

Final Checklist: Is Your Open Shelving Winning?

  • Can you touch every item on your shelves without moving something else? ✓
  • Does the shelf have at least 2-3 inches of breathing room? ✓
  • Are items grouped in clusters (not spread out)? ✓
  • Is your material story consistent? ✓
  • Would you leave your kitchen like this if a friend stopped by? ✓

If you hit all five, your open shelving is functional and beautiful.

Living Room Layout: The Measurements Nobody Tells You

Why your furniture is pushed against the walls and why that is the problem. Conversation distances, rug sizes and the float that makes a room work.

The short version

  • Facing seats want 180-240cm between them; that single distance separates a room people talk in from one that feels like a waiting area.
  • Floating the sofa 20-30cm off the wall makes the room read larger, not smaller.
  • A rug that is too small is the most damaging error in a living room — every seat needs at least its front legs on it.
  • Leave 90cm clear for the main route through the room and 60cm for secondary ones.
  • Pick one focal point and aim the primary seating at it; a room serving two never resolves.

Almost every living room that feels wrong has the same layout: every piece of furniture pushed flat against a wall, a large empty rectangle in the middle, and a rug that is too small floating somewhere near the coffee table. It is the arrangement people default to because it seems to maximise space, and it is precisely why the room does not work.

The room does not need more space in the middle. It needs the seating close enough for people to talk.

The conversation distance

Two people can hold a comfortable conversation with 180 to 240cm between them. Under 180cm feels close for anyone who is not family. Over 240cm and people raise their voices slightly, which is enough to make a room feel unwelcoming without anyone knowing why.

Measure across your seating right now — sofa front edge to the chair opposite. In most rooms with wall-hugging furniture it is well over 300cm, and the room feels cold as a result.

The fix is to float the furniture. Pull the sofa 20–30cm off the wall at minimum, and bring the opposing seat in. That small gap behind the sofa does something odd and reliable: it makes the room read as larger, because the eye registers space continuing behind the furniture rather than stopping at it.

A room with everything against the walls looks like a waiting room, because waiting rooms are arranged for circulation rather than conversation. Yours should be arranged for conversation.

The numbers to design around

Seating and tables

  • Sofa to coffee table: 40–45cm. Close enough to reach a cup without standing, far enough for knees.
  • Coffee table height: level with the sofa seat, or up to 5cm below. Higher looks wrong and is awkward to reach into.
  • Coffee table length: roughly two-thirds the length of the sofa.
  • Side table height: level with the arm of the chair it serves, ±5cm.
  • Seat to TV: 1.5–2.5× the screen diagonal. A 55” screen wants roughly 2.1–3.5m.

Circulation

  • Main walking route through the room: 90cm clear
  • Secondary routes (between coffee table and sofa, around a chair): 60cm
  • In front of a fireplace: 90cm clear, and nothing flammable within a metre

Wall and hanging

  • Art centre: 145–150cm from the floor — gallery standard, and it works.
  • Art above a sofa: the bottom edge 20–25cm above the sofa back; the piece should be roughly two-thirds the sofa’s width.
  • Curtain pole: as high as possible, ideally 10–15cm below the ceiling, and 15–25cm wider than the window each side so the curtains stack off the glass. This single change makes windows look substantially larger.

Rug size — where most rooms go wrong

A rug that is too small is the most common and most damaging error in a living room. It shrinks the seating area visually and makes every piece of furniture look unrelated to every other.

Three correct approaches, in order of preference:

1. All legs on. Every piece of seating sits entirely on the rug, with at least 15–20cm of rug showing beyond. Needs a large rug — usually 240×340 for a normal room — and it is the most generous, expensive and best-looking option.

2. Front legs on. The front legs of every seat sit on the rug, the back legs on the floor. This is the sensible middle path and works in most rooms with a 200×290. Critically, every piece must follow the same rule — one chair floating off the rug breaks the whole arrangement.

3. All legs off. Only acceptable for a small rug used as a deliberate accent in a tiny room. In a normal room it looks like a mistake.

Leave 20–45cm of bare floor between the rug edge and the walls. A rug that runs almost to the skirting reads as failed wall-to-wall carpet.

Find the focal point, then commit

Every living room has one natural focus. Usually a fireplace, sometimes a window with a view, occasionally — reluctantly — the television.

Pick it, then aim the primary seating at it. Rooms feel unresolved when the sofa faces the fireplace and the chairs face the TV on another wall, because the arrangement is trying to serve two masters.

If the TV and the fireplace are on different walls, the honest answer is to choose. Angle the seating to favour one and accept the other is a secondary view, or put the TV above the fireplace if the height works — bottom of the screen no more than 120cm from the floor, or you will be craning.

Three layouts that work

The standard pairing. Sofa facing a fireplace, two chairs at right angles forming a U, coffee table in the middle, everything on one large rug. Works in most rectangular rooms 350cm wide and up. Seats five, conversation distance around 200cm.

The facing sofas. Two sofas parallel, 200cm apart, coffee table between, console or fireplace at one end. Formal, excellent for conversation, hopeless for television. Needs a room at least 400cm wide.

The L with a float. Sofa along the longest wall but pulled 25cm off it, chaise or chair perpendicular forming an L, rug anchoring both. The best answer for narrow rooms, and the arrangement that most often rescues a room that “just does not work.”

Long narrow rooms

The special case, and the one that defeats most people. The instinct is to line both long walls with furniture, which creates a corridor.

Instead, break the room into two zones across its width:

  • Main seating group at one end, arranged around its own rug
  • A second function at the other end — a small dining table, a desk, a reading chair
  • A console table, an open shelf or the back of the sofa marking the division

Two square-ish zones read far better than one long thin one. The zoning principles are much the same as in our studio zoning guide, just with fewer functions to fit.

The test

When you think you are done, sit in every seat.

  • Can you reach a surface to put a drink down without standing? If not, you need another side table.
  • Can you talk to the person opposite without projecting?
  • Is there a light within reach that you can turn on without crossing the room?
  • Can you get from the door to your seat without turning sideways?

A room that fails any of those will quietly go unused, however good it looks in a photograph.

Still wondering

Common questions

How far apart should a sofa and chairs be?

180 to 240cm between facing seats. Closer than 180cm feels intimate to the point of awkward with guests. Further than 240cm and people raise their voices slightly, which makes a room feel unwelcoming without anyone being able to say why.

What size rug do I need for a living room?

Large enough that the front legs of every seat sit on it — usually 200x290cm. For all legs on, with 15-20cm of rug showing beyond the furniture, you generally need 240x340cm. Leave 20-45cm of bare floor between the rug and the walls.

Should living room furniture be pushed against the walls?

No. Pull the sofa at least 20-30cm off the wall. The gap lets the eye register space continuing behind the furniture, so the room reads as larger, and it brings the seating close enough for people to hold a conversation.

How far should the coffee table be from the sofa?

40-45cm — close enough to set a cup down without standing, far enough for knees. Keep the table level with the sofa seat or up to 5cm below it, and roughly two-thirds the length of the sofa.

How high should art hang above a sofa?

The bottom edge 20-25cm above the sofa back, with the piece roughly two-thirds the sofa's width. Art on an empty wall should be centred 145-150cm from the floor, which is the gallery standard and works in almost every room.

How do I lay out a long narrow living room?

Break it into two zones across its width instead of lining both long walls, which only creates a corridor. Main seating around its own rug at one end, a second function at the other, with a console or the back of the sofa marking the division.

Rumi from K-Pop Demon Hunters has become one of the most searched Halloween costumes of the year, and it is easy to see why. The look is specific enough to be recognisable but wearable enough to last a full night out. The combination of dragon braids, pink argyle, and combat-ready layering is genuinely striking.

The ideas below cover solo looks, duo options, and full squad builds. Start with the elements that are easiest to source and build outward.

The Core Elements

1. Get the Dragon Braids Right First

Dragon braids are the single most recognisable part of the Rumi look. Two thick braids with a slight wave, secured with dark ribbon or cord, read immediately to anyone who knows the character. Everything else is secondary.

If your hair is too short for braids, clip-in extensions in a matching colour work well and take about twenty minutes to install.

2. Pink Argyle Knitwear

Rumi’s signature pink argyle vest or sweater is the centrepiece of the costume. Look for dusty pink rather than hot pink — the palette is muted and slightly vintage, not neon. A thrifted argyle vest over a dark long-sleeve top is the most accurate and affordable option.

3. Dark Combat Layers Underneath

Under the knitwear, Rumi wears dark, combat-ready layers — a fitted black or charcoal long-sleeve top, dark trousers, and boots with some weight to them. The contrast between the soft pink argyle and the harder underlayers is what makes the look work.

4. The Colour Palette

Dusty pink, charcoal, deep burgundy, and off-white. Avoid anything too bright or too clean — the aesthetic is slightly worn-in and battle-ready, not pristine idol.

Solo Costume Builds

5. The Accurate Build

Pink argyle vest, dark fitted long-sleeve, black or charcoal straight-leg trousers, chunky boots, dragon braids, dark ribbon. This is the closest to screen-accurate and requires no sewing.

6. The Elevated Build

Commission or buy a custom pink argyle vest with the exact diamond pattern from the show. Pair with tailored dark trousers and leather-look boots. Add a small prop — a charm or pendant that references the show — for the finishing detail.

7. The Budget Build

Thrifted argyle knitwear in any pink tone, dark jeans, boots you already own, and clip-in braids. The total cost can be under twenty pounds if you shop secondhand.

8. The Warm-Weather Build

For indoor parties or warmer climates, swap the long-sleeve underlayer for a dark fitted tank and keep the argyle vest as the main piece. Add a light dark jacket you can remove.

9. The Cold-Weather Build

Layer a dark oversized coat over the full look. Rumi’s coat in later episodes is a long charcoal or dark burgundy style — this doubles as a practical outer layer for outdoor events.

Makeup and Accessories

10. The Makeup

Rumi’s makeup is clean with one strong element — a deep burgundy or berry lip. Keep the base natural, add a subtle smoky eye in charcoal or taupe, and finish with the dark lip. Avoid heavy contouring.

11. The Accessories

Dark cord or ribbon for the braids, a simple silver or dark metal ring or two, and boots with some visual weight. Avoid anything too delicate or sparkly — the aesthetic is grounded, not glamorous.

12. The Prop

A small prop referencing the show — a charm, a card, or a handmade badge — adds a layer of detail that fans will notice immediately. Keep it small enough to carry easily.

Duo and Group Builds

13. Rumi and Mira Duo

Rumi in pink argyle and dragon braids; Mira in the show’s darker colour palette with her signature hair. The contrast between the two looks makes the duo immediately recognisable.

14. Full Demon Hunters Squad

Assign each person one of the main Demon Hunters characters. Rumi is the most visually distinctive, so whoever does Rumi anchors the group. Coordinate the colour palettes so the group reads as a unit.

15. Rumi and Civilian Contrast

One person in full Rumi costume, one in a plain civilian outfit from the show’s world. The contrast plays well for photos and is easy to execute.

16. Gender-Swapped Rumi

The argyle vest and dragon braids translate well across genders. Keep the core colour palette and silhouette — the costume reads regardless of who is wearing it.

17. Casual Rumi

A pink argyle crewneck (rather than vest), dark jeans, and white trainers is a more casual interpretation that works for daytime events or low-key parties.

18. Elevated Rumi

A tailored pink argyle blazer over a dark turtleneck, with wide-leg dark trousers and heeled boots, takes the look in a more fashion-forward direction while keeping the character recognisable.

19. Couples Costume with a Non-Fan Partner

If your partner does not know the show, put them in a simple dark outfit with one Demon Hunters-adjacent detail — a dark coat, a charm, a specific colour. You do Rumi in full; they do a supporting character in a simplified version.

20. Last-Minute Rumi

Dragon braids, any pink knitwear, dark jeans, dark boots. If you have those four elements, the costume works. The braids are the non-negotiable — everything else can be approximated.

Final Thoughts

The Rumi costume works because it is specific without being complicated. Get the dragon braids and the pink argyle right and the rest follows naturally. Start with what you already own, fill the gaps with thrifted pieces, and keep the palette muted. The result is one of the most recognisable costumes of the season without requiring a single piece of specialist kit.

Mudroom Ideas for Small Homes

A mudroom is a luxury most homes don’t have. What most of us have is a back door, a patch of floor, and a growing pile of boots.

The good news: a mudroom is a function, not a room. You can build one into a corner, a wall, a closet or a garage entry — and it’ll work almost as well as the purpose-built version.

What a mudroom actually needs

Strip it back and there are four requirements:

  1. A place to sit to take shoes off
  2. A place shoes drain and dry without soaking the floor
  3. Hooks for coats and bags
  4. Flooring that survives water and grit

Everything else is nice-to-have. If your space delivers those four, you have a mudroom.

The minimum footprint

You can build a functional mudroom in 36 inches of wall. That gives you:

  • A 36-inch bench
  • Three hooks above it
  • A boot tray underneath

For a family of four, aim for 60 inches so everyone gets a hook and a cubby. Beyond 72 inches you’re into genuine comfort with room for a cabinet.

Depth matters more than width. You need 16–18 inches for a bench people can actually sit on, plus 30 inches of clear floor in front of it.

1. The bench-and-hook wall

The simplest and most effective layout. A bench against the wall, a rail of hooks above at 60 inches, baskets underneath.

Buy a storage bench or build one from a stock kitchen cabinet laid on its side with a wood top screwed on — a common trick that costs a fraction of purpose-built mudroom furniture and looks identical once painted.

2. Individual cubbies

If you have kids, cubbies solve arguments. One vertical slot per person, each with a hook, a shelf above for hats, and a basket below for shoes.

Cubby width: 12–16 inches per person. Any narrower and coats won’t hang properly.

Label them. Sounds fussy, works remarkably well.

3. Turn a closet into a mudroom

If there’s a coat closet near your back door, take the doors off. Remove the single rod and shelf, and rebuild the inside as a mini mudroom: bench across the bottom, hooks on the back wall, shelf above.

You gain far more usable storage than the closet ever provided, because a rod-and-shelf closet wastes most of its volume.

Paint the interior a contrasting colour and it reads as a designed nook rather than a stripped closet.

4. Garage entry mudroom

For homes where everyone comes in through the garage, build the mudroom on the garage side of the door. Boots come off before they ever enter the house.

A wall-mounted rack, a bench and a mat handle it. Add a bin for sports equipment and a hook for the dog lead.

5. Bench seating with storage inside

Lift-top benches hide seasonal items — winter gloves in summer, sunhats in winter. They’re the highest-value storage per square foot in the whole space.

The trade-off is you have to move everything off the bench to open it, so use it for things you access seasonally rather than daily.

Flooring that survives

This is where a mudroom is won or lost. Choose one:

Tile — the traditional choice. Waterproof, tough, easy to mop. Choose textured or matte finish (wet tile is slippery) and a mid-tone colour that hides grit. Dark grout.

Luxury vinyl plank — waterproof, warmer underfoot, cheaper to install, and forgiving of dropped boots. The most practical choice for most homes now.

Sealed concrete — perfect in a garage entry. Basically indestructible.

Avoid unsealed wood, laminate and light-coloured grout. All three will look ruined within a year.

The drainage detail people forget

Wet boots need somewhere for water to go. A boot tray with a raised rim and ridged base keeps the water off your floor and lets the boots dry.

For a bigger family, a low-sided galvanised tray or a purpose-made boot mat with a lip works better than individual trays that slide around.

Add a small mat inside the door too — grit stopped at the door is grit you don’t have to sweep.

6. Hooks over rods, always

In a mudroom, hooks beat a hanging rail every time. Coats come off and go straight on. Nobody uses a hanger when they’re carrying groceries.

Use double hooks — one arm for the coat, one for the bag. Rated for at least 15 lbs.

Height: 60–66 inches for adults, 40 inches for kids, 44 inches for bags.

7. Small storage that pulls its weight

  • Basket per person for shoes, under the bench
  • A single drawer or bin for gloves, hats, sunscreen
  • Wall pocket for mail and papers
  • Hooks at the side for umbrellas and dog leads
  • Small shelf for sunglasses and keys

Resist adding more than this. Mudrooms fill to capacity instantly, and extra storage just means more stuff accumulating in the busiest spot in the house.

8. Make it easy to clean

You will be cleaning this space more than any other. Design for it:

  • Wall paint in satin or semi-gloss, not matte — it wipes
  • Bench with a wipeable top
  • Nothing on the floor that can’t be picked up in one movement
  • A small broom and dustpan stored right there

9. Add warmth so it isn’t purely utilitarian

A mudroom can look good. A patterned runner, painted beadboard on the wall behind the hooks, woven baskets instead of plastic bins, and a warm light fixture instead of a bare bulb — all cheap, all make the space feel like part of the home.

10. Seasonal rotation

The habit that keeps a small mudroom functional: twice a year, take everything out and put back only what’s in season.

Winter coats go to a bedroom closet in April. Summer hats leave in October. A small mudroom holding one season’s gear works beautifully. The same mudroom holding all four seasons is a disaster.

Minimum viable mudroom shopping list:

  • 36-inch storage bench
  • Hook rail, 3–5 double hooks
  • Boot tray with a rim
  • Washable runner
  • Two baskets
  • Warm light fixture

That’s a functional mudroom in a hallway corner, and it can be done in an afternoon.

15 Pink Halloween Decor Ideas — Pink-o-ween Is Taking Over Pinterest

Decorate for Halloween in dusty pink with 15 pink Halloween decor ideas using blush pumpkins, pink candles, pastel skeletons, and a soft feminine palette.

  • The pink Halloween palette is dusty blush, white, and black — not hot pink.
  • Blush or white pumpkins are the centrepiece of the pink-o-ween aesthetic.
  • Pink skeletons and pastel skulls are the most-pinned single objects in this trend.

Pink-o-ween is the fastest-growing Halloween aesthetic on Pinterest, and it is a genuine alternative to the traditional orange-and-black palette. The look — dusty blush, white, and black with pastel skeletons and blush pumpkins — is feminine, photogenic, and surprisingly easy to execute in a real home.

The ideas below cover the core palette, the key objects, and how to build the look room by room.

The Palette

1. Dusty Blush, White, and Black

The pink Halloween palette is dusty blush, white, and black. Hot pink reads as modern and loses the slightly eerie quality that makes the aesthetic work. Dusty rose, pale blush, and soft mauve are the right tones.

Black is essential as a grounding accent — without it, the look becomes a generic pink room rather than a Halloween display.

2. Add Metallics Sparingly

Rose gold or antique gold accents — in candle holders, picture frames, or small accessories — add warmth without introducing a new colour. Use them sparingly so they read as accent rather than theme.

Pumpkins

3. Blush and White Pumpkins

Blush, white, and pale pink pumpkins are the centrepiece of the pink-o-ween aesthetic. Real white pumpkins are widely available in autumn; blush ones are easier to find in ceramic or painted form. Group three together in different sizes.

4. Painted Pumpkins

Paint real or faux pumpkins in dusty rose, pale blush, or white. Add simple details — a small black bat, a moon, a spider — in black paint for contrast. The combination of soft pink and black graphic detail is the most-pinned version of this look.

5. Glitter Pumpkins

A light dusting of fine rose gold or white glitter on a blush pumpkin adds a festive quality without looking childish. Use craft glitter and a light adhesive spray for an even finish.

Skeletons and Skulls

6. Pink Skeletons

A pink or blush skeleton — posed on a chair, propped against a wall, or arranged on a shelf — is the single most recognisable object in the pink-o-ween aesthetic. Paint a standard white plastic skeleton with dusty rose spray paint for a custom result.

7. Pastel Skulls

Ceramic skulls in blush, white, or pale mauve add a more refined version of the skeleton detail. Group two or three on a tray or shelf with candles and dried flowers.

8. Skull Candle Holders

Skull-shaped candle holders in white or blush ceramic are widely available and add the Halloween reference without any obvious orange or black. Use them with white or pale pink candles.

Candles and Light

9. Pink Taper Candles

Dusty rose or blush taper candles in simple white or black candlesticks are one of the easiest ways to build the pink Halloween palette. Group three candlesticks of different heights together.

10. Pink Fairy Lights

Warm pink or rose-tinted fairy lights along a shelf, around a mirror, or draped across a mantel add a soft glow that suits the aesthetic. Use battery-powered lights to avoid visible cords.

Florals and Botanicals

11. Dried Pink Roses

Dried roses in dusty pink or deep blush are the botanical centrepiece of the pink Halloween look. Arrange them in a white or black ceramic vase. They last the entire season and dry further as the weeks pass, which adds to the aesthetic.

12. Dark Florals with Pink Accents

A mixed arrangement of dark dahlias, dried grasses, and a few blush roses creates a more complex botanical display. The contrast between the dark stems and the pink flowers is more interesting than an all-pink arrangement.

Textiles and Surfaces

13. Blush Velvet Cushion Covers

Swapping a cushion cover for a blush or dusty rose velvet version is the fastest way to shift the room’s palette. Pair with a black or charcoal throw for contrast.

14. Black and Pink Table Runner

A black linen table runner with a few blush objects on top — candles, a small pumpkin, a skull — creates a display that reads as pink Halloween rather than generic autumn.

Finishing Details

15. Pink Cobwebs and Bats

Pale pink or white faux cobwebs and small black bat cutouts are the finishing details that tie the look together. Use them sparingly — one cobweb on a shelf, a few bats on a wall — rather than covering every surface.

Final Thoughts

Pink-o-ween works because it takes the Halloween palette in an unexpected direction without abandoning the seasonal references entirely. The blush pumpkins, pastel skeletons, and dusty rose candles are still clearly Halloween — they are just doing it in a different colour family. Start with the pumpkins and the candles, add one skeleton detail, and keep the black as a grounding accent throughout.

Narrow Hallway Decor Ideas for Tight Spaces

Narrow hallway decor ideas that add warmth without blocking the walkway — lighting, art, colour, runners and shallow storage that works in tight corridors.

  12. 12What to avoid in a narrow hallway

Hallways get skipped. They’re transition spaces, so nobody budgets for them, and they end up as long blank tunnels with one sad overhead light.

But a hallway is the space you walk through most often in a day. It’s also the easiest room in the house to transform, because it’s small and almost everything you do to it is cheap.

Work out your real usable depth first

Before anything else, measure the width of the hallway. Then subtract 30 inches — that’s the walkway you need to keep clear for comfortable passage.

Whatever’s left is what you can use.

  • 36 inch hallway → 6 inches of depth. Wall-mounted only.
  • 42 inch hallway → 12 inches. A very narrow console fits.
  • 48 inch hallway → 18 inches. A proper console or slim bench works.

Most people’s hallways fall in the first two categories, which is why floor furniture usually fails and wall solutions usually win.

1. Paint it darker than you think

The instinct in a narrow space is white, to open it up. It rarely works — white walls in a windowless corridor just look flat and institutional.

A deep colour does something more interesting: it blurs where the walls are. Charcoal, forest green, deep clay or a moody blue makes the corridor feel like an intentional passage rather than a leftover.

If that feels like too much, paint the lower third in a darker tone with a picture rail or moulding as the break. You get depth without committing the whole space.

2. Fix the lighting

One overhead fixture down the centre is what makes hallways feel like corridors. Layered light along the length changes everything.

  • Wall sconces every 6–8 feet at 60 inches high — the single best hallway upgrade
  • Plug-in sconces if you can’t wire new ones (cord covers painted wall colour disappear completely)
  • Picture lights above artwork
  • Warm bulbs, 2700K, always

Two soft pools of light along a hallway beat one bright ceiling fixture every time.

3. Gallery wall, but hung correctly

Hallways are ideal for art because you walk past slowly and see it up close.

Hang the centre of the arrangement at 57–60 inches — eye level. In a narrow hall you’ll be viewing it from an angle, so favour a horizontal run of frames rather than a tall stacked cluster.

Keep frames slim. Chunky frames with deep profiles catch shoulders and make a narrow hall feel narrower.

Mixing frame colours is fine, but keep the mat colour consistent — that’s what makes a mixed gallery wall look curated instead of random.

4. A runner is non-negotiable

A bare hallway floor echoes and looks unfinished. A runner absorbs sound, adds warmth and draws the eye down the length of the space.

Sizing: leave 4–6 inches of floor visible on each side. Don’t run it wall to wall.

Length: it should stop about 6 inches short of doorways at each end.

Pattern: busy patterns hide the dirt that hallways attract. Persian-style, kilim and geometric runners all work and forgive a lot.

5. Use shallow wall storage

If you need function from your hallway, keep everything under 6 inches deep.

  • Picture ledges (3.5 inches) for art you can rearrange
  • Peg rails for hats, bags and baskets
  • Slim floating shelves for plants and small objects
  • Wall-mounted baskets for gloves and dog leads

A picture ledge running the length of a hallway at 60 inches is one of the best-value decor moves there is — it gives you display space, costs very little, and doesn’t intrude at all.

6. Mirrors, but not the whole wall

A mirror at the far end of a hallway makes the corridor read longer. A mirror along the side wall makes it read wider.

You want one, not both, and not a wall of mirrored panels — that reads dated and makes people uneasy in a tight space.

A single large arched or round mirror at the end wall, or two smaller ones spaced along one side, does the job.

7. Add a runner of colour with the doors

Hallways usually have three or four doors opening off them. Painting all the doors one accent colour — while the walls stay neutral — turns a repetitive corridor into something rhythmic.

Deep green doors against warm white walls. Black doors against clay. It costs a tin of paint and changes the entire character.

8. Treat the end wall as a destination

Every hallway ends somewhere, and that end wall is the thing you look at every time you walk down it.

Give it something: a large piece of art, a narrow console with a lamp, a tall plant, a mirror. Anything is better than a blank wall, which makes the hallway feel like it just stops.

9. Plants that tolerate low light

Hallways rarely have windows. These handle it:

  • Snake plant (tolerates almost anything)
  • ZZ plant
  • Pothos on a high shelf, trailing down
  • Cast iron plant

Keep pots small and place them high — on a shelf or the console — so they don’t narrow the walkway.

10. Trim and moulding

Picture rail, panelling or a simple chair rail adds architectural interest to a hallway that has none.

Slat panelling on one wall is popular right now and works especially well in halls because the vertical lines make ceilings feel higher. It’s a weekend project with basic tools.

What to avoid in a narrow hallway

  • Furniture deeper than your usable measurement — you’ll bang into it daily
  • Bright overhead-only lighting
  • Wall-to-wall carpet runners with no floor showing
  • Too many small objects — a narrow space needs fewer, larger things
  • Doors that swing into the walkway if you can rehang them the other way

The three-step version if you only do one thing:

  1. Paint (colour, or panelling on one wall)
  2. Layered warm lighting at eye level
  3. A runner with pattern

Those three alone will transform a corridor, and together they cost less than a piece of furniture.

15 Navy Boys Bedroom Ideas That Feel Modern, Not Dark

Use navy in a boys bedroom without making it feel heavy with 15 ideas covering paint, bedding, accent colors, lighting, and furniture that keep the room bright.

Elena Marsh/September 22, 2026/4 min read

The short version

  • Use navy on one wall or as an accent color rather than on all four walls in a small room.
  • Pair navy with white, cream, or warm wood to prevent the room from feeling heavy.
  • Warm lighting at 2700K counteracts the coolness of navy and makes the room feel inviting.
  • Keep large furniture light-colored so the navy reads as an accent rather than the dominant tone.

Navy is one of the most versatile colors for a boys bedroom. It reads as calm and grown-up without being dull, and it works with almost every accent color. The challenge is using it in a way that feels modern and bright rather than heavy and enclosed.

These ideas show how to use navy effectively at different scales — from a single accent wall to full bedding — while keeping the room feeling open and comfortable.

1. Use Navy on One Accent Wall

A single navy wall behind the bed creates a strong focal point without making the room feel enclosed. Paint the other three walls white or a warm off-white to keep the room bright.

This is the most flexible approach — it works in small rooms and large ones equally well.

2. Choose White or Cream Furniture

White or cream furniture against a navy wall creates a clean contrast that prevents the room from feeling heavy. Avoid dark wood furniture on a navy wall in a small room — it absorbs too much light.

A white bed frame, white desk, and white shelving create a cohesive look that lets the navy do the work.

3. Use Navy Bedding on White Walls

If painting is not an option, navy bedding on white walls achieves a similar effect. A navy duvet with white or cream pillowcases is a classic combination that suits most ages.

Add a textured throw in a complementary color — rust, forest green, or warm grey — to add depth.

4. Pair Navy With Warm Wood Tones

Warm wood — oak, pine, or walnut — softens the coolness of navy and adds a natural, modern quality. A wooden desk, wooden shelves, or a wooden bed frame all work well against navy.

Avoid mixing too many wood tones — choose one and repeat it through the room.

5. Add White or Cream Curtains

White or cream curtains against a navy wall keep the window area light and prevent the room from feeling too enclosed. Hang them high and wide to maximize the sense of space.

Blackout lining is worth adding in a child’s bedroom regardless of the curtain color.

6. Use Warm Lighting

Navy absorbs light, so warm lighting at 2700K is important. A bedside lamp, a desk lamp, and a ceiling light on a dimmer give the room enough light at every time of day.

Avoid cool white bulbs — they make navy look grey and the room feel clinical.

7. Add a Light-Colored Rug

A cream, oatmeal, or light grey rug on a dark floor keeps the floor area feeling open. In a room with navy walls, a dark rug can make the space feel smaller than it is.

Size the rug correctly — it should extend at least 18 inches beyond the sides and foot of the bed.

8. Use Navy as an Accent in a Neutral Room

If full navy walls feel too bold, use navy as an accent color in a neutral room. Navy cushions, a navy lamp shade, navy storage boxes, or a navy desk chair all add the color without committing to it on the walls.

This approach is also easier to update as the child’s tastes change.

9. Add Brass or Gold Hardware

Brass or gold hardware — drawer handles, curtain rings, lamp bases — adds warmth to a navy room and gives it a more finished, grown-up look. It works particularly well with navy and white.

Even small details like a brass hook or a gold picture frame make a difference.

10. Use Navy in the Wardrobe or Storage

Painting the inside of a wardrobe navy, or choosing navy storage boxes and baskets, adds the color in a contained way that does not affect the overall brightness of the room.

This is a good option for rentals where wall painting is not allowed.

11. Add a Star or Map Print

A framed star map, world map, or constellation print suits a navy room and adds a personal, educational element. Use a white or light frame to keep it from disappearing against a dark wall.

One large print looks more considered than several small ones.

12. Keep the Ceiling White

A white ceiling reflects light back into the room and prevents the navy walls from making the space feel low. This is especially important in rooms with standard ceiling heights.

A white ceiling also makes the room easier to repaint in the future.

13. Use Navy and Red for a Classic Combination

Navy and red is a classic combination that suits boys bedrooms at most ages. Use red as the accent color — a red throw, red cushion, or red lamp — against a navy and white base.

Keep the red to 10% of the room’s color to avoid it competing with the navy.

14. Add a Pegboard in White or Natural Wood

A white or natural wood pegboard on a navy wall creates a practical display area that stands out clearly. Use it for medals, caps, headphones, or small accessories.

The contrast between the pegboard and the navy wall makes the display feel intentional.

15. Use Navy Sparingly in a Very Small Room

In a room under 100 square feet, limit navy to bedding, cushions, and small accessories rather than the walls. A small room with navy walls can feel like a cupboard, even with good lighting.

Use the navy accent wall approach only if the room has a window on the same wall or good natural light.

Final Thoughts

Navy works in a boys bedroom when it is balanced with light colors, warm lighting, and natural materials. Start with one navy element — a wall, bedding, or a few accessories — and build from there. The goal is a room that feels calm and considered, not dark and heavy.

How to Choose a Paint Colour and Not Regret It

Why the swatch lies, how light orientation changes everything, and the sample method that takes three days but saves you repainting the whole room.

The short version

  • Undertone, not the colour name, is what ruins a paint choice — hold every sample against plain printer paper to expose the bias.
  • North-facing rooms flatten and cool every colour, so they need warm pigment or genuine depth, never a weak pastel.
  • Paint samples onto A2 white card rather than the wall, and move them around the room across three days.
  • Sheen changes the shade: the same pigment reads deeper in matt and lighter in eggshell.
  • One litre covers roughly 12m² per coat — calculate the wall area, plan two coats, then buy 10% more.

Almost every paint disaster comes from the same mistake: choosing the colour somewhere other than the room it is going in. A swatch under shop lighting, held against a white card, at eye level, in the middle of the day, tells you almost nothing about how that colour will behave on four walls in your north-facing living room in November.

Here is what actually determines how a colour reads, and a three-day sampling method that has never let us down.

Undertone is the thing that ruins colours

Every neutral has a bias hiding under it. Two greys that look identical on the card can be violently different on a wall, because one is green-grey and the other is purple-grey.

The main undertone families in “neutral” paint:

  • Green-grey — calm, slightly cool, plays well with wood and brass
  • Blue-grey — crisp, can go cold and institutional in low light
  • Purple-grey (greige) — soft and flattering, but goes pink under warm bulbs
  • Yellow-beige — warm and forgiving, tips into cream and can look dated
  • Pink-beige — very warm, difficult next to cool flooring

How to find the undertone: put the sample next to a sheet of plain printer paper. The paper reads as true white and the bias in the sample becomes obvious. Do this for three candidate colours side by side and the differences that were invisible on the card become impossible to miss.

The undertone matters most where the paint meets something you are not changing — the floor, the worktop, a fixed fireplace. A green-grey wall above an orange-toned oak floor will fight; a warm greige will not.

Which way does the room face?

Orientation changes a colour more than the paint choice itself.

North-facing (south-facing in the southern hemisphere) — cool, blue-tinged, indirect light all day. Colours go greyer, flatter and colder than the card. Cool colours become icy. This is the orientation where people paint a room pale grey and end up with something that feels like a waiting room.

Choose: warm-based colours with some pigment in them. Warm off-whites, ochres, clay, deep greens, or lean into it and go genuinely dark — north rooms are excellent in strong colour and terrible in weak pastel.

South-facing — warm, bright, generous light for most of the day. Nearly everything works. Cool colours are lifted and made pleasant; warm colours can become almost too yellow at midday.

Choose: almost anything. If a colour is going to work anywhere it will work here.

East-facing — bright and slightly blue in the morning, then flat and grey from lunchtime.

Choose: colours you will mostly see in the morning. A bedroom works well east; a room you use in the evening needs a warmer colour to survive the afternoon flatness.

West-facing — dull and cool in the morning, warm and golden in the late afternoon.

Choose: with the evening in mind. Greens and warm neutrals are stunning in western afternoon light and perfectly fine at 9am.

Test any colour at 9am, at 2pm and again at 9pm with the lamps on. A colour that looks right in only one of those three is the wrong colour.

Sheen changes the colour

The same pigment at a different finish reads as a different shade, because sheen changes how much light bounces back.

  • Matt / flat — deepest colour, hides wall imperfections, marks easily. Best for ceilings and low-traffic walls.
  • Eggshell — slight sheen, much more washable, reads a touch lighter than matt. The sensible default for living rooms.
  • Satin — noticeable sheen, very durable, shows every bump in the plaster. Woodwork.
  • Gloss — maximum durability and maximum reflection. Doors, trim, and radiators.

A dark colour in matt absorbs light and recedes. The same dark colour in satin reflects and can look plasticky. If you are going dark, go matt.

The three-day sample method

This is slower than everyone wants it to be, and it is the difference between one coat of the right colour and two coats of the wrong one.

Do not paint patches directly on the wall. The existing colour bleeds through, the edges bias your eye, and you will end up painting over patchwork.

Instead:

  1. Buy sample pots of your three or four candidates.
  2. Paint A2 sheets of white card — two full coats, edge to edge, letting each dry properly. White card gives you a true reading with no existing wall colour underneath.
  3. Leave a white border of about 2cm around each, so you can see the colour against true white.
  4. Move them around the room over three days. Tape one to each wall. Look at them in the morning, at midday, and at night under your actual lamps.
  5. Hold them against the fixed things — the floor, the sofa, the curtains, the worktop. This is where undertone clashes appear.
  6. Look at them flat on the floor as well. Light bounces off the floor onto your walls, and a card lying flat approximates what the lower half of the wall will do.

Then narrow to two, buy larger sample pots, and repeat with bigger cards for a day. Yes, this takes most of a week. Repainting a living room takes a weekend and £150.

Practical rules that hold up

  • Go one shade lighter than you think for large walls. Colour intensifies across a big area — a card’s worth of pigment becomes a room’s worth.
  • Ceiling: the wall colour cut 25–50% with white reads better than default brilliant white in almost every room. Brilliant white ceilings above a coloured wall create a hard line that lowers the room.
  • Trim in the same colour as the walls, in a different sheen, makes a small room feel bigger — the eye stops registering the boundaries.
  • Keep whole-house cohesion by choosing colours from the same undertone family throughout. Rooms visible from one another should not swap between green-grey and pink-beige.
  • Buy from one brand per project. Undertone consistency within a brand’s range is far better than across brands.

How much paint

For estimating: one litre covers roughly 12m² per coat. Wall area is (perimeter × height) minus windows and doors. Two coats is standard; three if you are going lighter over a dark colour, or using a strong red or yellow, which are the poorest-covering pigments.

Buy 10% more than the calculation. Touch-ups two years later never match a fresh batch.

Once the walls are settled, the furniture matters less than you think. See our minimalist living room guide for the ratios that make a room feel finished.

Still wondering

Common questions

Why does my grey paint look purple or green on the wall?

Every neutral carries an undertone — green, blue, purple, yellow or pink. Under your room's light, and next to your floor, that bias becomes obvious even though it was invisible on the card. Hold the sample beside a sheet of plain printer paper and it shows immediately.

How many paint samples should I test before choosing?

Three or four candidates on A2 white card, then narrow to two for a second round with larger cards. Fewer than three and you never see the undertone differences; more than four and you stop being able to tell them apart.

What colour should I paint a north-facing room?

Something with pigment in it. North light is cool and indirect all day, so it drains colour — pale greys end up looking institutional. Warm off-whites, ochre, clay and deep green all work, and north rooms are genuinely excellent in strong dark colour.

What paint finish should I use in a living room?

Eggshell is the sensible default: enough sheen to wash down, little enough to forgive imperfect plaster. Use matt on ceilings and on any dark colour, since dark paint in satin reflects light and looks plasticky. Satin or gloss belong on woodwork.

Should the ceiling always be brilliant white?

Usually not. The wall colour cut 25-50% with white reads better in almost every room. A brilliant white ceiling above a coloured wall draws a hard line at the top of the wall, which visually lowers the whole room.

How much paint do I need for one room?

One litre covers about 12m² per coat. Take the wall perimeter multiplied by the height, subtract windows and doors, and plan for two coats — three if you are going lighter over dark, or using a strong red or yellow. Buy 10% more than that.

18 Pumpkin Painting Ideas That Look Better Than Carving

Paint pumpkins with 18 ideas from simple solid colors to detailed botanical designs. No carving required — these last longer and suit every skill level.

The short version

  • Painted pumpkins last longer than carved ones — up to several months on foam pumpkins.
  • A solid color in a non-traditional shade — cream, sage, charcoal — looks more sophisticated than orange.
  • Acrylic paint works on both real and foam pumpkins and dries in under an hour.
  • Seal with matte varnish spray to protect the paint and extend the pumpkin's life.

Painted pumpkins have one significant advantage over carved ones: they last. A foam pumpkin painted with acrylic paint and sealed with varnish will look the same in five years as it does today. A real pumpkin painted and sealed will last several weeks longer than a carved one.

The ideas below range from beginner-friendly solid colors to more detailed designs. Start with the simplest option and build from there.

Solid Colors

1. Cream Pumpkin

Paint a pumpkin in a warm cream or off-white. This is the most versatile painted pumpkin — it suits almost any interior and works with both Halloween and autumn decor. Use two coats for full coverage.

Use a warm cream rather than a stark white — it reads as more natural.

2. Sage Green Pumpkin

Paint a pumpkin in a muted sage green. This is an unusual, sophisticated color that suits a neutral or earthy interior. Pair it with cream and terracotta pumpkins for a cohesive group.

Use a matte finish — sage green looks far better matte than glossy.

3. Charcoal Pumpkin

Paint a pumpkin in a deep charcoal or near-black. This is a dramatic, modern color that suits a minimalist or gothic interior. Pair it with cream pumpkins for contrast.

Use two or three coats for full, even coverage.

4. Terracotta Pumpkin

Paint a pumpkin in a warm terracotta. This is a natural, earthy color that suits a rustic or bohemian interior. It also photographs beautifully in natural light.

Terracotta paint is available at most craft stores in the clay and earth tone section.
