Most people working from home don’t have a spare room. They have a corner of the bedroom, an alcove under the stairs, or one end of the dining table.

A small workspace can work genuinely well — but only if you get three things right: the desk depth, the light, and the ability to make the whole thing disappear when you’re done.

How much space you actually need

Less than you’d think.

  • Desk width: 40 inches is comfortable for a laptop setup. 30 inches works if you’re tight.
  • Desk depth: 24 inches for a monitor, 20 inches for laptop-only. Below 18 inches your keyboard hangs off the edge.
  • Clearance behind the chair: 30 inches to push back and stand up. This is the measurement people forget.

So a functional home office is roughly 40 x 54 inches of floor. That fits in a corner, an alcove, or the end of a bedroom wall.

1. The closet office

Take the doors off a small closet, remove the rod, and build in a desk at 29–30 inches high with shelves above.

You get a workspace that’s fully enclosed, with the whole back wall available for a pinboard or shelving. Add a curtain or put the doors back on and the office vanishes at 6pm — the single biggest advantage of this setup if the office is in a bedroom.

Depth is the thing to check: standard closets are 24 inches deep, which is exactly right for a desk.

2. Corner desk

An L-shaped or corner desk uses the least useful floor space in a room. Corners are dead zones for most furniture, so putting the desk there costs you almost nothing.

A corner setup also gives you two walls for shelving and pinboards.

3. Floating desk

A wall-mounted desk with no legs. The clear floor underneath makes a small room feel much less crowded, and you can slide a stool or a small filing cabinet under it.

Mount at 29 inches. Make sure it’s into studs — a floating desk with a monitor and elbows on it takes real load.

4. Under the stairs

The triangular space under a staircase fits a desk beautifully if you place it at the tall end. Add a wall light, a shelf, and it becomes a proper nook.

Check the headroom where you’ll be sitting — you want 40 inches minimum above the seat.

5. Narrow console desk in a hallway or bedroom

A console table 12–16 inches deep works as a laptop desk. Not enough for a monitor setup, but perfectly fine for a few hours of laptop work, and it reads as furniture rather than as an office.

Ideal for a bedroom where you don’t want a workspace dominating the room.

6. Fold-down wall desk

A drop-leaf or murphy-style desk mounted to the wall. Folds flat when closed, opens to a 20-inch work surface.

Best for spaces that have to do two jobs — a guest room, a dining room, a small living room. The office genuinely disappears.

Lighting is the thing most people get wrong

A small office in a corner is usually in the darkest part of the room. Overhead ceiling light behind you creates screen glare and shadows on your work.

What you need:

  • A task lamp on the desk, positioned to the side opposite your writing hand
  • Natural light from the side, not in front (glare) or behind (silhouette on video calls)
  • A warm ambient source — a lamp elsewhere in the room — so you’re not staring at a bright screen in a dark corner

If you’re on video calls, put a light in front of you, above eye level. A small ring light or a lamp on a shelf facing you solves the “why do I look terrible” problem instantly.

Storage: go up, not out

Floor space is what you don’t have. Wall space above the desk is free.

  • Floating shelves at 18 inches and 30 inches above the desk
  • Pegboard — the most flexible option for a small office; holds pots, hooks, small shelves, and reconfigures freely
  • Wall pockets or magazine files for papers
  • A single drawer unit on castors that rolls under the desk

Keep the desk surface for what you’re working on today. Everything else lives on the wall.

The cable problem

In a small space, visible cables make everything look chaotic. Three cheap fixes:

  • Adhesive cable channel along the back edge of the desk
  • A cable tray screwed underneath the desktop
  • Velcro ties bundling everything into one run down a single leg

A power strip mounted underneath the desk, not on the floor, cleans up 80% of it.

Chair — don’t compromise here

A dining chair is fine for 30 minutes and painful after two hours. If you work more than a couple of hours a day, a proper task chair matters more than the desk does.

In a small space, look for:

  • No arms, or removable arms — the chair tucks fully under the desk
  • A smaller footprint base
  • Neutral colour so it reads as furniture in a bedroom or living room

Making it look like part of the room

If the office is in a bedroom or living room, it should look like furniture, not like an office.

  • Wooden desk rather than white laminate
  • A lamp instead of a clip light
  • Art on the wall above, not just a calendar and sticky notes
  • A basket or closed box for the ugly essentials
  • One plant

The goal is that when you’re not working, you don’t see a workstation sitting in your bedroom.

The shut-down habit

The hardest part of a small home office isn’t the layout — it’s that work is now in the room where you relax.

Clear the desk at the end of the day. Laptop closed or put away, papers in the drawer, chair pushed in. It takes two minutes and it’s what lets the space stop being an office.

Minimum viable small office:

Item Spec
Desk 40 x 24 inches, 29–30 inches high
Clearance behind 30 inches
Task lamp Warm, adjustable, on the desk
Shelf One, 18 inches above the desk
Chair Armless task chair
Cable management Channel + underdesk power strip

If you are looking for small space Halloween decor ideas, the best place to start is with function rather than decoration. A space feels better when the layout is easy to use and the styling supports everyday life instead of getting in the way.

The ideas below are designed to be practical for real homes. You do not need to use every idea. Choose the changes that suit your space and your normal decor first, then build from there.

1. Use One Wall for Removable Bats

Cut-paper or card bats arranged on one wall add a playful seasonal note that is easy to remove and costs almost nothing. Use removable adhesive strips so there is no wall damage.

Keep frequently used items at an easy height and reserve higher storage for lighter or less-used things.

2. Choose Tabletop Pumpkins

In a small space, tabletop pumpkins take up far less room than floor-standing ones. Group two or three on a tray on the coffee table or console.

Keep walking paths, doors, drawers, and frequently used surfaces easy to access.

3. Hang Decor Instead of Using Floor Space

Wreaths, garlands, and hanging lanterns use wall and ceiling space rather than floor space. This keeps walkways clear and makes the room feel less cluttered.

Repeat a few materials and colors instead of using many unrelated decorations.

4. Use One Small Halloween Tray

A tray containing a candle, a small pumpkin, and one or two dark objects keeps the seasonal display contained and easy to move. Leave enough empty surface for everyday use.

A tray is useful because the whole group can be moved at once.

5. Choose a Restrained Color Palette

Black, cream, and muted orange read as Halloween without the garish brightness of primary colors. Repeat these tones through candles, pumpkins, and small accessories.

A common mistake is introducing a different strong color in every object. In a small room, a limited palette usually feels larger, calmer, and easier to update later.

6. Use Pumpkins in Different Sizes

Grouping pumpkins of different heights and sizes creates a more natural, editorial look than a row of identical ones. Mix real, ceramic, and fabric pumpkins to reduce yearly waste.

Choose pieces that are easy to store and that work with your normal decor.

7. Add Black Candles or Flameless Candles

Black candles are one of the simplest ways to signal the season without adding themed products. Use them in existing candlesticks or lanterns you already own.

Choose pieces that are easy to store and that work with your normal decor.

8. Create One Spooky Focal Point

Rather than decorating every surface, choose one area and make it the seasonal focal point. Keep the rest of the apartment calm.

Repeat a few materials and colors instead of using many unrelated decorations.

9. Use Dried Branches in a Tall Vase

A few bare or dark-painted branches in a tall vase add height and a slightly eerie quality without any obvious Halloween imagery. They also last the entire season.

Choose pieces that are easy to store and that work with your normal decor.

10. Add a Simple Black Garland

A thin black garland of leaves, stars, or geometric shapes adds a subtle seasonal note to a mantel, shelf, or windowsill without overwhelming the space.

Choose pieces that are easy to store and that work with your normal decor.

11. Decorate With Vintage-Inspired Prints

A framed vintage-style print of a moon, botanical skull, or dark landscape adds atmosphere without looking childish. Swap it into an existing frame you already own.

Choose pieces that are easy to store and that work with your normal decor.

12. Use Dark Linen or Velvet Textiles

Swapping a cushion cover or throw for a dark linen, velvet, or jacquard version adds seasonal depth without any obvious Halloween imagery.

Choose washable or easy-care materials in high-use areas.

13. Style a Coffee Table Tray

A tray containing a candle, a small pumpkin, and one or two dark objects keeps the seasonal display contained and easy to move.

A tray is useful because the whole group can be moved at once.

14. Add Subtle Skeleton Details

A small ceramic skull or a single skeleton figurine adds a touch of Halloween without dominating the room. Use one or two pieces rather than a collection.

Choose pieces that are easy to store and that work with your normal decor.

15. Use Warm Amber Lighting

Warm amber bulbs or candles create a moody atmosphere that suits Halloween without any additional decoration. Swap a standard bulb for an amber one in a lamp you already own.

For cozy rooms, warm-white bulbs around 2700K are a useful starting point.

16. Decorate the Entryway First

The entryway is the first thing guests see. A wreath, a pumpkin, and one candle lantern can create a strong seasonal impression without decorating the whole apartment.

Choose pieces that are easy to store and that work with your normal decor.

17. Add a Few Paper Bats to One Wall

Cut-paper bats arranged on one wall add a playful seasonal note that is easy to remove and costs almost nothing. Keep the arrangement loose and asymmetric for a more editorial look.

In rentals, removable adhesive strips mean no damage to walls.

Final Thoughts

The strongest small space Halloween decor ideas are the ones that make the room feel atmospheric without cluttering it. Start with one focal point, use wall and tabletop space rather than floor space, and choose pieces that store flat and work with your existing decor. Small, deliberate choices are usually more successful than covering every surface.

An apartment patio is often 6 x 8 feet of bare concrete with a railing. It’s also the only outdoor space you have, so it’s worth doing properly.

Here’s how to make it usable, starting with what actually fits.

Measure and plan the zones

Most apartment patios are 30–80 square feet. That’s enough for one function, done well — not three done badly.

Pick one:

  • Dining — a bistro table and two chairs
  • Lounging — two chairs and a small side table
  • Green space — plants, one chair, a stool

Trying to fit a dining set, loungers and a garden onto 50 square feet is why most small patios end up unusable.

Leave 24 inches of walkway to the door.

Furniture that fits

Bistro set — a 24–30 inch round table with two chairs. Needs about 6 x 6 feet including pull-out room.

Folding furniture — folds flat against the wall when you need the floor. Best for very small balconies.

Bench against the railing with a small table — uses the perimeter, leaves the middle clear.

Balcony rail table — a narrow shelf that hooks over the railing. Takes zero floor space.

Stackable stools — seating that stores in a corner.

Materials that survive outdoors: powder-coated aluminium, teak or acacia, resin wicker. Avoid untreated softwood and untreated steel.

Flooring over concrete

Bare concrete is what makes a patio feel like a fire escape. Covering it is the biggest single change.

Interlocking deck tiles — wood or composite squares that click together over concrete. No adhesive, no damage, and you take them with you. The best renter option.

Outdoor rug — polypropylene, which handles rain and dries fast. Cheap and instant.

Artificial grass tiles — soft underfoot, good if you have a dog.

Check your lease. Some buildings prohibit covering balcony drainage.

Privacy

Usually the main complaint about an apartment patio.

  • Balcony privacy screen — fabric or reed, cable-tied to the railing. Cheap and effective.
  • Bamboo or reed fencing attached to the rail
  • Tall planters with grasses — living screen, no attachment needed
  • An outdoor curtain on a tension rod, if there’s structure to hang from
  • A trellis with climbing plants in a large pot

Check building rules first — many have restrictions on what can be attached to railings or visible from outside.

Lighting

The thing that makes a small patio usable in the evening.

  • Solar string lights — no wiring, no socket needed. The most popular option for good reason.
  • Solar lanterns on the floor or a table
  • Battery LED candles
  • Clip-on rail lights
  • A solar-powered floor lamp

Warm white, not cool. String lights zigzagged overhead or along the railing transform the space at night.

Plants in containers

Everything on a patio lives in a pot, which changes what survives.

Easy and tough:

  • Lavender — loves sun and dry soil
  • Rosemary and thyme — useful and hardy
  • Geraniums
  • Succulents in a sunny spot
  • Boxwood in a large pot for structure
  • Ornamental grasses for movement and screening

For shade: ferns, hostas, impatiens, begonias.

Container rules: drainage holes are essential, pots dry out much faster than ground soil (daily watering in summer), and bigger pots are far more forgiving than small ones.

Vertical growing: a wall planter, a tiered plant stand, or railing planters. Uses no floor space.

Weight check: wet soil is heavy. Large planters on a balcony need to respect the load limit — check with your building if you’re planning several big pots.

Storage

  • A storage bench — seating plus a box for cushions
  • A slim deck box against a wall
  • A waterproof bag for cushions
  • Hooks on the wall for tools and a folded chair

Cushions must come inside or into a box, or they’ll be mouldy within a month.

Adding comfort

  • Outdoor cushions in a weather-resistant fabric
  • A throw for cool evenings
  • A small side table — even a stool works
  • A rug to define the seating area
  • A wind chime or lantern for character

Shade

If the patio gets direct sun, it’ll be unusable at midday.

  • A clamp-on balcony umbrella that fixes to the railing
  • A shade sail, if there are fixing points
  • A tall plant positioned to block afternoon sun
  • An outdoor curtain that draws across

Small details that matter

  • A doormat at the door
  • A bin for the small rubbish that accumulates
  • A watering can — carrying a jug from the kitchen gets old fast
  • A saucer under every pot so runoff doesn’t stain the concrete or drip on neighbours below

That last one causes more neighbour complaints than anything else on a balcony.

The starter setup for a 6 x 8 foot patio:

Interlocking deck tiles, one bistro set, a privacy screen on the railing, solar string lights overhead, three large planters, and a storage bench.

That’s a complete patio, nothing permanent, and it all comes with you when you move.

Zoning a Studio: Making One Room Behave Like Three

A studio fails when every activity happens everywhere. Rugs, backs of sofas, height changes and light are how you build rooms without building walls.

Elena Marsh/August 8, 2026/5 min read

The problem with a studio is almost never the square metreage. It is that one undivided space means every activity leaks into every other one — you eat where you work, sleep where you entertain, and the room never signals that anything has ended. The fix is not more storage. It is boundaries.

You can build convincing boundaries without touching a wall, and most of them are free.

Decide the zones before you move anything

Write down what the room genuinely has to do. For most studios it is three or four things:

  • Sleep
  • Sit / entertain
  • Eat
  • Work (only if you actually work from home — do not build a desk zone you use twice a month)

Then rank them by hours used per week. The zone with the most hours gets the best light and the best position; everything else fits around it. This sounds obvious and almost nobody does it — the bed usually ends up in the best spot by default, despite being the zone you are unconscious in.

If you work from home eight hours a day, the desk gets the window. The bed can go in the darkest corner, where it will sleep better anyway.

The five tools for building a boundary

1. Rugs — the cheapest walls you can buy

A rug defines a zone more effectively than almost anything else, because the floor is the one surface your eye reads as continuous. Break the floor and you break the room.

Rules that matter:

  • One rug per zone, with bare floor between them. The gap is the boundary.
  • Get the size right: in a seating zone, at least the front legs of every seat should sit on the rug. A small rug floating in the middle of a seating area makes the whole zone look unmoored.
  • Vary the texture between zones — a flat-weave under the dining area, something with pile under the sofa. Different underfoot means different room.

2. The backs of furniture

The back of a sofa is a wall. Face it into the seating zone and let its back form the edge of the sleeping area. A console table or narrow shelf behind it strengthens the line and gives you a surface.

An open-backed shelving unit does the same job while still passing light through, which matters if the boundary sits between the window and the rest of the room.

3. Height changes

Zones read as separate when the eye travels up and down between them.

  • Tall bookshelf at the edge of the sleeping zone
  • Low, long furniture in the seating zone
  • Pendant light dropped over the dining table

The pendant is particularly effective: a light hung at 75–85cm above a table draws a hard vertical boundary in a way nothing at floor level can.

4. Light

Each zone needs its own switchable light. This is the tool people skip and it is arguably the strongest of the five, because you can turn a zone off.

At 10pm, the desk light goes off and the work zone stops existing. That is a boundary no screen or curtain can match, and it does more for the psychological separation of work and rest than any amount of furniture.

5. Curtains and screens — last resort

Ceiling-track curtains around a bed do work, and they are the standard advice, but they cost light and make a small room smaller. Use them only if the bed is genuinely visible from the front door and it bothers you.

The best studio dividers are things you were going to own anyway, turned ninety degrees. Buying a “room divider” is usually a sign that the furniture is in the wrong places.

Scale: the thing that makes small rooms feel cramped

Counter-intuitively, too many small pieces make a room feel smaller than a few larger ones. Ten small objects create ten visual stops; three larger ones create three.

  • One large piece of art beats a gallery wall of nine small frames
  • A full-size sofa beats a loveseat plus two chairs
  • One big plant beats five small ones on every surface
  • Fewer, larger rugs beat several small ones

The exception is depth. Slim-depth furniture — a 30cm console instead of a 45cm one, a 80cm-deep sofa instead of 95cm — buys you circulation space, which is what actually makes a room feel liveable. Prioritise reducing depth over reducing width or length.

Circulation: the 60cm rule

Leave at least 60cm of clear walking width on every route you use daily, and 90cm on the main route from door to the rest of the flat. If a path is narrower than that, you will feel the room as cramped no matter how it looks.

Walk your actual routes before you commit to a layout: door to bed, bed to bathroom, kitchen to table. Furniture that blocks a nightly route will annoy you for years.

Storage that does not eat the room

  • Go vertical. Shelving to the ceiling in one place is less oppressive than waist-height storage on three walls, and holds more.
  • Under the bed is the largest unused volume in most studios. Flat boxes on castors; measure the clearance first.
  • One closed unit per zone, so each area can be tidied independently. Open storage everywhere means the whole flat looks messy when one corner is.
  • Furniture that stores: ottoman with a lid, bed with drawers, a bench at the table with a hinged seat.

For a compact sleeping area, our small bedroom ideas offer ways to layer bedding, lighting and storage without crowding the room.

A worked example: 32m² studio, window on one wall

  • Window wall: desk across the window, side-on so you look out to the left. Best light to the zone with the most hours.
  • Middle: sofa with its back to the desk, facing into the room, on a 200×290 rug. The sofa back is the wall between work and living.
  • Far corner, darkest: bed, low frame, one tall shelf at its foot marking the edge. Sconce on the wall — no bedside table needed.
  • Near the kitchen: small round table, two chairs, pendant dropped low over it, small flat-weave rug underneath.
  • Circulation: a clear 90cm run from the front door past the sofa to the kitchen; 60cm around three sides of the bed.

Four zones, no walls, no divider bought.

The one habit that matters

Reset the room every night. Ten minutes: desk cleared, throw folded, table wiped, everything back to its zone.

In a house with doors you can close a mess away. In a studio, every surface is on display from every angle, so the room is only ever as calm as its worst corner. That is the real cost of studio living — and the ten minutes is genuinely the whole solution.

16 Spooky Basket Ideas for Halloween Gifting Done Right

Build a spooky Halloween gift basket with 16 ideas covering themes, fillers, presentation, and recipients. From gothic to cozy-spooky to kid-friendly.

Elena Marsh/September 15, 2026/7 min read

The short version

  • A themed basket — cozy witch, gothic apothecary, movie night — looks more intentional than a random collection.
  • One splurge item plus several smaller treats feels more generous than all small items.
  • Black, orange, or deep purple tissue paper and a matching basket make the presentation.
  • Personalize with the recipient's favorite scent, snack, or hobby for maximum impact.

A spooky basket works best when it has a clear theme. A random collection of Halloween items looks like a last-minute grab from the seasonal aisle. A basket built around one idea — a cozy witch night in, a gothic apothecary, a horror movie marathon — looks intentional and personal.

The ideas below are organized by theme and recipient so you can build a basket that suits the person you are gifting.

Themed Basket Ideas

1. Cozy Witch Night In

Fill a black cauldron or a dark wicker basket with a fall candle, a face mask, a pair of witch-print socks, a mug, a hot chocolate mix, and a small bag of Halloween candy. Add a handwritten note that says “A little magic for your evening.”

This theme works for almost any woman and is the most universally appreciated spooky basket.

2. Gothic Apothecary

Fill a dark basket with glass apothecary jars filled with bath salts, a botanical candle, a dried flower bundle, a small crystal or stone, and a book of spells or a gothic novel. Label each jar with a handwritten potion name.

This theme suits someone with a gothic or witchy aesthetic.

3. Horror Movie Marathon

Fill a basket with a bag of popcorn, a bag of candy, a horror movie recommendation list printed on card, a cozy blanket, and a pair of Halloween socks. Add a small flashlight for watching in the dark.

This theme works for anyone who enjoys horror films.

4. Pumpkin Spice Everything

Build this as an evening-at-home kit for someone who genuinely likes the scent: pair their preferred warm drink with one edible treat and one scented item, then add a card suggesting a quiet autumn night in. A washable tray or lidded box can hold the set and be used again after Halloween.

Avoid stacking several competing fragrances. If you do not know the recipient’s scent preferences or food restrictions, choose the more flexible gift basket guide by recipient instead.

5. Haunted Spa Night

Fill a basket with a bath bomb, a face mask, a body scrub, a candle, a pair of cozy socks, and a small bottle of essential oil in a fall scent. Add a handwritten note with a self-care ritual suggestion.

This theme suits someone who enjoys self-care and relaxation.

6. Trick-or-Treat Candy Basket

Fill a large black cauldron with a generous selection of Halloween candy — full-size bars, not fun-size — plus a few specialty treats like caramel apples, pumpkin chocolates, and seasonal cookies. This is the most straightforward spooky basket and works for any age.

Full-size candy bars are always more impressive than fun-size ones.

7. Spooky Snack Attack

Fill a basket with savory and sweet snacks — spiced nuts, beef jerky, Halloween popcorn, dark chocolate, and a seasonal drink. This theme suits someone who prefers snacks over beauty products.

Choose a mix of sweet and savory for the most interesting basket.

8. Kid’s Trick-or-Treat Basket

Fill a small orange or black basket with Halloween candy, a small toy or game, a Halloween book, a pair of Halloween socks, and a small decoration for their room. Keep the candy to a reasonable amount and focus on the non-candy items.

Choose age-appropriate toys and games.

Presentation Tips

9. Use a Black Cauldron

A black plastic cauldron is the most thematic container for a spooky basket. It is inexpensive, reusable, and immediately signals Halloween. Fill the bottom with black tissue paper before adding the items.

Cauldrons are available at most craft stores and online from August onward.

10. Use a Dark Wicker Basket

A dark wicker basket in black, deep brown, or charcoal is a more elegant container than a plastic cauldron. It can be reused for other purposes after the season.

Line the basket with black or orange tissue paper before adding the items.

11. Layer with Tissue Paper

Layer the contents with black, orange, or deep purple tissue paper so nothing looks thrown in. Place the largest items at the back and the smallest at the front. Scrunch the tissue paper around the items to fill the gaps.

Use two colors of tissue paper — black and orange — for the most festive look.

12. Add a Handwritten Tag

A handwritten tag on kraft paper with the recipient’s name and a short Halloween message makes the basket feel personal. Tie it to the handle with a black ribbon.

Use a fine-tip black marker for the most legible handwriting.

Filler Ideas

13. Halloween Candy

A mix of Halloween candy — candy corn, pumpkin chocolates, caramel apples, and seasonal favorites — is the most essential spooky basket filler. Choose a mix that includes the recipient’s favorites.

Avoid candy the recipient is allergic to.

14. Small Halloween Decorations

A small ceramic pumpkin, a skull candle holder, or a Halloween-print tea towel is a decorative filler that adds value to the basket. Choose something in a neutral palette — cream, terracotta, or black.

Choose a piece that suits the recipient’s home decor style.

15. Seasonal Tea or Coffee

A small bag of seasonal tea — pumpkin spice, apple cinnamon, or chai — or a single-serve coffee packet is a practical filler that adds warmth to the basket.

Choose a flavor the recipient already likes if you know it.

16. Halloween Stickers or Washi Tape

A sheet of Halloween stickers or a roll of Halloween washi tape is an inexpensive filler that adds a playful touch. It suits a basket for a creative person or a child.

Choose stickers in a style that suits the recipient — cute, gothic, or classic Halloween.

Final Thoughts

The best spooky basket is the one that feels personal and intentional. Start with a theme, choose one item you know the recipient will love, and build the rest of the basket around it. Presentation — a quality container, layered tissue paper, and a handwritten tag — makes even a modest collection of gifts look impressive.

Still wondering

Common questions

What is a spooky basket?

A spooky basket is a Halloween gift basket filled with themed items — candles, candy, cozy treats, and small decorations — presented in a black, orange, or dark-colored basket or cauldron. It is the Halloween equivalent of an Easter basket, often left anonymously as part of the 'boo' gifting tradition.

How do you make a spooky basket look expensive?

Use a quality basket or a black cauldron rather than a plastic bin. Layer the contents with black or orange tissue paper so nothing looks thrown in. Include one genuinely good item — a quality candle, a nice chocolate bar, a real book — and fill around it with smaller treats. A handwritten tag on kraft paper completes the look.

20 Toy Story and Inside Out 2 Group Halloween Costume Ideas

Find the perfect group Halloween costume with 20 Toy Story and Inside Out 2 ideas for families, friend groups, and couples at every budget and group size.

The short version

  • Toy Story works for any group size from two to ten — every character has a distinct, recognisable look.
  • Inside Out 2 adds Anxiety, Envy, Ennui, and Embarrassment to the original five emotions.
  • Both franchises work for mixed-age groups including children and adults.
  • The emotions from Inside Out are the easiest to execute — solid colour outfit plus matching makeup.

Toy Story and Inside Out 2 are the two most-searched group Halloween costumes of the year, and both work for a reason: every character has a distinct, recognisable look that is achievable without specialist costume-making skills.

The ideas below cover both franchises, with options for different group sizes, ages, and budgets.

Toy Story

1. Woody and Buzz Duo

The classic two-person Toy Story costume. Woody needs a cowboy hat, a yellow plaid shirt, jeans, and brown boots. Buzz needs a white and purple outfit — a white top with purple and green details, or a full Buzz Lightyear suit from a costume shop.

2. The Core Four

Woody, Buzz, Jessie, and Rex. Jessie adds a red hat, red hair, a white shirt with red details, and jeans. Rex is a green dinosaur costume — widely available and immediately recognisable.

3. The Full Toy Box

Woody, Buzz, Jessie, Rex, Hamm, Slinky, and Mr Potato Head. Hamm is a pink outfit with a coin slot detail. Slinky is a brown outfit with a spring accessory. Mr Potato Head is a brown outfit with oversized felt features attached.

4. Woody and Bo Peep Couple

Woody in cowboy gear; Bo Peep in a blue and white shepherdess dress with a crook and a small sheep prop. A strong couple costume that is recognisable to anyone who has seen the films.

5. The Aliens Trio

Three people in green outfits with three-eyed alien headbands. One of the easiest and cheapest Toy Story group costumes — the look is immediately recognisable and requires almost no construction.

6. Lotso and the Sunnyside Gang

Lotso in a pink outfit with a strawberry-scented bear aesthetic; supporting characters in pastel outfits. Works well for a larger group that wants a villain-led theme.

7. Forky and Friends

Forky — a plastic fork with googly eyes, pipe cleaner arms, and a clay foot — is one of the most creative and low-cost Toy Story costumes. Pair with Woody and Buzz for a trio.

8. Andy’s Room Group

Everyone dresses as a different toy from Andy’s room. The group works at any size and allows each person to choose their favourite character.

Inside Out 2

9. The Original Five Emotions

Joy (yellow), Sadness (blue), Anger (red), Fear (purple), and Disgust (green). Each emotion is a solid colour outfit with matching hair and makeup. The five together are immediately recognisable.

10. Joy and Sadness Duo

The most recognisable Inside Out duo. Joy in a yellow dress with a blue streak in her hair; Sadness in a blue turtleneck and glasses. Both looks are easy to execute with existing clothing.

11. The New Emotions from Inside Out 2

Anxiety (orange), Envy (teal), Ennui (dark blue/purple), and Embarrassment (large, pink). Adding the new emotions to the original five creates a larger group costume that references the new film specifically.

12. Anxiety Costume

Anxiety from Inside Out 2 is orange with wild, slightly frantic energy. An orange outfit, orange hair or wig, and slightly manic makeup captures the character. One of the most topical costumes of the year.

13. Ennui Costume

Ennui is dark blue-purple, tall, and perpetually bored. A dark blue or purple outfit, dark makeup, and a permanently unimpressed expression. One of the easiest emotions to execute and one of the funniest.

14. Embarrassment Costume

Embarrassment is large, pink, and shy. A pink outfit — the larger and fluffier the better — with pink makeup and a hunched, self-conscious posture. Works especially well for someone tall.

15. Riley and Her Emotions

One person as Riley in a casual outfit; the rest as her emotions in their respective colours. The group works at any size and the contrast between the human character and the colourful emotions reads well in photos.

Mix characters from Toy Story, Inside Out, The Incredibles, and other Pixar films. The shared Pixar aesthetic makes the group read as a unit even with characters from different films.

Half the group as Toy Story characters, half as Inside Out emotions. The contrast between the toy aesthetic and the emotion aesthetic creates an interesting visual dynamic.

Family Options

18. Family Toy Story

Parents as Woody and Buzz; children as Jessie, Rex, and the aliens. The costumes scale well across ages and the characters are recognisable to every generation.

19. Family Inside Out

Each family member as a different emotion. Assign emotions based on personality for an extra layer of humour — the most anxious family member as Anxiety, the most enthusiastic as Joy.

20. Baby as a Toy

A baby or toddler dressed as a specific toy — a small Buzz Lightyear, a mini Woody, a tiny alien — while the adults dress as the other characters. Baby costumes for both franchises are widely available.

Final Thoughts

Both Toy Story and Inside Out 2 work as group costumes because every character has a distinct, recognisable look that is achievable at any budget. Start by assigning characters based on who wants to wear what, then coordinate the colour palettes so the group reads as a unit. The emotions from Inside Out are the easiest to execute; the Toy Story characters require slightly more construction but are more immediately recognisable to a wider audience.

Still wondering

Common questions

What are the best Halloween costumes for a trio?

The best trio costumes are the ones where all three characters are instantly recognizable as a set. The Sanderson Sisters, the Powerpuff Girls, the Scooby-Doo trio, and the Three Musketeers are perennially popular because they have distinct, recognizable looks for each member. Punny trios like rock, paper, scissors are reliably funny and easy to execute.

How do you assign trio costume characters fairly?

Start with the most distinctive character — the one with the most recognizable look — and assign it to the person who most resembles or most wants to play that character. Then assign the remaining characters based on personality and preference. If there is disagreement, draw lots.

The short version

  • Layer at least four different textures — smooth, rough, soft, and woven — for a rich, grounded look.

A warm neutral bedroom is one of the most enduring and comfortable interiors you can create. The combination of wood, linen, and layered neutrals creates a room that feels calm without being cold, and personal without being busy.

These ideas focus on the specific materials, textures, and choices that make a warm neutral bedroom feel genuinely inviting rather than simply beige.

1. Choose Warm Neutrals With Yellow or Pink Undertones

Warm neutrals — cream, oatmeal, caramel, warm grey, and soft terracotta — have yellow or pink undertones that make them feel inviting under artificial light. Avoid cool neutrals with grey or blue undertones, which can feel clinical in a bedroom.

Test paint colors in the room at different times of day before committing.

2. Use an Oak or Walnut Bed Frame

An oak or walnut bed frame is the anchor of a warm neutral bedroom. The natural grain and warm tone of the wood adds depth and character that painted furniture cannot replicate.

Choose a simple, clean-lined frame — ornate carved wood can feel heavy in a neutral room.

3. Layer Linen Bedding

Linen bedding in a natural, undyed, or warm white tone is the most effective way to add texture to a neutral bedroom. Layer a linen duvet with a cotton fitted sheet, a linen pillowcase, and a textured throw.

Linen softens and improves with every wash.

4. Add a Chunky Knit Throw

A chunky knit throw in oatmeal, cream, or a warm caramel adds a soft, tactile layer to the bed. Drape it loosely over the foot of the bed rather than folding it flat.

A throw in a slightly different shade from the bedding adds depth without introducing a new color.

5. Use a Jute or Wool Rug

A jute, sisal, or wool rug in a natural or caramel tone grounds the room and adds texture to the floor. Choose a rug that extends at least 18 inches beyond the sides and foot of the bed.

Natural fiber rugs are durable and improve with age.

6. Add Warm Wood Accessories

Repeat the wood tone from the bed frame in smaller accessories — a wooden lamp base, a wooden tray on the dresser, a wooden picture frame. This creates a cohesive look without making the room feel themed.

Stick to one wood tone — mixing too many creates a cluttered look.

7. Use Warm Lighting at 2700K

Warm neutrals look their best under warm lighting at 2700K. Cool white light makes neutrals look grey and flat. Use warm bulbs in every light source in the room.

A dimmer switch on the overhead light lets you adjust the warmth of the room in the evening.

8. Add Rattan or Wicker Details

Rattan and wicker accessories — a lamp base, a mirror frame, a small basket — add a natural, organic quality that suits a warm neutral bedroom. They also add texture without introducing a strong color.

One or two rattan pieces are enough — more can start to feel like a beach house.

9. Use Linen Curtains

Linen curtains in a natural or warm white tone add softness and warmth to the window area. Choose a fabric with a slight texture — a loose weave or a subtle slub — rather than a flat, shiny fabric.

Hang them high and wide — rod 4–6 inches above the frame, extending 6–10 inches past each side.

10. Add Dried Flowers or Pampas Grass

Dried flowers, pampas grass, or dried seed heads in a simple ceramic vase add a natural, textural element that suits a warm neutral bedroom. They last for months and require no maintenance.

Use a terracotta or matte ceramic vase rather than a glass one for a warmer look.

11. Use a Boucle or Textured Headboard

A boucle, linen, or textured fabric headboard adds a soft, tactile focal point to the bed wall. Choose a warm white, oatmeal, or caramel tone that suits the rest of the room.

A fabric headboard also improves acoustics in a hard-floored room.

12. Add a Terracotta or Rust Accent

A single warm accent color — terracotta, rust, or burnt orange — prevents a neutral bedroom from feeling bland. Use it in one or two cushions, a throw, or a piece of art.

Keep the accent to 10% of the room’s color — one or two pieces is enough.

13. Use Ceramic or Terracotta Accessories

Ceramic and terracotta accessories — a vase, a lamp base, a small bowl — add a natural, handmade quality that suits a warm neutral bedroom. Choose matte finishes rather than shiny glazes.

Group two or three pieces together on a tray or shelf rather than scattering them around the room.

14. Add a Plant in a Simple Pot

A plant in a simple ceramic or terracotta pot adds a natural accent color and a living quality that no other accessory can replicate. A snake plant, a pothos, or a small fiddle-leaf fig all work well in a neutral bedroom.

Place it where it will get enough light — near the window or in a bright corner.

15. Keep the Room Uncluttered

A warm neutral bedroom looks its best when the surfaces are clear and the room is uncluttered. Neutrals show mess more than darker colors — a few well-chosen objects look far better than a crowded surface.

Edit the room regularly and remove anything that does not contribute to the calm, warm quality of the space.

Final Thoughts

A warm neutral bedroom works when the materials are natural, the textures are layered, and the lighting is warm. Start with the bed frame and the bedding, then add wood, linen, and one or two accent colors. The goal is a room that feels grounded and inviting rather than plain and empty.

Winter at Home: Warmth That Is Not Just a Blanket on a Sofa

Hygge is usually sold as throws and candles. The real levers are light temperature, texture contrast, scent and one properly warm corner. Here is the method.

In this article

  1. 01Lever one: drop the colour temperature
  2. 02Lever two: texture contrast, not texture quantity
  3. 03Lever three: scent, used sparingly

Hygge got flattened into a shopping list somewhere around 2016 — buy a chunky throw, light a candle, photograph a mug. The idea underneath it is better than that, and it is mostly about contrast: a room feels warm in winter because something about it is set against the cold outside, not because it contains soft objects.

Four levers do almost all of the work.

Lever one: drop the colour temperature

The fastest change, and the one people notice without knowing why.

Winter daylight is cold and blue — around 6500K at midday under cloud. If your indoor lighting is also cool, the house never feels like a refuge from it. Swapping to warm bulbs makes the interior read as a different environment the moment you walk in.

  • Replace 4000K bulbs with 2700K everywhere you spend evenings
  • Add one or two 2200K sources at low level for after dark
  • Get everything onto dimmers, and actually turn them down

The other half of this is height. Winter light should sit low. Table lamps, floor lamps and candles at hip and shoulder height make a room feel enclosed; a bright ceiling fitting makes it feel like a corridor. We go further into the mechanics in our guide to bedroom lighting layers, and the same three-source logic applies to a living room.

A room lit from above at 4000K in January feels like somewhere you are waiting. The same room lit from three low points at 2700K feels like somewhere you live.

Lever two: texture contrast, not texture quantity

Piling on soft things does not make a room feel warm. What registers is the difference between rough and smooth, matte and glossy, hard and soft — placed next to each other.

Aim for at least four distinct textures in any seating area:

  • Something woolly — a chunky knit throw, a boucle cushion
  • Something flat and matte — linen, brushed cotton
  • Something hard and cool — ceramic, stone, glass, a wooden bowl
  • Something with pile — a rug, sheepskin, velvet

The hard element is the one people leave out, and it is the one that makes the soft elements read. A ceramic lamp base next to a wool throw makes the wool look woollier. Six wool things next to each other just look like laundry.

Rugs do more than you think

A rug in winter is thermal as well as visual — bare floor pulls heat out of a room through your feet, and the perceived temperature difference between a rug and a cold board is genuinely a couple of degrees.

If you have hard floors, this is the highest-value winter purchase. Layering a smaller wool or sheepskin rug over a larger flat-weave gives you the texture contrast and the insulation in one move.

Lever three: scent, used sparingly

Scent is the sense most directly wired to memory, which is why it does so much for atmosphere and why overdoing it is so unpleasant.

What works in winter: woodsmoke, beeswax, pine, cedar, clove, orange peel, vetiver, tobacco leaf.

What to avoid: anything described as “fresh linen” or “ocean”, which read as summer, and cheap synthetic vanilla, which reads as a car.

One scent source per room, maximum. Two competing scents cancel into a headache. A simmer pot — orange peel, a cinnamon stick, a few cloves, water, lowest heat — costs nothing and beats most candles.

Lever four: build one properly warm corner

This is the part that turns a decorated room into a used one. Pick a single spot and make it genuinely the best place in the house to sit for two hours.

It needs all five:

  1. A chair you can stay in — one with arms and a back you can lean into
  2. Light over your shoulder — a floor lamp behind and to one side, not in front
  3. A surface within reach — for a cup, at roughly the height of the chair arm
  4. Something to put over you — throw, folded on the arm, not draped decoratively
  5. A view of something — a window, a fire, a bookshelf. Not a blank wall.

Most living rooms are arranged around a television and contain no such corner. Building one changes how much the room gets used far more than anything you can buy.

The winter swap, room by room

A seasonal change should take an hour, not a weekend. Keep a single box.

Living room: swap cotton cushion covers for wool or velvet; heavier throw out; layer a sheepskin over the rug; move the reading lamp closer to the chair.

Bedroom: flannel or brushed cotton sheets instead of percale; add a wool blanket between the sheet and the duvet rather than swapping the duvet; heavier curtains if you have them.

Kitchen: a bowl of citrus out on the counter, which is decoration you can eat; tea towels in a deeper colour; the simmer pot on Sunday.

Hall: somewhere for wet coats that is not the banister. Unglamorous, and the single thing that most affects whether the house feels calm in January.

What to skip

  • Fake snow, anywhere. It reads as a shop window.
  • Blankets folded into perfect squares. A throw needs to look used; fold it in half and drape it over an arm.
  • Filling every surface. Winter interiors work through pools of warmth surrounded by dimness — clutter fights that.
  • Buying a whole new palette. Winter is a shift in texture and light, not a repaint.

When to take it down

Late February, when the light starts changing. Heavy textures held into spring make a house feel stale, and the first genuinely bright morning is a good prompt: take up the sheepskin, put the cotton covers back on, and let the room get lighter with the season.

Working the other direction? Our autumn mantel guide covers the seasonal step just before this one.

17 Wicked Halloween Costume Ideas — Elphaba and Glinda Duo Looks

Recreate the most iconic duo of the year with 17 Wicked Halloween costume ideas covering Elphaba, Glinda, solo builds, group looks, and budget options.

The short version

  • Elphaba needs three things: all-black clothing, green face paint, and a pointed hat.
  • Glinda's bubble dress is the centrepiece — pale pink or white with volume is the priority.
  • The duo works best when the two looks are clearly contrasted in colour and silhouette.
  • Both costumes can be built from thrifted pieces for under thirty pounds each.

Wicked is the duo costume of the year. Elphaba and Glinda are visually opposite — black versus pink, angular versus soft, grounded versus ethereal — which makes them one of the most striking pairs you can do. The looks are also genuinely achievable without a costume shop.

The ideas below cover both characters individually, the duo build, group options, and budget alternatives.

Elphaba

1. The Core Elphaba Build

All-black clothing from head to toe, green face and neck paint, a wide-brimmed pointed black hat, and black boots. This is the minimum viable Elphaba and it reads immediately. The hat is the non-negotiable element.

2. The Accurate Elphaba

A fitted black dress or black corset top with a full black skirt, long black gloves, a dramatic black cape, the pointed hat, and full green makeup from hairline to collarbone. Add a small broom prop for the finishing detail.

3. The Budget Elphaba

Black jeans, a black long-sleeve top, a black hat from a costume shop or charity shop, and green face paint. Total cost under fifteen pounds. The green skin is what makes it work — do not skip it.

4. Elphaba Makeup

Green face paint applied from the hairline down to the collarbone, blended at the edges. Use a setting spray to prevent transfer. Add dark eye makeup — deep green or black eyeshadow, strong liner — and a dark lip in plum or deep berry.

Shop this costume makeup 54-Color Face Painting Kit See details & availability Check current price On Amazon · Opens in a new tab

5. Elphaba Hair

Elphaba’s hair is dark and worn down or loosely styled under the hat. If your hair is not dark, a simple black wig works well. The hat covers most of the hair anyway.

Glinda

6. The Core Glinda Build

A pale pink or white dress with volume — a prom dress, a bridesmaid dress, or a tulle skirt with a fitted top — a small crown or tiara, a wand, and an updo. The silhouette is the priority: full skirt, fitted bodice, pale colour.

7. The Accurate Glinda

A pale pink ball gown or bubble dress, a sparkly tiara, a star-tipped wand, white or pale pink gloves, and an elaborate updo with curls. Add a beauty mark above the lip for the finishing detail.

8. The Budget Glinda

A thrifted pale pink or white dress, a tiara from a pound shop, a star wand made from card and a wooden dowel, and any updo. The silhouette matters more than the specific dress.

Shop this Halloween look Women's Black Halloween Costume Set See details & availability Check current price On Amazon · Opens in a new tab

9. Glinda Makeup

Soft and luminous — a glowing base, pink blush, a light pink or nude lip, and a subtle shimmer on the eyelids. Add a small beauty mark above the lip. The look is polished and pretty, not dramatic.

10. Glinda Hair

An updo with volume and soft curls. A high bun with loose curls framing the face is the most recognisable option. Add the tiara at the crown.

The Duo

11. The Classic Duo

Elphaba in full black with green makeup; Glinda in full pale pink with tiara and wand. The contrast does all the work. Stand together for photos and the costumes read from across the room.

12. The Elevated Duo

Commission or buy higher-quality versions of both costumes — a structured black gown for Elphaba, a proper ball gown for Glinda. Add matching accessories and coordinate the makeup for a more polished result.

Shop this costume makeup 42-Color Costume Makeup Kit See details & availability Check current price On Amazon · Opens in a new tab

13. The Casual Duo

Elphaba in black jeans, black top, hat, and green face paint; Glinda in a pink midi skirt, white top, and tiara. Both looks are comfortable enough for a full evening and easy to move in.

Group Options

14. Add the Wizard

A third person in a green suit or waistcoat with a top hat and a slightly pompous expression completes the core trio. The Wizard’s look is more interpretive than the two leads.

15. Add Doctor Dillamond

A fourth person in a grey or white outfit with goat-like accessories — ears, a simple horn headband — adds a recognisable supporting character that fans will appreciate.

16. The Full Oz Group

Assign each person a character from the show — Elphaba, Glinda, Fiyero, the Wizard, Nessa. Coordinate the colour palettes so the group reads as a unit even to people who do not know the show.

Alternatives

17. Gender-Swapped or Non-Binary Wicked

Both looks translate across genders. Elphaba’s silhouette works in trousers and a structured black jacket; Glinda’s works in a pink suit with a tiara. Keep the core colour and the signature prop — hat or wand — and the costume reads regardless.

Final Thoughts

Wicked costumes work because the two characters are so visually distinct. The contrast between Elphaba’s black and Glinda’s pink is the whole costume — get that right and everything else is detail. Start with what you already own in those colour families, fill the gaps with thrifted pieces, and do not skip the green face paint.

17 Y2K Apocalypse Halloween Party Decor Ideas

Throw a Y2K apocalypse Halloween party with 17 decor ideas using glitchy screens, silver metallics, caution tape, neon accents, and retro-futurist styling.

Elena Marsh/October 5, 2026/6 min read

The short version

  • The Y2K apocalypse palette is silver, black, neon green, and electric blue — not orange.
  • Glitchy screen effects, caution tape, and static noise are the three core aesthetic elements.
  • Silver mylar balloons and metallic streamers are the fastest way to build the look.
  • Old CRT monitors, floppy disks, and Y2K-era tech props add authentic period detail.

The Y2K apocalypse aesthetic takes the millennium panic — the fear that computers would fail, systems would crash, and civilisation would end at midnight on 1 January 2000 — and turns it into a party. The look is silver metallics, glitchy screens, caution tape, neon accents, and the specific visual language of late-1990s technology.

It is one of the most original Halloween party themes of the year and genuinely easy to execute with a mix of craft supplies and thrifted tech.

The Palette

1. Silver, Black, and Neon

The Y2K apocalypse palette is silver, black, neon green, and electric blue. Avoid orange entirely — it breaks the aesthetic. Add red sparingly as a warning or danger accent.

Repeat these colours through every element and the party will feel cohesive even with a mix of sources.

Balloons and Streamers

2. Silver Mylar Balloons

Silver mylar balloons — round, star-shaped, or in Y2K-relevant numbers — are the fastest way to build the metallic aesthetic. Cluster them in corners or hang them from the ceiling.

3. Metallic Streamers

Silver and black metallic streamers hung from the ceiling or doorways create an immediate Y2K atmosphere. Add a few neon green or electric blue streamers for colour contrast.

4. Caution Tape

Yellow and black caution tape draped across doorways, around furniture, and along walls is one of the most recognisable Y2K apocalypse elements. It is also extremely cheap.

Screens and Tech

Shop this party decoration Halloween Balloon Garland Arch Kit See details & availability Check current price On Amazon · Opens in a new tab

5. Glitchy Screen Displays

Loop a glitchy screen effect, a Y2K countdown, or a static noise video on a TV or monitor. Free glitch effect videos are widely available online. This single element does more for the atmosphere than almost anything else.

6. Old CRT Monitors as Props

A CRT monitor — found at a charity shop or recycling centre — displaying a glitchy image or a Y2K countdown is the most authentic prop you can add. Even a non-functional one works as a visual element.

7. Floppy Disks and CD-ROMs

A pile of floppy disks, CD-ROMs, and old tech accessories scattered on a table or displayed in a bowl adds period-accurate detail. They are widely available at charity shops and car boot sales.

8. Printed Error Messages

Print large-format versions of classic Windows error messages — “FATAL ERROR”, “SYSTEM FAILURE”, “Y2K CRITICAL” — and tape them to walls, mirrors, and windows. Use a pixelated font for authenticity.

Lighting

Shop this party essential Halloween Party Tableware Kit for 50 See details & availability Check current price On Amazon · Opens in a new tab

9. Neon Green or Blue Lighting

Neon green or electric blue bulbs or LED strips create the most atmospheric Y2K lighting. Use them in corners, under furniture, or behind screens for a glow effect.

10. Strobe or Flicker Effect

A strobe light or a flickering bulb adds a glitchy, unstable quality to the lighting. Use it in one area rather than throughout the whole space.

11. Black Light

A black light makes white and neon elements glow and adds an eerie quality to the space. Pair with neon green or white decorations for maximum effect.

Table and Surface Styling

12. Foil Table Covers

Silver foil table covers on the food and drinks tables add metallic texture and reflect the lighting. They are cheap, widely available, and easy to dispose of after the party.

Shop this party accessory Halloween Photo Booth Props, 18-Piece Set See details & availability Check current price On Amazon · Opens in a new tab

13. Y2K Countdown Centrepiece

A printed or handmade Y2K countdown clock — showing the time ticking toward midnight on 31 December 1999 — as a table centrepiece adds a narrative element to the decor.

14. Survival Kit Display

A “Y2K survival kit” display — tinned food, bottled water, a torch, a first aid kit — styled on a table with a handwritten label adds a darkly humorous element that fits the theme perfectly.

Finishing Details

15. Hazmat Suit Photo Booth

A simple photo booth area with a yellow caution tape frame, a printed “QUARANTINE ZONE” sign, and a few props — gas masks, hazmat gloves, a clipboard — gives guests a place to take photos and adds a strong visual element to the party.

16. Printed Newspaper Headlines

Print fake newspaper front pages with Y2K apocalypse headlines — “COMPUTERS TO FAIL AT MIDNIGHT”, “CIVILISATION ENDS AT 00:00” — and tape them to walls and windows. Use a period-accurate newspaper layout for authenticity.

17. Y2K Playlist

A playlist of late-1990s pop, nu-metal, and electronic music playing throughout the party completes the aesthetic in a way that no visual element can. The music is as important as the decor.

Final Thoughts

The Y2K apocalypse party works because the aesthetic is specific, nostalgic, and genuinely funny. The silver metallics, glitchy screens, and caution tape create an immediately recognisable atmosphere. Start with the balloons and the screen display, add the caution tape, and fill in the details from there. The survival kit and the error message prints are the elements that will get the most reactions.

17 Vintage Halloween Decor Ideas — The Trend Everyone Is Copying

Decorate for Halloween with 17 vintage Halloween decor ideas using antique prints, mercury glass, dried botanicals, and a muted Victorian-inspired palette.

The short version

  • The vintage Halloween palette is sepia, black, deep burgundy, and aged cream — not bright orange.
  • Antique-style prints in existing frames are the fastest way to shift the aesthetic.
  • Mercury glass, taper candles, and dried botanicals are the three core material groups.
  • Thrift shops and estate sales are the best sources — new reproductions rarely have the right patina.

Vintage Halloween decor has grown 200% on Pinterest year on year, and it is easy to understand why. The aesthetic — sepia tones, Victorian silhouettes, mercury glass, and dried botanicals — creates atmosphere without the garish brightness of modern Halloween products. It also works with a neutral interior rather than fighting it.

The ideas below are organised by material and placement. Start with the elements that are easiest to source and build from there.

The Palette

1. Sepia, Black, and Aged Cream

The vintage Halloween palette is sepia, black, deep burgundy, and aged cream. Avoid bright orange entirely — it reads as modern and breaks the aesthetic immediately. Muted terracotta is the closest acceptable warm tone.

Repeat these four colours through every element and the room will feel cohesive even with a mix of sources and styles.

2. Deep Burgundy as the Accent

Deep burgundy — in candles, dried flowers, velvet ribbon, or a single textile — adds warmth and depth without introducing a modern colour. It also photographs beautifully in low light.

Prints and Artwork

3. Antique-Style Halloween Prints

Victorian-era Halloween imagery — black cats, owls, moons, witches in silhouette, botanical skulls — printed and framed in existing frames is the fastest way to shift the aesthetic. Look for public domain images from the 1890s–1920s, print them at home, and swap them into frames you already own.

4. Botanical Skull Prints

A botanical illustration style applied to skulls or dark flowers is one of the most-pinned vintage Halloween aesthetics. Frame two or three together in mismatched antique-style frames for a gallery wall effect.

Shop this Halloween decor Black Flameless Candles, Set of 9 See details & availability Check current price On Amazon · Opens in a new tab

5. Moon Phase Charts

A vintage moon phase chart or astronomical diagram adds a slightly occult quality without any obvious Halloween imagery. It works year-round and transitions easily into November.

Candles and Light

6. Taper Candles in Antique Holders

Black or deep burgundy taper candles in brass, pewter, or verdigris candlesticks create the most authentic vintage look. Group three candlesticks of different heights together rather than spacing them evenly.

Use flameless tapers near dried materials.

7. Mercury Glass Votives

Mercury glass votives and lanterns in silver or aged gold scatter light in a way that modern glass does not. Group several together on a tray for a mantel or console display.

8. Candelabras

A single candelabra — real or flameless — is one of the most effective vintage Halloween props. It adds height, drama, and period authenticity in one object.

Botanicals and Natural Materials

Shop this Halloween decor 16-Piece Mini Pumpkin Decor Set See details & availability Check current price On Amazon · Opens in a new tab

9. Dried Flowers in Dark Tones

Dried dahlias, roses, and grasses in deep burgundy, black, and aged cream are the botanical centrepiece of the vintage Halloween aesthetic. Arrange them in a ceramic or earthenware vase rather than glass.

10. Bare Branches

Bare branches in a tall vase — left natural or sprayed black — add height and a slightly eerie quality. They last the entire season and cost almost nothing if you collect them from the garden.

11. Dried Herb Bundles

Bundles of dried sage, lavender, or rosemary tied with dark ribbon add a witchy, apothecary quality. Hang them from a hook, lay them on a shelf, or tuck them into a vase arrangement.

Objects and Props

12. Apothecary Bottles

Dark glass bottles, cork-stoppered vials, and small ceramic pots labelled with handwritten tags create an apothecary display that is one of the most-copied vintage Halloween aesthetics. Fill them with dried herbs, dark sand, or leave them empty.

13. Vintage Books

A stack of old books — dark spines, aged covers — on a shelf or coffee table adds period authenticity. Look for old encyclopaedias, botanical references, or anything with a worn leather cover at charity shops.

14. Ceramic Skulls and Bones

A ceramic skull in cream, black, or terracotta reads as vintage rather than cheap when the material is right. Avoid plastic entirely. One well-chosen ceramic piece is worth more than ten plastic props.

15. Antique Mirrors

A dark-framed or slightly foxed mirror adds depth and a slightly unsettling quality. Lean it against a wall rather than hanging it for a more casual, collected look.

Textiles

16. Velvet and Lace

Deep burgundy or black velvet cushion covers, a lace table runner, or a velvet throw add the textile richness that defines the vintage Halloween aesthetic. Both materials photograph well in candlelight.

17. Dark Linen

A dark linen table runner or shelf liner in charcoal or deep navy creates a base for a display that feels aged and considered rather than modern. Layer objects on top rather than placing them directly on a light surface.

Final Thoughts

Vintage Halloween decor works because it treats the season as an aesthetic rather than a theme. The goal is atmosphere — candlelight, dried botanicals, aged materials, and a muted palette — rather than coverage. Start with the prints and the candles, add one or two antique-style objects, and let the patina do the work.

17 Bathroom Organization Ideas for Small Spaces

Maximize every inch of a compact bathroom with 17 bathroom organization ideas for small spaces covering under-sink storage, vertical shelving, and decluttering.

If you are looking for bathroom organization ideas for small spaces, the best place to start is with function rather than decoration. A room feels better when the layout is easy to use, storage has a clear purpose, and the styling supports everyday life instead of getting in the way.

The ideas below are designed to be practical for real homes. You do not need to use every idea. Choose the changes that solve the biggest problem in your space first, then build from there.

1. Prioritize the Vanity and Under-Sink Area

The vanity and under-sink cabinet are the highest-impact storage zones in a small bathroom. Measure the space carefully and choose containers that fit around the plumbing.

Measure width, depth, and height before choosing containers, especially around plumbing. Use low or pull-out bins when possible so items at the back remain easy to reach.

2. Use Shallow Wall Shelves

Shallow floating shelves above the toilet or beside the mirror add storage without reducing floor space. Use them for everyday items you reach for often.

Measure the wall before drilling or ordering storage, and check that doors, cabinets, and people can still move comfortably.

3. Add Hooks Where Towels Actually Land

Hooks placed where towels naturally land — beside the shower, near the door, or on the back of the door — are more likely to be used than a towel rail in an inconvenient location.

In rentals, removable adhesive hooks are a good no-drill alternative.

4. Keep Only One Backup of Each Product

Storing more than one backup of shampoo, conditioner, or body wash quickly fills a small bathroom cabinet. Keep one backup of each product and restock when it runs out.

Before buying anything, measure the available area and think about how the item will be used every day.

5. Declutter Before Buying Organizers

Removing unused, expired, duplicate, or outgrown items immediately creates space and makes every later storage decision easier. This is often more effective than buying another organizer.

Set a short review schedule rather than waiting for the room to become overwhelming.

6. Measure the Under-Sink Cabinet

The under-sink cabinet is often underused because of the plumbing. Measure the available space carefully and choose U-shaped drawers, pull-out bins, or stackable containers that fit around the pipes.

Measure width, depth, and height before choosing containers.

7. Use Clear or Labeled Bins

Clear bins let you see what is inside without opening every container. Use them for makeup, hair accessories, or small items that tend to get lost.

Use labels only where they genuinely help.

8. Add Stackable Drawers

Stackable plastic or acrylic drawers make efficient use of vertical space inside a cabinet. Use them for makeup, skincare, or small bathroom accessories.

Measure width, depth, and height before choosing containers.

9. Install Storage Above the Toilet

The wall above the toilet is almost always unused. A shelf, cabinet, or freestanding over-toilet unit there can hold towels, toilet paper, and bathroom supplies.

Measure the wall before drilling or ordering storage.

10. Use Drawer Dividers

Drawer dividers prevent small items from mixing together and make it faster to find what you need. Use them for makeup, hair accessories, or bathroom tools.

Before buying anything, measure the available area and think about how the item will be used every day.

11. Keep Only Daily Essentials on the Counter

A clear counter makes a small bathroom feel larger and easier to clean. Keep only the items you use every day on the surface and store everything else in a cabinet or drawer.

Group a small number of items together and leave visible empty space so the surface can still do its real job.

12. Use a Tray to Contain Small Items

A tray on the counter groups small items together and makes them easy to move when cleaning. Choose a tray that fits the counter without taking up too much space.

A tray is useful because the whole group can be moved at once.

13. Add Hooks Instead of More Furniture

Hooks on the wall or back of the door hold towels, robes, and bags without using any floor space. This is often more practical than adding another piece of furniture.

Measure the wall before drilling or ordering storage.

14. Use the Back of the Door

An over-door organizer on the bathroom door holds small items, cleaning supplies, or hair tools without using any wall or floor space.

Before buying anything, measure the available area and think about how the item will be used every day.

15. Add a Lazy Susan for Bottles

A lazy Susan inside a cabinet or on a shelf lets you reach items at the back without moving everything in front. Use it for bottles, jars, and containers that tend to get lost at the back.

Before buying anything, measure the available area and think about how the item will be used every day.

16. Move Toothbrushes Off a Tiny Counter

A wall-mounted toothbrush holder or a cup on a shelf frees up counter space and keeps the surface looking tidy.

Group a small number of items together and leave visible empty space so the surface can still do its real job.

17. Store Backup Products Separately

Keep backup products in a separate cabinet, under the sink, or in a linen closet rather than in the main bathroom storage. This prevents the bathroom from feeling overcrowded.

Before buying anything, measure the available area and think about how the item will be used every day.

Final Thoughts

The strongest bathroom organization ideas for small spaces are the ones that make the room easier to use, not simply more decorated. Start with a declutter, prioritize the under-sink area, and use vertical space and hooks to add storage without reducing floor space. Small, deliberate improvements are usually more successful than changing everything at once.

If you are looking for bathroom over the toilet storage ideas, the best place to start is with function rather than decoration. A room feels better when the layout is easy to use, storage has a clear purpose, and the styling supports everyday life instead of getting in the way.

The ideas below are designed to be practical for real homes. You do not need to use every idea. Choose the changes that solve the biggest problem in your space first, then build from there.

1. Install Two Shallow Floating Shelves

Two shallow floating shelves above the toilet create a clean, open look and provide useful storage for towels, plants, and bathroom accessories. Keep the lower shelf at a comfortable height.

Measure the wall before drilling or ordering storage, and check that doors, cabinets, and people can still move comfortably.

2. Use a Freestanding Over-Toilet Unit

A freestanding over-toilet unit requires no drilling and can be moved if needed. It is a good option for rentals or bathrooms where wall drilling is not permitted.

Before buying anything, measure the available area and think about how the item will be used every day.

3. Add a Closed Wall Cabinet

A closed wall cabinet above the toilet hides items you do not want on open display — medications, cleaning supplies, or personal care products.

Measure the wall before drilling or ordering storage.

4. Use Baskets to Hide Extra Toilet Paper

A basket on a shelf above the toilet holds extra toilet paper while keeping the shelf looking tidy. Choose a basket that fits the shelf depth without overhanging.

Use labels only where they genuinely help.

5. Declutter Before Buying Organizers

Removing unused, expired, duplicate, or outgrown items immediately creates space and makes every later storage decision easier.

Set a short review schedule rather than waiting for the room to become overwhelming.

6. Measure the Under-Sink Cabinet

The under-sink cabinet is often underused because of the plumbing. Measure the available space carefully and choose containers that fit around the pipes.

Measure width, depth, and height before choosing containers.

7. Use Clear or Labeled Bins

Clear bins let you see what is inside without opening every container. Use them for makeup, hair accessories, or small items that tend to get lost.

Use labels only where they genuinely help.

8. Add Stackable Drawers

Stackable plastic or acrylic drawers make efficient use of vertical space inside a cabinet. Use them for makeup, skincare, or small bathroom accessories.

Measure width, depth, and height before choosing containers.

9. Install Storage Above the Toilet

The wall above the toilet is almost always unused. A shelf, cabinet, or freestanding over-toilet unit there can hold towels, toilet paper, and bathroom supplies.

Measure the wall before drilling or ordering storage.

10. Use Drawer Dividers

Drawer dividers prevent small items from mixing together and make it faster to find what you need.

Before buying anything, measure the available area and think about how the item will be used every day.

11. Keep Only Daily Essentials on the Counter

A clear counter makes a small bathroom feel larger and easier to clean. Keep only the items you use every day on the surface.

Group a small number of items together and leave visible empty space so the surface can still do its real job.

12. Use a Tray to Contain Small Items

A tray on the counter groups small items together and makes them easy to move when cleaning.

A tray is useful because the whole group can be moved at once.

13. Add Hooks Instead of More Furniture

Hooks on the wall or back of the door hold towels, robes, and bags without using any floor space.

Measure the wall before drilling or ordering storage.

14. Use the Back of the Door

An over-door organizer on the bathroom door holds small items, cleaning supplies, or hair tools without using any wall or floor space.

Before buying anything, measure the available area and think about how the item will be used every day.

15. Add a Lazy Susan for Bottles

A lazy Susan inside a cabinet or on a shelf lets you reach items at the back without moving everything in front.

Before buying anything, measure the available area and think about how the item will be used every day.

Final Thoughts

The strongest bathroom over the toilet storage ideas are the ones that make the room easier to use, not simply more decorated. Start with the wall above the toilet, choose between open shelves and a closed cabinet based on what you need to store, and keep the display tidy with baskets and trays. Small, deliberate improvements are usually more successful than changing everything at once.
